subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define health according to WHO.
answer_html:
Definition WHO (1948): "Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity."

Points to remember

  1. It is a positive and holistic concept – not just "no disease"
  2. It includes body, mind and social life; many experts also add a spiritual dimension
  3. The Ottawa Charter (1986) describes health as a resource for everyday life, not the objective of living
  4. Health is dynamic – a person's state of health keeps changing

Dimensions of health: physical, mental, social, spiritual, emotional, vocational and environmental.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the health–illness continuum.
answer_html:
Introduction Health and illness are not two separate boxes; they are two ends of a continuous scale (continuum).

Key points

  1. One end is high-level wellness (optimum health) and the other end is severe illness and death
  2. In the middle is a neutral point where there is neither obvious illness nor full wellness
  3. A person's position on the continuum keeps changing from day to day
  4. Halbert Dunn introduced the idea of high-level wellness; John Travis described the illness–wellness continuum: premature death ← disability ← symptoms ← signs ← neutral point → awareness → education → growth → high-level wellness
  5. Nursing use: the nurse helps each person move towards the wellness end through treatment, education and healthy lifestyle

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Differentiate between illness and disease.
answer_html:
Introduction The words illness, disease and sickness are often used together, but they have different meanings.

Illness Disease
a subjective feeling of being unwell an objective, pathological change in the structure or function of the body
described by the person ("I feel weak") diagnosed by signs, investigations and tests
may exist without a disease (anxiety) may exist without illness (early hypertension, diabetes)
includes the person's experience and reaction a medical concept

Sickness is the social aspect – the state of social dysfunction, the role the person takes when ill (sick role).

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: List the stages of illness behaviour.
answer_html:
Introduction Illness behaviour is the way a person recognises, interprets and responds to symptoms. Suchman described five stages:

  1. Symptom experience – the person feels that something is wrong (pain, fever, weakness)
  2. Assumption of the sick role – accepts being ill, seeks advice from family and friends, may take home remedies, is excused from duties
  3. Medical care contact – seeks professional help for diagnosis and treatment
  4. Dependent patient role – depends on health professionals, follows treatment
  5. Recovery and rehabilitation – gives up the sick role and returns to normal roles

Factors affecting illness behaviour: age, culture, beliefs, education, income, previous experience and access to health care.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the concept of health.
answer_html:
Introduction Health is a fundamental human right and a worldwide social goal. The meaning of health has changed over time – from "absence of disease" to "complete well-being".

1. Changing concepts of health

  • Biomedical concept – health is the absence of disease; the body is seen as a machine. Limitation: ignores the mind and social factors
  • Ecological concept – health is dynamic harmony between man and his environment; disease is maladjustment to the environment
  • Psychosocial concept – health is influenced by social, psychological, cultural, economic and political factors as well as biology
  • Holistic concept – the whole person – body, mind, spirit and environment – is considered together; it is the most accepted concept today

2. WHO definition (1948)

  • "Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity"
  • Merits: positive, holistic, gives a goal
  • Criticism: "complete" well-being is an ideal that few persons ever reach; it is difficult to measure

3. Dimensions of health

  • Physical – the body works perfectly; normal vital signs, good appetite, sleep and bowel habits
  • Mental – the person can cope with stress, work productively and realise his abilities
  • Social – good relationships and the ability to fulfil roles in family and society
  • Spiritual – a purpose in life, values, faith and inner peace
  • Emotional – feeling and expressing emotions appropriately
  • Vocational – satisfaction from work
  • Environmental – living in a safe, clean environment

4. Positive health

  • A state in which every part of the body and mind is functioning at its best, with a high capacity to resist disease

5. Spectrum of health

  • Health is a range, from positive health → better health → freedom from sickness → unrecognised sickness → mild sickness → severe sickness → death

6. Health as a right and a responsibility

  • The state must provide health services, and every person must also take responsibility for his own health

Nursing importance

  • Nurses use the holistic concept to plan care that meets physical, emotional, social and spiritual needs, and they promote health, not just cure disease

Conclusion Health is a dynamic, holistic state of physical, mental, social and spiritual well-being; nurses work to move every person towards positive health.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain Maslow's hierarchy of needs with its application in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Abraham Maslow, an American psychologist, proposed in 1943 that human needs are arranged in a hierarchy (pyramid) of five levels. Lower, basic needs must usually be satisfied before higher needs motivate behaviour. Nurses use this hierarchy to set priorities in patient care.

1. Physiological needs (base of the pyramid)

  • Oxygen, fluids, nutrition, elimination, temperature regulation, rest and sleep, activity, shelter and sexual needs
  • Nursing: maintaining airway and breathing, giving oxygen, IV fluids, feeding, bowel and bladder care, ensuring sleep

2. Safety and security needs

  • Physical safety (protection from injury, infection, falls) and psychological safety (freedom from fear and anxiety)
  • Nursing: side rails, infection control, correct medication, explaining procedures to reduce fear

3. Love and belonging needs

  • The need to give and receive affection, to belong to a family and group
  • Nursing: allowing family visits, involving the family in care, showing warmth and acceptance

4. Esteem needs

  • Self-respect, dignity, recognition, independence and status
  • Nursing: addressing patients respectfully, maintaining privacy, encouraging self-care, praising efforts

5. Self-actualisation (top of the pyramid)

  • Reaching one's full potential – "what a man can be, he must be"
  • Nursing: helping patients accept limitations, set new goals and achieve independence after illness or disability

Deficiency and growth needs

  • The first four levels are deficiency needs – their lack causes tension
  • Self-actualisation is a growth need

Characteristics of the hierarchy

  • Lower needs are more urgent; a person struggling to breathe is not interested in health teaching
  • Needs may overlap; a person can work on several levels at once
  • Unmet needs cause tension and illness; met needs no longer motivate

Application in nursing

  • Priority setting – airway, breathing and circulation first, then safety, then emotional and educational needs
  • Holistic assessment and care planning
  • Patient teaching is effective only after basic needs are met

Conclusion Maslow's hierarchy arranges human needs from physiological to self-actualisation; it guides nurses to meet urgent physical needs first and then psychological and social needs.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the types of illness and the risk factors for developing illness.
answer_html:
Introduction Illness is a state in which a person's physical, emotional, intellectual, social or spiritual functioning is reduced or impaired compared with his previous condition. Illnesses differ in onset, duration and course, and the chance of developing them depends on risk factors.

A. Types of illness

1. Acute illness

  • Sudden onset, severe symptoms, short duration (usually less than 6 months); usually responds to treatment and the person returns to normal
  • Examples: common cold, appendicitis, typhoid, fracture

2. Chronic illness

  • Gradual onset, lasts 6 months or longer, often lifelong; periods of remission (symptoms disappear) and exacerbation (symptoms worsen)
  • Examples: diabetes mellitus, hypertension, asthma, arthritis, chronic kidney disease

3. Terminal illness

  • An illness that cannot be cured and is expected to lead to death; e.g. advanced cancer

4. Other classifications

  • Communicable (tuberculosis, malaria) and non-communicable (heart disease, cancer)
  • Congenital (present at birth – cleft lip) and acquired
  • Physical and mental illness

B. Risk factors for developing illness A risk factor is any situation, habit, environmental condition or physiological state that increases the chance of a person developing a disease.

1. Genetic and physiological factors

  • Family history of diabetes, hypertension, cancer or mental illness; obesity; pregnancy

2. Age

  • Infants and the elderly are more prone to infections; the risk of heart disease and cancer increases with age

3. Lifestyle (behavioural) factors

  • Smoking, alcohol, drug use, unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, unsafe sex, stress, poor sleep

4. Environmental factors

  • Polluted air and water, poor sanitation, overcrowding, occupational hazards (dust, chemicals, noise), climate

5. Socio-economic factors

  • Poverty, illiteracy, unemployment, poor housing, poor access to health care

6. Psychological factors

  • Chronic stress, anxiety, loneliness

7. Cultural factors

  • Harmful practices and delay in seeking care

Nursing importance

  • Identify risk factors during assessment and give health education on lifestyle changes, screening and early treatment

Conclusion Illnesses may be acute, chronic or terminal; risk factors – genetic, age, lifestyle, environment and socio-economic status – increase the chance of illness, and many of them can be modified by health education.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define health. Explain the dimensions of health and the factors influencing health. (2 + 6 + 7)
answer_html:
(a) Definition of health (2 marks)

  • WHO (1948): "Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity"
  • Webster's dictionary: "the condition of being sound in body, mind or spirit, especially freedom from physical disease or pain"
  • Operational definition: a condition in which there is no obvious evidence of disease, and a person's various organs and systems are functioning normally and in harmony with the environment
  • Ottawa Charter (1986): health is a resource for everyday life, a positive concept emphasising social and personal resources as well as physical capacities
  • In simple words: health is a dynamic state in which the body, mind and social life of a person work well, so that he can live a productive and satisfying life

(b) Dimensions of health (6 marks) Health is multi-dimensional. All dimensions are interconnected; a problem in one affects the others.

1. Physical dimension

  • The perfect functioning of the body – every cell and organ working at its best and in harmony
  • Signs of physical health: good complexion, clean skin, bright eyes, lustrous hair, firm flesh, sweet breath, good appetite, sound sleep, regular bowel and bladder habits, smooth coordinated movements, and normal pulse, BP, weight and exercise tolerance
  • Assessed by clinical examination, nutrition and dietary assessment, and laboratory tests

2. Mental dimension

  • A state of balance between the person and his surroundings; the ability to cope with the normal stresses of life
  • Characteristics: free from internal conflicts, well adjusted, accepts criticism, has self-control, faces problems, has a good self-image and works productively
  • Mental health and physical health affect each other (psychosomatic illness)

3. Social dimension

  • Quantity and quality of a person's relationships and the extent of involvement with family and community
  • A socially healthy person has good relationships, social skills and the ability to fulfil roles (son, parent, worker, citizen)

4. Spiritual dimension

  • The part of the person that reaches out for meaning and purpose in life
  • Includes values, ethics, faith, integrity, principles and inner peace; may or may not be religious
  • Spiritual strength helps patients cope with suffering and death

5. Emotional dimension

  • Relates to feelings – the ability to recognise, express and control emotions such as love, fear, anger and sorrow
  • Mental health is more about knowing and thinking; emotional health is about feeling

6. Vocational dimension

  • Satisfaction and achievement from work; loss of a job or retirement affects health

7. Intellectual dimension

  • Curiosity, learning, creativity and problem-solving

8. Environmental dimension

  • Living and working in a safe, clean and healthy environment

9. Other dimensions (Park)

  • Philosophical, cultural, socio-economic, educational, nutritional, curative and preventive dimensions

(c) Factors influencing health (determinants of health) (7 marks) Health is influenced by many factors acting within the individual and in the society in which he lives. Lalonde (Canada, 1974) grouped them into four "health fields": human biology, environment, lifestyle and health care organisation.

1. Biological (genetic) factors

  • The genetic make-up of a person is fixed at conception
  • Inherited diseases – haemophilia, thalassaemia, sickle cell anaemia, colour blindness – and a tendency to diabetes, hypertension and some cancers
  • Age and sex also matter – infants and the elderly are more vulnerable; some diseases are more common in one sex

2. Behavioural and socio-cultural factors (lifestyle)

  • Lifestyle means the way people live – their habits, diet and behaviour
  • Harmful: smoking, tobacco chewing, alcohol, drug abuse, junk food, physical inactivity, unsafe sex, stress
  • Healthy: balanced diet, regular exercise, adequate sleep, personal hygiene, avoidance of addictions
  • Most non-communicable diseases (heart disease, diabetes, cancer) are lifestyle-related
  • Culture, customs and beliefs – food taboos during pregnancy, early marriage, open defecation, delay in seeking treatment

3. Environmental factors

  • Physical environment – air, water, soil, housing, climate, noise, radiation; polluted water causes diarrhoea, typhoid and hepatitis
  • Biological environment – disease-causing organisms, vectors such as mosquitoes and flies, animals
  • Psychosocial environment – family relationships, social support, stress, crime, violence

4. Socio-economic factors

  • Economic status – income decides the ability to buy nutritious food, good housing and health care; poverty and ill health form a vicious cycle
  • Education – especially of women; illiteracy is linked with high infant mortality and poor hygiene
  • Occupation – unemployment causes stress and poverty; certain occupations expose people to hazards (silicosis in miners, injuries in construction workers)
  • Political system – government policies, health budget and commitment decide the availability of health services

5. Health services

  • Availability, accessibility, affordability and acceptability of health services – immunisation, safe delivery, clean water, sanitation, family planning, early treatment
  • Coverage of health insurance (e.g. Ayushman Bharat – PM-JAY) reduces the cost burden on families

6. Ageing of the population

  • Increasing numbers of elderly increase chronic disease and disability

7. Gender

  • Discrimination against girls and women in food, education and health care affects their health

8. Other factors

  • Food and agriculture, industry, transport and communication, social welfare and family welfare programmes, the media and technology

Summary of determinants

Group Examples
Biological genes, age, sex
Lifestyle diet, exercise, smoking, alcohol
Environment water, air, housing, vectors
Socio-economic income, education, occupation, politics
Health services availability, accessibility, affordability

Indicators of health (how health is measured)

  • Mortality indicators – crude death rate, infant mortality rate, maternal mortality ratio, under-five mortality, life expectancy
  • Morbidity indicators – incidence and prevalence of diseases, hospital admission rates
  • Disability indicators – disability-adjusted life years (DALYs)
  • Nutritional status – stunting, wasting and underweight in children, low birth weight
  • Health care delivery and utilisation – doctor–population ratio, immunisation coverage, institutional deliveries
  • Socio-economic and environmental indicators – literacy, per-capita income, safe water and sanitation coverage
  • Composite indicators – Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI), Human Development Index (HDI)

Responsibility for health

  • Individual – self-care, healthy lifestyle and seeking timely treatment
  • Community – sanitation, community participation, support for health programmes
  • State – Article 47 of the Constitution makes improvement of public health a duty of the state; health services, policies and laws
  • International – WHO, UNICEF and other agencies; global control of diseases

Role of the nurse

  • Assess all dimensions of health during the nursing assessment
  • Health education on lifestyle, hygiene, nutrition and preventing addictions
  • Improve environmental sanitation through community work
  • Help people use available health services and government schemes
  • Support women's education and empowerment
  • Act as a role model of healthy living

Conclusion Health is a positive, multi-dimensional state of physical, mental, social, spiritual and emotional well-being. It is determined by biology, lifestyle, environment, socio-economic conditions and health services; most of these can be improved, and the nurse plays a key role through care, education and advocacy.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain Maslow's hierarchy of needs and the impact of illness on the patient and the family. (8 + 7)
answer_html:
(a) Maslow's hierarchy of needs (8 marks)

Introduction Abraham Maslow (1943) described human needs as a pyramid of five levels. The most basic needs are at the bottom; higher needs are at the top. A person is motivated first by the lower needs, and only when these are reasonably met do the higher needs become important. Basic human needs are common to all people, but the way they are met differs with age, culture and health.

1. Physiological needs

  • Oxygen – the most urgent need; a person can live only a few minutes without it
  • Fluids – water and electrolyte balance
  • Nutrition, elimination (urine and stool), temperature regulation
  • Rest, sleep and activity, shelter, sexual needs
  • Nursing actions: clearing the airway, oxygen therapy, positioning, IV fluids, feeding, catheter care, maintaining temperature, promoting sleep and mobility

2. Safety and security needs

  • Physical safety – protection from injury, infection, falls, burns and medication errors
  • Psychological safety – freedom from fear and anxiety; knowing what to expect
  • Nursing actions: side rails, call bell within reach, infection control, the "rights" of medication, explaining procedures, keeping promises, a familiar routine

3. Love and belonging needs

  • The need to give and receive affection, to be accepted and to belong to a family, friends and community
  • Illness and hospitalisation separate a person from loved ones
  • Nursing actions: flexible visiting hours, involving the family in care, warm and caring attitude, spending time with lonely patients

4. Esteem needs

  • Self-esteem – self-respect, confidence, independence
  • Esteem from others – recognition, respect, status
  • Illness that causes dependence, disfigurement (mastectomy, colostomy) or loss of job threatens self-esteem
  • Nursing actions: address the patient by name, maintain privacy and dignity, encourage self-care and decision-making, appreciate progress

5. Self-actualisation

  • The need to realise one's full potential and become everything one is capable of becoming
  • Self-actualised people are creative, accept themselves and others, solve problems and have a purpose
  • Nursing actions: help the patient accept limitations, set realistic new goals, learn new skills (e.g. a paraplegic person learning to use a wheelchair and return to work)

Deficiency and growth needs

  • Levels 1–4 are deficiency (D) needs; level 5 is a growth (being) need

Characteristics of the hierarchy

  • Needs are universal, but priorities can change – a mother may give her child's needs priority over her own hunger
  • Needs are interrelated; one unmet need affects others
  • Unmet needs produce tension and illness

Kalish's modification

  • Richard Kalish added a level of stimulation needs – sex, activity, exploration, manipulation and novelty – between physiological and safety needs; a child must explore and play before feeling secure

Example: applying Maslow to a patient on the first day after abdominal surgery

  1. Physiological – maintain airway, give oxygen if needed, IV fluids, pain relief, check urine output, encourage deep breathing
  2. Safety – raise side rails, prevent infection of the wound, check drain and IV site, explain each procedure
  3. Love and belonging – allow the spouse to stay, speak warmly, answer the family's questions
  4. Esteem – keep the patient covered, knock before entering, involve him in decisions about early ambulation
  5. Self-actualisation – before discharge, help him plan a safe return to work and a healthy lifestyle

Application of Maslow's hierarchy in nursing

  • Assessment of the patient's needs at all levels
  • Setting priorities – life-threatening physiological needs first (airway, breathing, circulation), then safety, then love, esteem and self-actualisation
  • Planning holistic care
  • Patient teaching – a patient in pain or hungry cannot learn; meet basic needs first

(b) Impact of illness on the patient and the family (7 marks)

A. Impact on the patient

1. Behavioural and emotional changes

  • Shock, denial, anger, fear, anxiety, depression, irritability and withdrawal
  • Short-term, mild illness causes little change; serious or chronic illness may cause long-lasting emotional reactions
  • The patient may become dependent and demanding

2. Changes in body image

  • Body image is the way a person sees his own body
  • Amputation, mastectomy, colostomy, burns, paralysis, loss of hair after chemotherapy alter body image; the patient may feel ashamed or unattractive
  • The patient passes through stages – shock, withdrawal, acknowledgement and acceptance

3. Changes in self-concept and self-esteem

  • Inability to fulfil roles (earner, parent) lowers self-worth; the patient may feel he is a burden

4. Changes in roles

  • The person may be unable to work, run the house or care for children; temporary or permanent role reversal occurs

5. Loss of independence and privacy

  • Hospital routines, exposure during procedures and dependence on others for basic needs

6. Financial impact

  • Loss of income, cost of treatment, medicines and travel

7. Spiritual distress

  • Questions such as "Why has God done this to me?"; loss of faith or increased religious practice

8. Physical effects of the illness itself

  • Pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance and loss of appetite

B. Impact on the family

1. Role changes

  • Other members take over the patient's roles – a wife may have to earn, a child may have to care for younger siblings or the sick parent

2. Emotional stress

  • Fear, anxiety, guilt, anger and grief, especially in serious, chronic or terminal illness

3. Financial burden

  • Cost of treatment, loss of the patient's income, loss of wages of the caregiver; debts and sale of property

4. Disruption of family routines

  • Changes in meals, sleep, children's studies and social activities; frequent hospital visits

5. Caregiver burden

  • Physical tiredness, emotional exhaustion and neglect of the caregiver's own health

6. Changes in family relationships

  • Some families come closer; others face conflicts and even breakdown

7. Social isolation and stigma

  • Especially in diseases such as TB, HIV, leprosy and mental illness

C. Factors that decide the extent of the impact

  • Nature, severity and duration of the illness – sudden, life-threatening or chronic illness has a greater impact
  • Age and role of the patient – illness of the main earner or of a young child affects the family most
  • Personality and coping style of the patient and family
  • Family structure and support – joint families share the burden more easily
  • Financial resources and health insurance
  • Cultural and religious beliefs about illness
  • Availability of health services nearby

Role of the nurse

  • Assess the impact of illness on the patient and family
  • Encourage expression of feelings; listen with empathy
  • Give clear information about the illness and treatment
  • Support adjustment to body-image changes; refer to support groups
  • Involve the family in care and teach home care
  • Inform about financial assistance – government schemes and health insurance
  • Arrange counselling and spiritual support; refer to the medical social worker

Conclusion Maslow's hierarchy of needs guides nurses to meet a patient's physiological, safety, love, esteem and self-actualisation needs in order of priority. Illness affects the patient's emotions, body image, roles, finances and spirit, and it also changes the roles, routines, finances and relationships of the whole family; holistic nursing care addresses both.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the models of health and illness.
answer_html:
Introduction Models of health and illness are frameworks that explain how people understand health, why they behave as they do and how illness develops. They help nurses assess health beliefs, motivate healthy behaviour and plan care and health education.

1. Biomedical model

  • Health is the absence of disease; illness is caused by a physical agent or bodily malfunction
  • Focus on diagnosis and cure; ignores psychological and social factors

2. Biopsychosocial model (George Engel)

  • Health and illness result from the interaction of biological, psychological and social factors
  • The basis of holistic care

3. Agent–host–environment model (epidemiological triad)

  • Disease results from the interaction of an agent (microbe, chemical, injury), a host (age, immunity, habits) and the environment (water, housing, climate)
  • A change in any one can cause or prevent disease – useful in community health

4. Health Belief Model (Rosenstock) A person is likely to take a health action (e.g. screening, vaccination) when he believes that:

  • he is susceptible to the disease (perceived susceptibility)
  • the disease is serious (perceived severity)
  • the action will be beneficial (perceived benefits)
  • the barriers – cost, pain, time, fear – are not too great (perceived barriers)
  • a cue to action is present – a symptom, advice, a media message, illness in a friend
  • he is able to do it (self-efficacy)
  • Modifying factors – age, sex, education, culture
  • Example: a woman goes for cervical cancer screening when she believes she is at risk, that cancer is serious and that early detection helps, after advice from an ASHA worker

5. Health Promotion Model (Nola Pender)

  • Explains why people adopt health-promoting behaviour (exercise, healthy diet) even without illness
  • Depends on individual characteristics and experiences, perceived benefits and barriers, self-efficacy, feelings about the activity, and the influence of family, peers and the environment
  • Leads to commitment to a plan of action

6. Holistic health model

  • The person is a whole – body, mind and spirit – in interaction with the environment
  • Uses complementary practices such as yoga, meditation, music therapy along with medical treatment

7. Basic human needs model (Maslow)

  • Health depends on meeting physiological, safety, love, esteem and self-actualisation needs in order of priority

Application in nursing

  • Assess the patient's health beliefs and readiness to change
  • Reduce barriers and provide cues to action (reminders, health talks)
  • Build self-efficacy through demonstration and praise
  • Plan holistic, individualised care and health education

Conclusion Models such as the biomedical, biopsychosocial, epidemiological triad, Health Belief Model, Health Promotion Model and holistic model explain health behaviour and illness; nurses use them to understand patients and motivate healthy behaviour.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: List the determinants of the health care delivery system.
answer_html:
Introduction The type and quality of health care that reaches people depends on several factors.

Determinants of health care delivery

  1. Size and characteristics of the population – age structure, rural or urban
  2. Disease pattern – communicable and non-communicable diseases
  3. Socio-economic status of the people
  4. Political commitment and health policies (National Health Policy, 2017)
  5. Financial resources – government budget, insurance
  6. Health manpower – doctors, nurses, paramedics
  7. Technology and infrastructure
  8. Geography and transport
  9. Culture, beliefs and health-seeking behaviour
  10. Community participation and people's expectations

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Mention the levels of prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction The aim of prevention is to stop disease from occurring or progressing.

Levels of prevention

  1. Primordial prevention – preventing the emergence of risk factors (healthy lifestyles in children)
  2. Primary prevention – before disease occurs:
    • health promotion (health education, nutrition, sanitation)
    • specific protection (immunisation, iodised salt)
  3. Secondary prevention – early diagnosis and prompt treatment (screening for cancer cervix, BP, diabetes)
  4. Tertiary prevention – after disease has occurred:
    • disability limitation
    • rehabilitation (physiotherapy after stroke)

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Name the levels of health care.
answer_html:
Introduction Health care in India is organised in levels, from the village to specialised hospitals, with referral between levels.

Levels of health care

  1. Primary level – the first contact of the people with the health system; essential, basic care
    • Sub-centres and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (Health and Wellness Centres), Primary Health Centres (PHCs)
  2. Secondary level – more complex problems referred from the primary level
    • Community Health Centres (CHCs), sub-district and district hospitals
  3. Tertiary level – specialised and super-specialised care
    • Medical college hospitals, regional institutes, AIIMS
  4. Some experts add a quaternary level – highly specialised care such as organ transplant

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the levels of prevention with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Prevention means actions that stop a disease from occurring, detect it early or limit its complications. Leavell and Clark related the levels of prevention to the natural history of disease – the course of a disease from its beginning to its end.

1. Primordial prevention

  • Prevention of the emergence or development of risk factors in populations where they have not yet appeared
  • Mainly through health education and healthy lifestyles from childhood
  • Example: encouraging school children to exercise, eat healthy food and avoid tobacco, so that obesity, hypertension and diabetes do not develop

2. Primary prevention – action taken before the onset of disease

  • (a) Health promotion – improves general health:
    • health education, good nutrition, environmental sanitation, safe water, good housing, lifestyle changes
    • personal hygiene, family life education
  • (b) Specific protection – protects against a particular disease:
    • immunisation (BCG, polio, measles-rubella)
    • iodised salt against goitre; vitamin A supplementation
    • chemoprophylaxis; use of helmets, seat belts and protective equipment at work
    • mosquito nets against malaria

3. Secondary prevention – action that halts the progress of a disease at its early stage

  • Early diagnosis and prompt treatment
  • Examples: screening for hypertension, diabetes and cancer of the cervix (Pap smear, VIA) and breast; sputum examination of TB suspects and starting treatment; screening of newborns for hypothyroidism
  • Prevents complications and spread of disease to others

4. Tertiary prevention – action taken when the disease has already caused damage

  • (a) Disability limitation – preventing or delaying the progress of disability (good control of diabetes to prevent amputation; physiotherapy to prevent contractures)
  • (b) Rehabilitation – restoring the person to the highest possible level of function:
    • medical (artificial limbs, hearing aids)
    • vocational (training for a new job)
    • social and psychological

Summary table

Level Stage of disease Measures Example
Primordial before risk factors lifestyle education healthy diet in schools
Primary before disease promotion, specific protection vaccination
Secondary early disease screening, early treatment Pap smear
Tertiary late disease disability limitation, rehabilitation prosthesis, physiotherapy

Role of the nurse

  • Health education, immunisation, screening camps, early referral, follow-up and rehabilitation at home

Conclusion Prevention works at four levels – primordial, primary, secondary and tertiary; nurses are involved at every level, from health education to rehabilitation.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Describe the types of health care agencies.
answer_html:
Introduction Health care agencies are the institutions and services through which health care is delivered to people. They range from village sub-centres to large hospitals and home care services, and they may be government, private or voluntary.

1. Hospitals

  • Provide in-patient and out-patient care, emergency services, diagnosis, treatment, education and research
  • Types: general and specialty hospitals; government, private, voluntary and teaching hospitals

2. Primary health care centres

  • Sub-centres / Ayushman Arogya Mandirs – staffed by a community health officer, ANMs and a multipurpose worker; give basic maternal and child health, immunisation, family planning and NCD screening
  • Primary Health Centres (PHCs) – a medical officer and nursing staff; first referral point for sub-centres
  • Community Health Centres (CHCs) – 30-bedded referral units with specialists

3. Clinics and out-patient departments

  • Physicians' clinics, polyclinics, specialty OPDs; ambulatory care without admission

4. Nursing homes and extended-care facilities

  • Small private hospitals; long-term care for the elderly and chronically ill who need nursing care but not acute hospital care

5. Rehabilitation centres

  • Restore function after stroke, spinal injury or amputation; de-addiction centres

6. Day-care centres

  • Day-care surgery, chemotherapy and dialysis units; day-care for the elderly

7. Home health care agencies

  • Nursing care, physiotherapy and palliative care at the patient's home

8. Hospice and palliative care centres

  • Comfort care for the terminally ill and support to their families

9. Diagnostic centres and laboratories

  • Laboratory, imaging and blood bank services

10. Voluntary and international agencies

  • Red Cross, CARE, missionary and charitable organisations; WHO and UNICEF support health programmes

11. Occupational and school health services

  • ESI dispensaries, industrial health centres, school health clinics

12. Telemedicine and e-health services

  • eSanjeevani tele-consultation, mobile health units

Nursing importance

  • Nurses work in all these agencies and must know the referral system so that patients reach the right level of care

Conclusion Health care is delivered through hospitals, primary care centres, clinics, nursing homes, rehabilitation, home care and hospice services run by government, private and voluntary bodies; together they provide preventive, curative and rehabilitative care.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define hospital. Explain the types of hospitals, the functions of a hospital and the members of the health team with their roles. (2 + 4 + 4 + 5)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • WHO: "A hospital is an integral part of a social and medical organisation, the function of which is to provide for the population complete health care, both curative and preventive, and whose out-patient services reach out to the family and its home environment; the hospital is also a centre for the training of health workers and for bio-social research."
  • In simple words: a hospital is an institution with beds, staff and equipment that provides diagnosis, treatment, nursing care, rehabilitation, education and research
  • The word comes from the Latin "hospes", meaning a host or guest

(b) Types of hospitals (4 marks)

1. According to ownership and control

  • Government (public) hospitals – run by the central government (AIIMS, central government hospitals), the state government (district and civil hospitals, medical college hospitals) or local bodies (municipal hospitals)
  • Semi-government and statutory hospitals – ESI hospitals, railway, defence and police hospitals
  • Private hospitals – owned by individuals, partnerships or corporate groups
  • Voluntary (charitable) hospitals – run by trusts, missionaries and non-governmental organisations on a non-profit basis

2. According to type of service

  • General hospitals – care for all types of patients and diseases
  • Specialty hospitals – for a particular group or disease: maternity, children's, cancer, cardiac, eye, mental, TB, orthopaedic and infectious disease hospitals
  • Super-specialty hospitals – cardio-thoracic surgery, neurosurgery, organ transplant

3. According to length of stay

  • Short-stay (acute care) hospitals – stay of less than 30 days
  • Long-stay hospitals – stay of more than 30 days; for chronic illness, psychiatric and rehabilitation care

4. According to level of care

  • Primary (PHC), secondary (CHC, district hospital) and tertiary (medical colleges, regional institutes)

5. According to teaching status

  • Teaching hospitals – attached to medical and nursing colleges
  • Non-teaching hospitals

6. According to system of medicine

  • Allopathic hospitals and AYUSH hospitals (Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha, Homoeopathy)

7. According to bed strength

  • Small (below 100 beds), medium (100–300 beds) and large (above 300 beds)

(c) Functions of a hospital (4 marks)

1. Patient care (curative function)

  • Diagnosis – history, examination, laboratory and imaging services
  • Treatment – medical, surgical and nursing care for in-patients and out-patients
  • Emergency and trauma services round the clock
  • Rehabilitation – physiotherapy, occupational therapy, vocational guidance

2. Preventive and promotive function

  • Immunisation, antenatal and post-natal care, family planning, health education, screening, control of communicable diseases and outreach camps

3. Education and training

  • Training of doctors, nurses, pharmacists, technicians and other health workers; continuing education for staff
  • Health education of patients and families

4. Research

  • Clinical and nursing research to improve care; maintaining medical records for research and statistics

5. Community service

  • Participation in national health programmes, disaster management, mobile clinics and outreach services

6. Administrative and support functions

  • Medical records, pharmacy, central sterile supply (CSSD), dietary services, laundry, housekeeping, biomedical waste management, stores and maintenance

Organisation of a hospital (in brief)

  • Governing body / board of management → medical superintendent / director
  • Clinical departments – medicine, surgery, obstetrics and gynaecology, paediatrics, orthopaedics, psychiatry, emergency
  • Nursing department – chief nursing officer (nursing superintendent) → deputy and assistant nursing superintendents → ward sisters (nursing officers) → staff nurses → student nurses
  • Diagnostic departments – laboratory, radiology, blood bank
  • Support services – pharmacy, CSSD, kitchen, laundry, maintenance
  • Administrative departments – accounts, human resources, stores, medical records

(d) Members of the health team and their roles (5 marks) The health team is a group of health professionals with different skills who work together towards the common goal of the patient's health. The patient and the family are the centre of the team.

1. Physician (doctor)

  • Diagnoses disease, prescribes treatment, performs procedures and surgery, and leads medical management

2. Nurse

  • Provides 24-hour care; assesses the patient, plans and gives nursing care, gives medicines, observes and reports changes, educates the patient and family, coordinates the team and acts as the patient's advocate

3. Pharmacist

  • Dispenses medicines, checks prescriptions for errors and interactions, advises on drug use and storage

4. Dietitian / nutritionist

  • Assesses nutritional needs, plans therapeutic diets (diabetic, renal, low-salt) and counsels patients

5. Physiotherapist

  • Exercises, mobilisation, chest physiotherapy, electrotherapy and rehabilitation after injury or surgery

6. Occupational therapist

  • Helps patients regain skills for daily living and work; provides adaptive devices

7. Medical social worker

  • Helps with financial, family and social problems; links patients with welfare schemes and agencies

8. Laboratory technician

  • Collects and analyses blood, urine and other specimens

9. Radiographer

  • Performs X-rays, ultrasound and other imaging under the radiologist

10. Clinical psychologist and counsellor

  • Psychological assessment, counselling and therapy

11. Respiratory therapist, speech therapist, optometrist

  • Specialised therapies

12. Support staff

  • Multipurpose workers, ward attendants and housekeeping staff maintain cleanliness, transport patients and assist in care

13. Medical records officer and administrators

  • Maintain records, manage resources and ensure smooth functioning

Principles of effective teamwork

  • A common goal, clear roles, mutual respect, good communication (team meetings, handover), coordination and shared decision-making

Characteristics of a good hospital

  • Patient-centred, with respect for patients' rights and dignity
  • Adequate, qualified staff and modern equipment
  • Clean, safe environment with effective infection control and biomedical waste management
  • Round-the-clock emergency services and a clear referral system
  • Quality assurance – standard protocols, audits, accreditation (e.g. NABH)
  • Good records and transparent administration
  • Links with the community and participation in national health programmes

Role of the nurse in the hospital

  • Care giver – direct, 24-hour patient care
  • Manager of the ward – staff, supplies, equipment and environment
  • Coordinator between the patient and other team members
  • Teacher of patients, families and students
  • Advocate of the patient's rights
  • Researcher – participating in studies to improve care

Conclusion A hospital is an integral part of the health system that provides curative and preventive care, training and research. Hospitals may be classified by ownership, service, length of stay, level of care and teaching status. Their work depends on a coordinated health team, in which the nurse plays a central, round-the-clock role.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: What is primary health care? List its elements.
answer_html:
Definition Primary health care is essential health care based on practical, scientifically sound and socially acceptable methods and technology, made universally accessible to individuals and families in the community through their full participation, at a cost the community and country can afford (Alma-Ata Declaration, 1978, WHO and UNICEF). Its goal was "Health for All".

Eight essential elements

  1. Education about health problems and their prevention
  2. Food supply and proper nutrition
  3. Safe water and basic sanitation
  4. Maternal and child health, including family planning
  5. Immunisation against major infectious diseases
  6. Prevention and control of locally endemic diseases
  7. Treatment of common diseases and injuries
  8. Provision of essential drugs

Principles: equitable distribution, community participation, intersectoral coordination and appropriate technology.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the organisation of a hospital.
answer_html:
Introduction Hospital organisation is the arrangement of authority, departments and relationships that allows all staff to work together for coordinated patient care. It is shown in an organisational chart, which gives the lines of authority and communication.

1. Governing body

  • Government hospitals – controlled by the Health Department and the Directorate of Health Services; in medical college hospitals, by the Medical Education Department
  • Private and trust hospitals – a board of directors or trustees
  • Hospital management committees, such as the Rogi Kalyan Samiti in government hospitals, involve the community

2. Administration

  • Medical Superintendent (or Dean in teaching hospitals, or Hospital Administrator) – the overall head
  • Deputy Medical Superintendent and administrative officers

3. Departments

a. Clinical (medical) services

  • Medicine, surgery, obstetrics and gynaecology, paediatrics, orthopaedics, ENT, ophthalmology, psychiatry
  • Emergency (casualty), intensive care units, operation theatres and out-patient department

b. Nursing service department

  • Chief Nursing Officer / Nursing Superintendent → Deputy and Assistant Nursing Superintendents → ward sister (ward in-charge) → nursing officers (staff nurses) → nursing aides
  • Responsible for nursing care, nursing staff management, ward management and clinical teaching of students

c. Diagnostic and therapeutic (paramedical) services

  • Laboratory, radiology, pharmacy, blood bank, physiotherapy, dietetics and the central sterile supply department (CSSD)

d. Supportive (hotel) services

  • Housekeeping, laundry, kitchen, maintenance, biomedical engineering, security, transport and biomedical waste management

e. Administrative services

  • Medical records, accounts, stores and purchase, human resources, information technology, public relations and medico-social work

4. Committees

  • Infection control committee, drug and therapeutics committee, ethics committee, quality (accreditation) committee, hospital management committee

5. Principles of good organisation

  • Unity of command – each person reports to one superior
  • Clear lines of authority and responsibility
  • Reasonable span of control
  • Division of work and specialisation
  • Coordination and communication between departments

6. Importance for the nurse

  • Knowing the chain of command helps the nurse report correctly, seek help and coordinate with other departments for smooth patient care

7. Types of organisational structure

  • Line organisation – authority flows directly from top to bottom (e.g. Nursing Superintendent → ward sister → nursing officer)
  • Line and staff organisation – line officers are supported by advisory staff (infection control nurse, quality manager); the commonest in hospitals
  • Functional organisation – specialists control particular functions across departments

Conclusion A hospital is organised under a governing body and administration into clinical, nursing, diagnostic, supportive and administrative departments, linked by clear lines of authority and committees; this organisation ensures coordinated, efficient patient care.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: History of Nursing and Nursing as a Profession
question: List the qualities of a nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction A nurse cares for people when they are most vulnerable, so she needs personal, professional and ethical qualities.

Qualities of a nurse

  1. Compassion and empathy – feels with the patient
  2. Patience, tolerance and a kind, cheerful nature
  3. Honesty and integrity
  4. Good communication and listening skills
  5. Sharp observation and critical thinking
  6. Responsibility and accountability
  7. Punctuality and discipline
  8. Tact and courtesy
  9. Physical and mental fitness
  10. Adaptability and teamwork
  11. Confidentiality and respect for others
  12. Willingness to learn and keep knowledge updated

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: History of Nursing and Nursing as a Profession
question: Enumerate the ethical principles in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Ethics is the study of right and wrong conduct. Nurses follow these principles while caring for patients.

Ethical principles

  1. Autonomy – respecting the patient's right to make his own decisions (informed consent)
  2. Beneficence – doing good for the patient
  3. Non-maleficence – doing no harm
  4. Justice – fair and equal treatment of all patients
  5. Veracity – telling the truth
  6. Fidelity – keeping promises and being faithful to commitments
  7. Confidentiality – protecting the patient's private information
  8. Accountability – being answerable for one's own actions

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: History of Nursing and Nursing as a Profession
question: Define nursing.
answer_html:
Definitions

  1. Florence Nightingale: nursing is "the act of utilising the environment of the patient to assist him in his recovery"
  2. Virginia Henderson: "The unique function of the nurse is to assist the individual, sick or well, in the performance of those activities contributing to health or its recovery (or to peaceful death) that he would perform unaided if he had the necessary strength, will or knowledge; and to do this in such a way as to help him gain independence as rapidly as possible"
  3. International Council of Nurses (ICN): nursing encompasses autonomous and collaborative care of individuals of all ages, families, groups and communities, sick or well, in all settings; it includes promotion of health, prevention of illness and care of the ill, disabled and dying

In simple words: nursing is both an art and a science of caring for people to promote, maintain and restore health.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: History of Nursing and Nursing as a Profession
question: Explain the code of ethics for nurses.
answer_html:
Introduction A code of ethics is a written set of moral principles and standards of conduct that guides members of a profession. It tells the public what to expect from nurses and helps nurses make right decisions. In India, the Indian Nursing Council (INC) has laid down the code of ethics for nurses; internationally, the International Council of Nurses (ICN) code is followed.

Purposes of a code of ethics

  • Guides nurses in ethical decision-making
  • Protects the rights of patients
  • Maintains public trust and the dignity of the profession
  • Provides a standard for self-evaluation and for disciplinary action

Code of ethics for nurses in India (INC) – main principles

1. The nurse respects the uniqueness of individuals

  • Provides care without discrimination of caste, creed, religion, culture, ideology, economic or social status
  • Considers the individual's culture, beliefs and values in planning care

2. The nurse respects the rights of individuals as partners in care

  • Gives information so that patients can make informed choices, and respects their decisions
  • Obtains informed consent before procedures

3. The nurse respects the right to privacy and maintains confidentiality

  • Shares information judiciously – only with those who need to know for the patient's care
  • Maintains privacy during examinations and procedures

4. The nurse maintains competence

  • Keeps knowledge and skills up to date through continuing education to give quality care

5. The nurse practises within ethical, professional and legal boundaries

  • Follows laws, hospital policies and the scope of nursing practice; is accountable for her actions

6. The nurse works harmoniously with members of the health team

  • Cooperates, respects and communicates with colleagues for the benefit of patients

7. The nurse commits to the demands of professional membership

  • Participates in professional organisations and contributes to the advancement of nursing

ICN Code of Ethics (in brief)

  • Four principal elements: nurses and patients (or other people requiring care), nurses and practice, nurses and the profession, and nurses and global health
  • The fundamental responsibilities: promote health, prevent illness, restore health and alleviate suffering

Nursing importance

  • The code guides daily situations such as keeping information confidential, refusing to falsify records, reporting errors honestly and treating all patients equally

Conclusion The code of ethics guides nurses to respect every individual, protect rights and privacy, maintain competence, work within legal limits, cooperate with the team and advance the profession.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: History of Nursing and Nursing as a Profession
question: Describe the contributions of Florence Nightingale to nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Florence Nightingale (1820–1910) is called the founder of modern nursing. She was born on 12 May 1820 in Florence, Italy, to a wealthy English family. Against her family's wishes, she chose nursing as a career. 12 May is celebrated worldwide as International Nurses Day in her honour.

1. Training and early work

  • Trained at the Kaiserswerth institution in Germany (under Pastor Theodor Fliedner)
  • In 1853 she became superintendent of a hospital for gentlewomen in Harley Street, London

2. Work in the Crimean War (1854–1856)

  • Went to Scutari (Turkey) with 38 nurses to care for wounded British soldiers
  • Found overcrowding, poor sanitation, lack of supplies and high death rates
  • Improved cleanliness, ventilation, water supply, diet, laundry and nursing care; the death rate of soldiers fell dramatically
  • Made night rounds with a lamp – known as the "Lady with the Lamp"

3. Founded nursing education

  • With the Nightingale Fund, she started the Nightingale Training School for Nurses at St Thomas' Hospital, London, in 1860 – the first organised, secular school of nursing
  • Set standards: selection of good-character students, a planned course, residence for students and trained nurses as teachers
  • This model spread across the world, including India

4. Writings

  • "Notes on Nursing: What It Is and What It Is Not" (1859) – the first nursing textbook, stressing fresh air, light, warmth, cleanliness, quiet, diet and observation
  • "Notes on Hospitals" and many reports on public health

5. Environmental theory

  • Health depends on the environment – ventilation, light, noise, cleanliness, warmth, drainage and pure water
  • The nurse's role is to put the patient in the best condition for nature to act upon him

6. Statistician and reformer

  • Used statistics and diagrams (the "polar area" or coxcomb diagram) to show that most deaths were due to preventable diseases
  • First woman elected Fellow of the Royal Statistical Society
  • Worked on health and sanitation of the army and people of India

7. Raised the status of nursing

  • Made nursing a respectable profession for women based on knowledge, discipline and compassion

Honours: Royal Red Cross; the Order of Merit (1907) – the first woman to receive it.

Conclusion Florence Nightingale transformed nursing from an untrained occupation into an educated, respected profession through her war work, training school, writings, environmental theory and use of statistics.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: History of Nursing and Nursing as a Profession
question: Explain the history of nursing in India.
answer_html:
Introduction Nursing in India has grown from untrained care by family members and attendants to a university-based profession regulated by law. Its history can be divided into ancient, medieval, British and post-independence periods.

1. Ancient period

  • Ayurveda: the Charaka Samhita describes the qualities of nurse attendants – knowledge of drug preparation, cleverness, devotion to the patient and purity of body and mind
  • Sushruta emphasised cleanliness in surgery
  • King Ashoka (3rd century BC) built hospitals for people and animals, with attendants for nursing care

2. Medieval period

  • Muslim rulers established hospitals (dar-ul-shifa); care was mostly given by family members and untrained attendants

3. British period

  • 1664 – the East India Company opened the first military hospital at Fort St George, Madras
  • 1797 – a lying-in (maternity) hospital in Madras
  • 1871 – the first school of nursing (for women) at the Government General Hospital, Madras
  • 1885 – the Lady Dufferin Fund to train women doctors, nurses and midwives
  • 1908 – the Trained Nurses' Association of India (TNAI) was formed; it grew out of the Association of Nursing Superintendents (1905)
  • 1926 – Madras became the first province to set up a registration council for nurses
  • 1946 – the first B.Sc. Nursing programmes at the College of Nursing, Delhi, and at CMC Vellore
  • Bhore Committee (1946) recommended improvement of nursing education and services

4. Post-independence period

  • 1947 – the Indian Nursing Council Act was passed and the Indian Nursing Council (INC) was formed to regulate nursing education
  • State Nursing Councils register nurses and midwives
  • 1959 – M.Sc. Nursing started at the Rajkumari Amrit Kaur College of Nursing, New Delhi
  • Post-basic B.Sc., M.Phil. and Ph.D. programmes followed
  • Nurse practitioner courses in critical care and midwifery have been introduced
  • 2021 – the INC introduced the revised competency-based B.Sc. Nursing curriculum with a semester system

5. Professional organisations

  • TNAI, Student Nurses' Association (SNA), INC and state councils, and specialty nursing associations

Nursing personnel today

  • ANM / MPHW (female), GNM, B.Sc., Post-basic B.Sc., M.Sc., Ph.D. nurses; community health officers; nursing officers, tutors and administrators

Conclusion From the attendants of Charaka and Ashoka to university-educated nurses regulated by the INC, nursing in India has developed into a recognised profession with its own education, registration and organisations.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: History of Nursing and Nursing as a Profession
question: Define nursing. Explain the nature and scope of nursing, the functions of a nurse and the criteria of nursing as a profession. (2 + 4 + 4 + 5)
answer_html:
(a) Definition of nursing (2 marks)

  • Florence Nightingale: nursing is "the act of utilising the environment of the patient to assist him in his recovery"
  • Virginia Henderson (1966): "The unique function of the nurse is to assist the individual, sick or well, in the performance of those activities contributing to health or its recovery (or to peaceful death) that he would perform unaided if he had the necessary strength, will or knowledge, and to do this in such a way as to help him gain independence as rapidly as possible"
  • ICN: nursing encompasses autonomous and collaborative care of individuals of all ages, families, groups and communities, sick or well, in all settings; it includes promotion of health, prevention of illness and care of the ill, disabled and dying, along with advocacy, research, education and participation in health policy
  • Nurse: a person who has completed a recognised programme of nursing education and is registered with the nursing council to practise nursing

(b) Nature and scope of nursing (4 marks)

Nature of nursing

  1. An art and a science – the science provides knowledge (anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, nursing principles); the art is the skilful, caring application of that knowledge
  2. Holistic – concerned with the physical, mental, social and spiritual needs of the whole person
  3. Caring and humanistic – based on compassion and respect for human dignity
  4. Helping and service-oriented – the welfare of people comes before personal gain
  5. Based on the nursing process – a scientific, problem-solving approach: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation
  6. Dynamic – changes with advances in science, technology and the needs of society
  7. Ethical and legal – governed by a code of ethics and laws
  8. Collaborative – works with other members of the health team

Philosophy of nursing (beliefs)

  • Every individual has worth and dignity and the right to quality health care without discrimination
  • Health is a basic human right; nursing contributes to the health of individuals, families and communities
  • Nursing education should prepare competent, ethical, caring and lifelong learners

Objectives of nursing

  • Promotion of health, prevention of illness, restoration of health and alleviation of suffering, including a peaceful death

Scope of nursing (where and how nurses work)

  1. Hospital nursing – wards, ICUs, operation theatres, emergency, specialty units
  2. Community health nursing – sub-centres, PHCs, CHCs, home visits, national health programmes; community health officers in Ayushman Arogya Mandirs
  3. School and occupational health nursing
  4. Military nursing – the Military Nursing Service
  5. Nursing education – tutors, lecturers, professors and principals
  6. Nursing administration – nursing officers, superintendents, directors of nursing
  7. Nursing research
  8. Specialised and advanced practice – critical care, oncology, cardiac, neonatal and psychiatric nursing; nurse practitioners and nurse midwives
  9. Home care, hospice and palliative care
  10. International nursing and service in WHO, Red Cross and other agencies
  11. Independent practice – nursing homes, consultation, entrepreneurship

(c) Functions of a nurse (4 marks)

1. Independent functions – actions the nurse performs on her own professional judgement, without a doctor's order

  • Nursing assessment and nursing diagnosis
  • Hygiene care, positioning, prevention of pressure ulcers
  • Monitoring of vital signs and observation
  • Health education and counselling
  • Comfort measures, emotional support
  • Maintaining a safe environment and infection control

2. Dependent functions – carried out on the written or verbal orders of a physician

  • Administration of medicines and injections
  • IV therapy and blood transfusion
  • Diagnostic tests and preparation for special procedures
  • Specific treatments such as dressing of surgical wounds with prescribed agents

3. Interdependent (collaborative) functions – carried out with other members of the health team

  • Planning care with doctors, physiotherapists and dietitians
  • Ward rounds, multidisciplinary meetings, discharge planning
  • Emergency care such as CPR

Roles of a nurse

Role What the nurse does
Care giver gives direct physical and emotional care
Communicator communicates with patients, families and the team
Teacher (educator) teaches patients, families, students
Counsellor helps patients cope with problems
Advocate protects patients' rights
Leader and manager manages the ward, staff and resources
Change agent introduces improvements
Researcher finds and uses evidence
Case manager and coordinator coordinates care across services

(d) Criteria of nursing as a profession (5 marks)

Definition of profession

  • A profession is an occupation that requires extensive education, specialised knowledge and skills, is guided by a code of ethics, and is devoted to service of society

Abraham Flexner's criteria (1915) – a profession:

  1. Involves intellectual activity with individual responsibility
  2. Is based on a body of science and learning
  3. Is practical, applying knowledge to definite ends
  4. Has a technique that can be taught through an educational discipline
  5. Is self-organised – has a professional association
  6. Is motivated by altruism – service to others

How nursing meets these criteria

1. Well-defined body of knowledge

  • Nursing has its own theories (Nightingale, Henderson, Orem, Peplau, Roy) and uses knowledge from biological and behavioural sciences

2. Long, specialised education in institutions of higher learning

  • University-level programmes – B.Sc., M.Sc., Ph.D. – with theory and supervised clinical practice

3. Service orientation (altruism)

  • Service to people is the main motive; nurses care for all, irrespective of caste, religion or status

4. Code of ethics

  • The INC and ICN codes of ethics and professional conduct guide nurses

5. Licensure and registration

  • Only nurses registered with a State Nursing Council may practise; the INC sets standards of education

6. Professional organisations

  • TNAI, INC, State Nursing Councils, ICN and specialty associations protect standards and the welfare of nurses

7. Autonomy and accountability

  • Nurses make independent nursing decisions within their scope and are accountable for them

8. Research and continuing education

  • Nursing research builds evidence-based practice; nurses update knowledge through continuing education

9. Career commitment

  • Nursing is a lifelong career with clear career paths in practice, education, administration and research

10. Recognised status in society

  • Recognised by law and by society as an essential health profession

Challenges to full professional status

  • Limited autonomy in some settings, shortage of nurses, heavy workload and low public image in some areas; these are improving with better education, research and leadership

Conclusion Nursing is the art and science of caring for people – sick or well – to promote, maintain and restore health. Its scope ranges from hospitals and communities to education, administration and research. Nurses carry out independent, dependent and interdependent functions, and nursing satisfies the criteria of a profession: a body of knowledge, higher education, a code of ethics, registration, professional organisations, autonomy and service to society.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: History of Nursing and Nursing as a Profession
question: Name the categories of nursing personnel in India.
answer_html:
Introduction Nursing personnel in India are prepared through different programmes and work at different levels.

1. By educational preparation

  • Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) – diploma, mainly for community work
  • General Nursing and Midwifery (GNM) – diploma
  • B.Sc Nursing (4 years) and Post-basic B.Sc Nursing
  • M.Sc Nursing, PhD; Nurse Practitioner programmes (e.g. critical care, midwifery)

2. By position in service

  • Hospitals – Nursing Officer (staff nurse), ward sister, nursing supervisor, Assistant and Deputy Nursing Superintendent, Nursing Superintendent, Chief Nursing Officer
  • Community – ANM, health supervisor, Public Health Nurse, Community Health Officer at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs
  • Education – clinical instructor, tutor, lecturer, associate professor, professor, principal

3. Support staff – nursing aides and ward attendants (non-professional).

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: History of Nursing and Nursing as a Profession
question: What are professional values in nursing?
answer_html:
Definition Professional values are the enduring beliefs and ideals that guide a nurse's behaviour and decisions in practice.

Core values (American Association of Colleges of Nursing)

  1. Altruism – concern for the welfare of others
  2. Autonomy – respecting the patient's right to make decisions
  3. Human dignity – respect for the worth and uniqueness of every person
  4. Integrity – honesty and acting according to the code of ethics
  5. Social justice – fair and equal treatment of all, regardless of caste, religion or income

Other important values

  • Caring and compassion, accountability, confidentiality, competence, respect and teamwork

Importance: guide ethical decisions, build patients' trust and give the profession its identity.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: History of Nursing and Nursing as a Profession
question: Describe the history of nursing in the world.
answer_html:
Introduction Nursing is as old as mankind – it began with a mother caring for her child and the sick in the family. Over centuries it developed from instinctive care to a scientific profession.

1. Ancient period

  • Care given by mothers, priests and medicine men; illness was blamed on evil spirits and gods
  • Egypt – embalming, medical papyri
  • Babylon – the Code of Hammurabi laid down rules for physicians
  • Hebrews – the Mosaic code gave rules of hygiene, isolation and sanitation
  • Greece – Hippocrates, the father of medicine, separated medicine from magic
  • Rome – military hospitals, aqueducts and public sanitation
  • India – Charaka and Sushruta described the qualities of an attendant (nurse); King Ashoka built hospitals for people and animals

2. Early Christian period

  • Christianity stressed love and service to the sick
  • Phoebe – the first deaconess and visiting nurse
  • Fabiola – founded the first free public hospital in Rome
  • Marcella – turned her palace into a religious house and taught women to nurse
  • Paula – built hospitals and hostels for pilgrims

3. Middle Ages

  • Care given by monastic orders and military nursing orders during the Crusades – the Knights Hospitallers (Order of St John), Teutonic Knights and Knights of St Lazarus (care of leprosy)
  • Hospitals such as the Hôtel-Dieu in Lyon and Paris

4. "Dark period" of nursing (about 1500–1850)

  • After the Reformation, monasteries were closed; nursing was done by untrained, poorly paid women of low social standing – shown by Charles Dickens' character Sairey Gamp
  • Reformers:
    • St Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac – founded the Sisters of Charity (1633) and trained them to nurse
    • Pastor Theodor Fliedner – opened the Kaiserswerth Deaconess Institute in Germany (1836), the first organised nurses' training school, where Florence Nightingale later trained
    • Elizabeth Fry – prison reform and an institute of nursing sisters in England

5. Modern period (Nightingale era)

  • Florence Nightingale – care of soldiers in the Crimean War (1854–56); founded the Nightingale Training School at St Thomas' Hospital, London (1860) – the beginning of modern nursing

6. Twentieth century onwards

  • International Council of Nurses (ICN) founded in 1899
  • Red Cross (Henry Dunant, 1863)
  • Registration of nurses – first in New Zealand (1901), then other countries
  • University education for nurses (University of Minnesota, 1909)
  • Nursing theories (Peplau, Henderson, Orem, Roy), research, specialisation and nurse practitioners
  • WHO (1948) and nursing's role in primary health care

Conclusion Nursing grew from family and religious care in ancient times, through the monastic and military orders and the dark period, to the modern profession founded by Florence Nightingale, and today it is a scientific, registered and university-based profession.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: History of Nursing and Nursing as a Profession
question: Explain the functions of professional organisations in nursing – INC, State Nursing Council, TNAI and ICN.
answer_html:
Introduction Professional organisations set standards, regulate practice and protect the interests of nurses and the public. Some are statutory (created by law) and others are voluntary associations.

1. Indian Nursing Council (INC)

  • A statutory body constituted under the Indian Nursing Council Act, 1947
  • Functions:
    • prescribes uniform standards and syllabi for nursing education
    • recognises nursing qualifications and inspects nursing institutions
    • prescribes norms for faculty, infrastructure and clinical facilities
    • maintains national registration data (nurse unique identification and tracking)
    • lays down the Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct
    • advises government on nursing matters
  • The National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act, 2023 provides for the INC to be replaced by a National Nursing and Midwifery Commission

2. State Nursing Councils (e.g. Maharashtra Nursing Council, under the Maharashtra Nurses Act, 1966)

  • Register nurses and midwives qualified to practise in the state; renewal of registration
  • Inspect and approve nursing schools; conduct examinations in some states
  • Disciplinary action – remove names from the register for professional misconduct
  • Maintain the state register

3. Trained Nurses' Association of India (TNAI) – founded in 1908

  • A voluntary professional association of nurses
  • Objectives and functions:
    • uphold the dignity and honour of the profession
    • promote the welfare of nurses – working conditions, salaries
    • continuing education – conferences, workshops
    • publishes The Nursing Journal of India
    • guides the Student Nurses' Association (SNA)
    • represents Indian nurses in the ICN

4. International Council of Nurses (ICN) – founded in 1899, headquarters in Geneva

  • A federation of national nurses' associations from more than 130 countries
  • Functions:
    • gives the ICN Code of Ethics for Nurses
    • sets international standards and promotes nursing education and research
    • represents nursing at WHO and other world bodies
    • promotes International Nurses Day (12 May), Florence Nightingale's birthday

5. Other organisations

  • Student Nurses' Association, Society of Midwives of India, Nursing Research Society of India, speciality nursing societies

Benefits of membership

  • Professional identity, updating of knowledge, networking, a voice in policy and protection of nurses' rights

Statutory and voluntary bodies compared

Statutory body (INC, SNC) Voluntary association (TNAI, ICN)
created by an Act of legislature formed voluntarily by nurses
regulates education and practice promotes the profession and nurses' welfare
registration is compulsory to practise membership is optional

Conclusion The INC and State Nursing Councils regulate nursing education and registration, while TNAI and ICN are professional associations that promote standards, welfare and the voice of nurses nationally and internationally.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: History of Nursing and Nursing as a Profession
question: Explain the rights of patients.
answer_html:
Introduction Patients' rights are the basic rights that every patient has while receiving health care. In India, the Charter of Patients' Rights was prepared by the National Human Rights Commission and recommended by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (2019) for adoption by all hospitals. It lists 17 rights.

Rights of patients

  1. Right to information – about the illness, investigations, treatment and expected costs
  2. Right to records and reports – copies of case papers and investigation reports
  3. Right to emergency medical care – without demand for advance payment
  4. Right to informed consent before procedures and treatment
  5. Right to confidentiality, human dignity and privacy
  6. Right to a second opinion
  7. Right to transparency in rates and care according to prescribed rates
  8. Right to non-discrimination – on grounds of disease (e.g. HIV), caste, religion, sex, age or economic status
  9. Right to safety and quality care according to standards
  10. Right to choose alternative treatment options, if available
  11. Right to choose the source for obtaining medicines or tests
  12. Right to proper referral and transfer, free from commercial influence
  13. Right to protection for patients involved in clinical trials
  14. Right to protection of participants in biomedical and health research
  15. Right to take discharge, or to receive the body of a deceased patient, without being detained over billing disputes
  16. Right to patient education
  17. Right to be heard and seek redressal of grievances

Responsibilities of patients

  • Give correct history; follow instructions; respect staff and other patients
  • Pay the agreed charges; never resort to violence

Role of the nurse

  • Patient advocate – protect patients' rights and speak up for them
  • Give information and obtain consent properly; maintain privacy and confidentiality
  • Treat every patient without discrimination
  • Display the patients' rights charter and help patients use grievance procedures

Rights in special situations

  • Persons with mental illness (Mental Healthcare Act, 2017) – right to access care, dignity, confidentiality, an advance directive and a nominated representative
  • People living with HIV (HIV and AIDS Act, 2017) – protection against discrimination; consent and confidentiality for testing
  • Children – consent from parents or guardians, with the child's assent when old enough
  • Dying patients – pain relief, palliative care, dignity and the company of family

Conclusion Patients have rights to information, records, emergency care, consent, privacy, second opinion, non-discrimination, safety, choice, proper referral, discharge, education and redressal; the nurse protects these rights as the patient's advocate.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Name the elements of communication.
answer_html:
Introduction Communication is the exchange of information, ideas and feelings between two or more persons.

Elements of communication

  1. Sender (source / encoder) – the person who starts the message
  2. Message – the information, idea or feeling to be conveyed
  3. Channel (medium) – the means: spoken words, writing, gestures, telephone
