  4. Receiver (decoder) – the person who receives and interprets the message
  5. Feedback – the receiver's response that shows the message was understood
  6. Environment (context) – the setting – place, time, privacy
  7. Noise (interference) – anything that disturbs the message

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Mention the levels of communication.
answer_html:
Introduction Communication takes place at different levels depending on the number of people involved.

Levels of communication

  1. Intrapersonal – communication within oneself – self-talk, thinking ("I must check this patient's BP again")
  2. Interpersonal – between two persons, face to face – nurse and patient
  3. Small group – among a few people with a common purpose – a team meeting, a group health talk
  4. Public – one speaker to a large audience – a lecture, a health exhibition
  5. Organisational – within an institution through formal channels – circulars, reports
  6. Mass communication – through media to the general public – radio, TV, newspapers, social media
  7. Transpersonal – communication in the spiritual domain – prayer, meditation

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: List the therapeutic communication techniques.
answer_html:
Introduction Therapeutic communication is purposeful communication by the nurse that helps the patient express feelings and cope with problems.

Techniques

  1. Active listening
  2. Using silence
  3. Open-ended questions ("How are you feeling today?")
  4. Restating and paraphrasing
  5. Reflecting feelings ("You seem worried about the surgery")
  6. Clarifying ("Can you explain what you mean?")
  7. Focusing on the main concern
  8. Giving information
  9. Offering self ("I will sit with you for a while")
  10. Acknowledging and giving recognition
  11. Summarising
  12. Therapeutic touch, used appropriately

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the process of communication.
answer_html:
Introduction Communication is the process of exchanging information, ideas, thoughts and feelings between two or more persons through verbal or non-verbal means, so that they understand each other. It is a two-way, continuous and dynamic process.

Steps (process) of communication

1. Idea or need (stimulus)

  • The process starts when the sender has an idea, information or feeling to share
  • Example: the nurse wants to tell a patient to remain fasting from midnight before surgery

2. Sender (source)

  • The person who starts the communication; his knowledge, attitude, culture and communication skills affect the message

3. Encoding

  • Converting the idea into a form that can be sent – words, symbols, gestures, pictures
  • The nurse chooses simple words in the patient's language: "Please do not eat or drink anything after 12 o'clock tonight"

4. Message

  • The actual content – verbal or non-verbal – that is sent
  • It should be clear, complete, concise, correct and courteous (the "5 Cs")

5. Channel (medium)

  • The route through which the message travels – face-to-face talk, telephone, written instructions, posters, gestures, electronic media
  • The nurse may give the instruction orally and also tie a "Nil by mouth" card on the bed

6. Receiver

  • The person for whom the message is meant
  • His attention, hearing, language, education, emotional state and culture affect how he receives it

7. Decoding

  • The receiver interprets the message and gives it meaning
  • If the patient understands "12 o'clock" as noon instead of midnight, the message has been decoded wrongly

8. Feedback

  • The receiver's response, which shows whether the message has been understood
  • The nurse asks: "Can you tell me until when you can eat?" – the patient's answer confirms understanding
  • Feedback makes communication a two-way process

9. Environment (context)

  • The physical and emotional setting – privacy, noise, lighting, time and relationship between the persons

10. Noise (barriers)

  • Anything that disturbs the message at any stage – physical noise, pain, anxiety, language differences, jargon

Models of communication

  • Linear model – one-way: sender → message → receiver
  • Interactive (circular) model – includes feedback; both persons send and receive at the same time

Nursing importance

  • Always check understanding through feedback, especially for medicine instructions, diet and preparation for procedures

Conclusion Communication is a continuous two-way process of encoding, sending, receiving, decoding and feedback, influenced by the environment and noise; effective communication is the basis of safe nursing care.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Describe the phases of the nurse–patient (helping) relationship.
answer_html:
Introduction The nurse–patient relationship is a therapeutic, helping relationship in which the nurse uses her knowledge, skills and personality to help the patient meet his health needs. It is goal-directed, patient-centred, time-limited and professional. It develops through four phases.

Purposes of the helping relationship

  • To build trust and cooperation
  • To understand the patient's needs and problems
  • To help the patient cope with illness and make decisions
  • To promote independence and recovery

1. Pre-interaction phase

  • Begins before the nurse meets the patient
  • The nurse collects information from records, the doctor and the family
  • She examines her own feelings, fears and prejudices (e.g. about caring for a patient with HIV or a suicide attempt)
  • She plans the first meeting – time, place and privacy

2. Orientation (introductory) phase

  • The nurse and patient meet and get to know each other
  • The nurse introduces herself, explains her role and the purpose of the interaction
  • Trust and rapport are built; confidentiality is explained
  • The patient's problems and needs are identified
  • A contract is made – time, place, frequency and goals of meetings, and the expected date of ending
  • The patient may test the nurse; consistency and honesty are important

3. Working phase

  • The longest and most productive phase
  • The patient explores his feelings and problems; the nurse uses therapeutic communication
  • Nursing care is given, the patient is taught, and coping skills are developed
  • The nurse encourages independence and self-care
  • Problems such as resistance, dependence or transference may arise and are handled patiently

4. Termination (resolution) phase

  • The relationship is brought to a planned end – at discharge or transfer
  • The nurse and patient review progress and goals achieved
  • Feelings about ending (sadness, anxiety) are discussed
  • The patient is prepared for self-care at home and referred to other services if needed
  • The nurse avoids sudden endings and does not continue a social relationship

Peplau's phases

  • Hildegard Peplau described the phases as orientation, identification, exploitation and resolution

Characteristics of a good helping relationship

  • Trust, respect, empathy, genuineness, acceptance, confidentiality and professional boundaries

Conclusion The nurse–patient relationship passes through pre-interaction, orientation, working and termination phases; at each phase the nurse builds trust, helps the patient solve problems and prepares him for independence.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain how the nurse communicates effectively with vulnerable groups.
answer_html:
Introduction Vulnerable groups are people who have special difficulty in expressing their needs or who are at greater risk of being misunderstood – children, women, the elderly, and physically and mentally challenged persons. The nurse must adapt her communication to their needs.

1. Children

  • Use simple words suited to the child's age; get down to the child's eye level
  • Use play, toys, pictures and dolls to explain procedures
  • Be honest – tell the child when something will hurt
  • Involve parents; let the child hold a favourite toy
  • Praise cooperation; never threaten
  • With adolescents – respect privacy, speak without judging, maintain confidentiality

2. Women

  • Ensure privacy and a female attendant during examinations
  • Be sensitive to cultural modesty and to women who may hesitate to speak in front of family
  • Be alert to signs of domestic violence; talk to the woman alone
  • Give information so that she can make her own decisions

3. The elderly

  • Address them respectfully by name; do not talk down to them
  • Speak slowly and clearly, face them, reduce background noise
  • Check that spectacles and hearing aids are in place
  • Give one instruction at a time; repeat and give written instructions in large print
  • Allow extra time to respond; listen to their stories (reminiscence)

4. Hearing-impaired persons

  • Get their attention before speaking; face the person so that he can lip-read
  • Use gestures, writing, pictures and sign language interpreters

5. Visually impaired persons

  • Announce yourself when entering and leaving; describe the surroundings
  • Explain before touching; use touch and voice to guide

6. Persons with speech problems (aphasia)

  • Ask yes/no questions; use picture boards and writing pads; be patient

7. Mentally challenged persons and persons with mental illness

  • Use short, simple, concrete sentences; be calm, consistent and patient
  • Do not argue with delusions; focus on reality
  • Use positive reinforcement; involve caregivers

8. Unconscious patients

  • Talk to them and explain every procedure – hearing may still be present

General principles

  • Empathy, respect, patience, privacy, feedback to check understanding, and the use of interpreters when there is a language barrier

Conclusion Effective communication with vulnerable groups needs patience, simple language, suitable aids and respect for their dignity, so that their needs are understood and met.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define communication. Explain the process of communication, the barriers to effective communication and the role of communication in patient care. (2 + 4 + 4 + 5)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • The word comes from the Latin "communis", meaning common – communication creates a common understanding
  • Communication is the process of exchanging information, ideas, thoughts and feelings between two or more persons through verbal and non-verbal means
  • Keith Davis: communication is "the process of passing information and understanding from one person to another"
  • It is a two-way, continuous, dynamic process, and it is the foundation of the nurse–patient relationship

Types of communication

  • Verbal – spoken and written words
  • Non-verbal – facial expression, eye contact, gestures, posture, touch, tone of voice, appearance, silence; non-verbal messages are often more powerful than words
  • Formal and informal; upward, downward and horizontal (in an organisation)

(b) Process of communication (4 marks)

  1. Sender – has an idea or information to share; the nurse wants to teach a diabetic patient about insulin
  2. Encoding – the idea is converted into words, symbols or gestures that the receiver can understand – simple Marathi or Hindi words and a demonstration with the pen
  3. Message – the content; it should be clear, concise, complete, correct and courteous
  4. Channel – the medium: face-to-face talk, demonstration, leaflet, telephone, video
  5. Receiver – the person who receives the message – the patient and family
  6. Decoding – the receiver interprets the message based on his knowledge, language, culture and emotional state
  7. Feedback – the receiver's response; the nurse asks the patient to return-demonstrate the injection, confirming understanding
  8. Environment – privacy, quiet, comfortable setting and the relationship between the persons
  9. Noise – anything that disturbs the message at any point

Modes of communication

  • Face-to-face, written (records, notices), telephonic, electronic (email, electronic health records) and audio-visual

(c) Barriers to effective communication (4 marks)

1. Physical (environmental) barriers

  • Noise from equipment, crowded wards, poor lighting, lack of privacy, distance, interruptions, uncomfortable temperature

2. Physiological barriers

  • Pain, fatigue, hunger, fever, medicines (sedation), hearing or visual impairment, speech defects, unconsciousness

3. Psychological (emotional) barriers

  • Anxiety, fear, anger, depression, embarrassment, low self-esteem, preoccupation with worries, defensiveness

4. Language (semantic) barriers

  • Different languages or dialects; medical jargon ("NPO", "ambulate", "void"); words with different meanings; unclear messages

5. Socio-cultural barriers

  • Differences in culture, religion, education, gender, age and social status; beliefs about illness; women hesitating to speak to male staff

6. Attitudinal barriers

  • Prejudice, stereotypes, a superior or rude attitude, lack of interest, judgemental remarks

7. Organisational barriers

  • Heavy workload, shortage of staff, lack of time, rigid hierarchy, poor handover systems

8. Barriers related to the nurse's communication (non-therapeutic techniques)

  • False reassurance ("Don't worry, everything will be fine")
  • Giving advice or imposing own opinions
  • Changing the subject or ignoring the patient's feelings
  • Asking "why" questions that make the patient defensive
  • Judging, criticising, arguing, belittling feelings ("Everyone feels that way")
  • Interrupting, giving stereotyped answers, using closed questions only

9. Poor listening

  • Day-dreaming, thinking of one's reply, selective listening

10. Information overload

  • Too much information at once; the patient remembers little

Ways to overcome barriers

  • Provide privacy and a quiet environment
  • Relieve pain and discomfort before important conversations
  • Use the patient's language; avoid jargon; use an interpreter when needed
  • Use therapeutic techniques – active listening, open-ended questions, reflection, clarification, silence and summarising
  • Match non-verbal and verbal messages; maintain eye contact and an open posture
  • Respect cultural differences; be non-judgemental
  • Give information in small amounts; use pictures and written leaflets
  • Always seek feedback

Therapeutic techniques with examples

Technique Example
Open-ended question "How have you been feeling since the operation?"
Reflecting "You sound worried about going home."
Clarifying "When you say you feel 'bad', what do you mean?"
Restating "You are saying the pain is worse at night."
Silence sitting quietly with a crying patient
Offering self "I'll stay with you until your son arrives."
Giving information "The drip will stay for about two days."
Summarising "So today we discussed your diet and insulin timing."

Characteristics of effective communication (the 7 Cs)

  • Clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete and courteous
  • Timely, suited to the receiver's level, and consistent in words and body language

(d) Role of communication in patient care (5 marks)

1. Building the nurse–patient relationship

  • Communication builds trust and rapport; the patient feels safe to share problems

2. Assessment

  • A good interview and observation of non-verbal cues provide an accurate nursing history; e.g. a patient who says "I am fine" but grimaces may be in pain

3. Planning and giving care

  • The patient's preferences are understood and he participates in decisions; informed consent depends on clear communication

4. Reducing anxiety and fear

  • Explaining procedures, the hospital routine and what to expect reduces anxiety before surgery and investigations

5. Patient and family education

  • Teaching about medicines, diet, exercise, wound care and warning signs improves compliance and prevents readmission

6. Emotional support and counselling

  • Listening with empathy helps patients cope with diagnosis, disability, loss and dying

7. Team communication and patient safety

  • Clear handover (e.g. the SBAR format – situation, background, assessment, recommendation), accurate reporting of changes and correct documentation prevent errors
  • Reading back telephone orders prevents medication errors

8. Continuity of care

  • Records and reports pass information from shift to shift and from hospital to home

9. Advocacy

  • The nurse communicates the patient's needs and wishes to the doctor and team

10. Patient satisfaction and outcomes

  • Most patient complaints are due to poor communication; good communication improves satisfaction, cooperation and recovery

11. Professional and legal protection

  • Clear communication and documentation protect the nurse and the institution in legal matters

Conclusion Communication is a two-way process of exchanging information and feelings through a sender, message, channel, receiver and feedback. Physical, physiological, psychological, language, cultural and organisational barriers can block it, but therapeutic techniques overcome them. Effective communication is central to assessment, care, education, emotional support, teamwork and patient safety.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the therapeutic communication techniques with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Therapeutic communication is purposeful, patient-centred communication that helps the patient express feelings, understand his condition and cope with illness. Its techniques encourage the patient to talk and make him feel understood.

Techniques with examples

  1. Active listening – giving full attention with eye contact and nodding; posture summarised as SOLER – Sit squarely, Open posture, Lean forward, Eye contact, Relaxed
  2. Using open-ended questions (broad openings) – "How are you feeling today?" "What would you like to talk about?"
  3. Restating (paraphrasing) – Patient: "I can't sleep at night." Nurse: "You are having trouble sleeping?"
  4. Reflecting feelings – "You sound worried about the operation."
  5. Clarifying – "I'm not sure what you mean by feeling strange. Could you explain?"
  6. Focusing – "Let us talk more about the pain in your leg."
  7. Exploring – "Tell me more about what happened at home."
  8. Using silence – allowing the patient time to think and express feelings
  9. Offering self – "I will sit with you for a while."
  10. Giving information – "Your blood test report will come this evening."
  11. Giving recognition – "I see you walked to the bathroom by yourself today."
  12. Encouraging description of perceptions – "What do you hear when you feel frightened?"
  13. Summarising – "Today we talked about your diet and your medicines."
  14. Validating – checking that the nurse has understood correctly
  15. Therapeutic touch – holding the hand of a distressed patient, when culturally acceptable

Non-therapeutic responses to avoid

  • False reassurance – "Don't worry, everything will be fine"
  • Giving advice – "If I were you, I would…"
  • Judging – "That was a foolish thing to do"
  • "Why" questions that sound accusing; changing the subject; using medical jargon

Importance

  • Builds trust; reduces anxiety
  • Helps in assessment and patient teaching
  • Encourages cooperation and self-care

Example – techniques used together

  • Patient: "I don't think this treatment is working."
  • Nurse (reflecting): "You feel worried that you are not improving?"
  • Patient: "Yes, the pain is the same."
  • Nurse (clarifying and focusing): "Tell me more about the pain – where is it, and is it better or worse at any time?"
  • Nurse (giving information): "Let me inform the doctor; we can also try a change of position."

Conclusion Therapeutic communication uses techniques such as active listening, open-ended questions, restating, reflecting, clarifying, silence and summarising to help patients express themselves, while avoiding false reassurance, advice-giving and judgement.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the characteristics of a therapeutic nurse–patient relationship.
answer_html:
Introduction A therapeutic (helping) relationship is a professional, goal-directed relationship between the nurse and the patient, aimed at the patient's health and wellbeing (Hildegard Peplau). It passes through orientation, working and termination phases.

Characteristics

  1. Trust – built by being reliable, consistent and keeping promises
  2. Respect – addressing the patient by name, protecting privacy and dignity
  3. Empathy – understanding the patient's feelings from his point of view
  4. Genuineness – being honest and sincere
  5. Acceptance (unconditional positive regard) – non-judgemental attitude
  6. Confidentiality – information shared only with those who need to know
  7. Patient-centred and goal-directed – focus on the patient's needs, not the nurse's
  8. Professional boundaries – no personal or romantic relationships, no accepting gifts or money, limited self-disclosure; avoid both over-involvement and under-involvement
  9. Time-limited – has a definite beginning and end
  10. Mutual participation – the patient takes part in decisions about his care
  11. Self-awareness of the nurse – recognising one's own feelings, prejudices and limits
  12. Effective communication – therapeutic techniques and active listening

Social and therapeutic relationship compared

Social relationship Therapeutic relationship
for friendship and mutual pleasure to meet the patient's health needs
needs of both are met focus on the patient
no fixed goals or time limits goal-directed and time-limited
personal sharing on both sides professional boundaries

Problems that can arise

  • Transference – the patient transfers feelings about an important person (e.g. a parent) onto the nurse
  • Countertransference – the nurse's emotional reaction to the patient based on her own past experiences
  • Boundary violations and resistance by the patient
  • The nurse handles these through self-awareness, supervision and maintaining professional limits

Actions that build trust

  • Introduce yourself by name and explain your role
  • Be punctual and keep promises ("I will come back in ten minutes")
  • Be consistent in what you say and do
  • Respect the patient's privacy, culture and choices
  • Admit when you do not know something and find out

Phases in brief

  • Pre-orientation – the nurse prepares herself
  • Orientation – getting to know each other, setting goals
  • Working – solving problems, teaching, supporting
  • Termination – reviewing progress and ending the relationship

Conclusion A therapeutic relationship is a trusting, respectful, empathetic, genuine, confidential, patient-centred and goal-directed relationship with clear professional boundaries; it is the foundation of effective nursing care.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: List the types of client records.
answer_html:
Introduction A client (patient) record is a written or electronic account of the patient's health, treatment and care. It is a legal document.

Types of client records

  1. Admission record (face sheet) – identification and admission details
  2. History and physical examination sheet
  3. Doctor's order sheet and progress notes
  4. Nursing notes (nurse's record)
  5. Nursing care plan / Kardex
  6. Graphic chart – temperature, pulse, respiration and BP
  7. Intake–output chart
  8. Medication administration record (MAR)
  9. Investigation reports – laboratory, X-ray, ECG
  10. Consent forms, operation and anaesthesia records
  11. Discharge summary, referral and transfer forms

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Name the methods (systems) of documentation.
answer_html:
Introduction Hospitals use different systems to record patient information.

Methods of documentation

  1. Narrative charting – a story-like, time-ordered description of care
  2. Source-oriented records – each discipline (doctors, nurses, lab) has a separate section
  3. Problem-oriented medical record (POMR) – organised around the patient's problems; notes written in SOAP format (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan)
  4. PIE charting – Problem, Intervention, Evaluation
  5. Focus charting (DAR) – Data, Action, Response
  6. Charting by exception – only abnormal findings are written in detail
  7. Flow sheets and checklists – vital signs, intake–output, diabetic charts
  8. Kardex – a quick-reference card file of each patient's care
  9. Electronic (computerised) health records

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: What is an incident report?
answer_html:
Definition An incident report is a written record of any unusual event (accident or error) that is not consistent with the routine care of a patient or the operation of the institution.

Examples of incidents

  • Patient falls, medication errors, burns, needle-stick injury, equipment failure, wrong patient or wrong site procedures, patient absconding, violence

Points to remember

  1. Write it as soon as possible (usually within 24 hours)
  2. Describe facts objectively – what happened, time, place, persons involved, action taken
  3. Do not blame anyone or give opinions
  4. It is sent to the nursing superintendent / quality department, not kept in the patient's chart
  5. Purpose: patient safety and quality improvement, not punishment

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the purposes of recording and reporting.
answer_html:
Introduction A record is a written or electronic account of a patient's health status, the care given and the patient's response. A report is an oral or written exchange of information among caregivers (e.g. change-of-shift report). Accurate records and reports are essential for safe, continuous and legally sound care.

Purposes of recording and reporting

1. Communication

  • Members of the health team communicate through records; the doctor, nurse, physiotherapist and dietitian all know what has been done and what is planned

2. Continuity of care

  • Information passes from shift to shift, from unit to unit and from hospital to home, so that care is not interrupted

3. Planning and evaluating care

  • Assessment data in records help in making nursing diagnoses and care plans and in evaluating the patient's progress

4. Legal documentation

  • Records are legal evidence of the care given; in court cases and consumer complaints, "not recorded means not done"
  • They protect the patient, the nurse, the doctor and the hospital

5. Quality assurance and audit

  • Records are reviewed to check the quality of care and compliance with standards (e.g. NABH accreditation)

6. Education

  • Students learn about diseases, treatments and nursing care from records and case studies

7. Research

  • Records provide data for clinical and nursing research

8. Statistics and planning

  • Data on admissions, diseases, births and deaths help hospital and government planning

9. Financial and insurance purposes

  • Records support billing, insurance claims (e.g. Ayushman Bharat – PM-JAY) and reimbursement

10. History for future reference

  • When the patient comes again, past records help diagnosis and treatment (allergies, previous surgeries)

11. Medico-legal and administrative purposes

  • Birth and death certificates, medico-legal cases (MLC), notification of communicable diseases

12. Evaluation of staff performance

  • Records reflect the quality of work of nurses and other staff

Purposes of reporting (in brief)

  • To inform the next shift or the doctor about the patient's condition, changes and pending work
  • To report emergencies and unusual events promptly so that action can be taken

Conclusion Recording and reporting serve communication, continuity of care, planning, legal protection, quality assurance, education, research, statistics and finance; good records reflect good nursing care.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the principles (guidelines) of documentation.
answer_html:
Introduction Documentation is the act of recording patient information in a permanent record. Because records are legal documents and the basis of communication, nurses must follow certain principles so that the record is accurate, complete and legally valid.

Principles of good documentation

1. Accuracy (factual and objective)

  • Write facts, not opinions – "Patient vomited 200 ml of greenish fluid at 10:30 a.m." instead of "Patient was sick"
  • Record the patient's own words in quotation marks ("I feel giddy")
  • Use correct measurements

2. Completeness

  • Include all relevant information – assessment, care given, response, teaching, refusals and omissions
  • An incomplete record suggests incomplete care

3. Conciseness

  • Brief and to the point; avoid unnecessary words

4. Timeliness (current)

  • Record immediately after giving care; never record in advance
  • Write the date and time of every entry (24-hour clock preferred)

5. Organisation

  • Record events in logical, chronological order

6. Legibility and permanence

  • Write clearly in permanent blue or black ink; never use pencil

7. Correct identification

  • The patient's name, age, registration (IP) number and ward on every page

8. Signature

  • Sign every entry with full name and designation; do not sign for others or let others sign for you

9. Use of approved abbreviations and terminology only

  • Use only abbreviations approved by the hospital; avoid error-prone ones (e.g. "U" for units)

10. Correct way of correcting errors

  • Do not erase, overwrite, scratch out or use correction fluid
  • Draw a single line through the wrong entry so that it remains readable, write "mistaken entry", put your initials and the date, and write the correct entry

11. No blank spaces

  • Draw a line through empty spaces so that nothing can be added later

12. Confidentiality

  • Records must be kept safely; information is shared only with authorised persons
  • Do not take records out of the ward or photograph them; protect computer passwords

13. Verbal and telephone orders

  • Write the order, read it back to confirm, and have it signed by the doctor within the time set by hospital policy (usually 24 hours)

14. Legal points (don'ts)

  • Do not chart actions done by others as your own; do not write criticism of colleagues; do not write "incident report filed" in the chart

Conclusion Good documentation is accurate, complete, concise, timely, legible, signed, confidential and correctly corrected; following these principles protects patients and nurses and ensures continuity of care.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Describe the change-of-shift report, transfer report and incident report.
answer_html:
Introduction Reporting is the oral or written exchange of information among health team members. Reports keep everyone informed about the patient's condition and ensure continuity and safety of care.

A. Change-of-shift (handover) report Meaning: the report given by the nurse going off duty to the nurse coming on duty.

Methods

  • Oral – face-to-face in the nurses' station
  • Bedside handover – at the patient's bedside; the patient can participate and the incoming nurse sees the patient
  • Written – ward report book
  • Recorded (audio) in some hospitals

Contents

  • Patient's name, age, bed number, diagnosis, surgery or procedure done
  • Current condition – vital signs, level of consciousness, pain, intake–output, drains, IV lines
  • Treatments and medicines given and due, investigations pending
  • New admissions, transfers, discharges, deaths, critically ill patients
  • Patients' and families' concerns

Format: SBAR – Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation (also ISBAR with "Identify")

Guidelines

  • Be brief, factual and organised; avoid gossip and personal opinions
  • Ensure privacy – do not discuss in front of other patients

B. Transfer report Meaning: given when a patient is moved from one unit to another (e.g. ICU to ward) or to another hospital.

Contents

  • Identification, diagnosis, reason for transfer
  • Present condition, recent vital signs, allergies
  • Treatment given, medicines and their last dose times, IV fluids
  • Investigations done and pending, special precautions (isolation, fall risk)
  • Family informed, patient's belongings and records sent

C. Incident report Meaning: a written report of any unexpected event that has caused or could cause harm to a patient, visitor or staff member.

Examples: patient fall, medication error, needle-stick injury, burns, equipment failure, absconding, violence.

Guidelines

  • Report immediately to the in-charge and complete the form within 24 hours
  • Describe what happened objectively – time, place, people involved, condition of the patient, actions taken
  • Do not blame, guess or admit guilt
  • Inform the doctor and record the patient's condition and care in the nursing notes (without mentioning the incident report itself)
  • Used for analysis and quality improvement

Other reports: 24-hour census report, medico-legal reports, birth and death reports, notification of communicable diseases.

Conclusion Change-of-shift, transfer and incident reports keep the health team informed, ensure continuity of care and improve patient safety; they must be accurate, brief, objective and timely.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define records and reports. Explain the types of records, the methods of documentation and the legal guidelines for documentation. (2 + 4 + 4 + 5)
answer_html:
(a) Definitions (2 marks)

  • Record: a permanent written or electronic communication that documents information about a patient's health status, the care given and the patient's response. It is a legal document
  • Report: an oral or written exchange of information among caregivers about the patient's condition, care and plans – e.g. change-of-shift report, incident report
  • Documentation: the process of making a written or electronic record of everything relevant to the patient's care
  • Confidentiality: information in records is private and is shared only with those directly involved in the patient's care

(b) Types of records (4 marks)

1. Patient (clinical) records

  • Admission record (face sheet) – name, age, sex, address, IP number, date of admission, diagnosis, consultant, next of kin
  • History sheet and physical examination
  • Doctor's order sheet – medicines, investigations, treatments
  • Progress notes – the doctor's daily notes
  • Nursing notes – observations, care given and the patient's response
  • Nursing care plan and Kardex
  • Graphic chart (TPR chart) – temperature, pulse, respiration and BP
  • Intake–output chart
  • Medication administration record
  • Special charts – diabetic chart, neuro-observation chart (Glasgow Coma Scale), fluid balance chart, partograph, pain chart, pressure ulcer risk chart
  • Investigation reports – laboratory, X-ray, ECG, ultrasound
  • Consent forms – for surgery, anaesthesia, blood transfusion, special procedures
  • Operation notes, anaesthesia record, post-operative notes
  • Discharge summary, referral and transfer forms, death summary

2. Ward (administrative) records

  • Admission and discharge register, census register
  • Narcotic (dangerous drugs) register, drug and stock registers
  • Indent book, inventory register, equipment register, linen register
  • Diet register, duty roster and attendance register
  • Ward report book, incident register, medico-legal case (MLC) register, birth and death registers

3. Community health records

  • Family folders, eligible couple register, antenatal and immunisation registers, birth and death registers, RCH registers

4. Educational records

  • Students' attendance, clinical experience records, evaluation records

(c) Methods (systems) of documentation (4 marks)

1. Narrative charting

  • The traditional method – care is described in a story-like, chronological manner
  • Merit: simple, flexible; limitation: lengthy, repetitive, time-consuming, important points may be missed

2. Source-oriented records

  • Each discipline writes in its own section – doctors' notes, nurses' notes, lab reports
  • Limitation: information about one problem is scattered across sections

3. Problem-oriented medical record (POMR)

  • Introduced by Lawrence Weed; organised around the patient's problems
  • Parts: database (history, examination, tests), problem list, plan of care, progress notes
  • Progress notes are written in the SOAP format:
    • S – Subjective data: what the patient says ("I have pain in my stomach")
    • O – Objective data: what the nurse observes or measures (BP 150/90 mmHg, guarding of abdomen)
    • A – Assessment: conclusion or nursing diagnosis (acute pain)
    • P – Plan: actions to be taken
  • Extended forms: SOAPIE and SOAPIER (Intervention, Evaluation, Revision)

4. PIE charting

  • P – Problem, I – Intervention, E – Evaluation; problems are numbered and followed in each shift

5. Focus charting (DAR)

  • Each entry focuses on a patient concern or event
  • D – Data, A – Action, R – Response

6. Charting by exception (CBE)

  • Standards of normal findings are pre-defined; only abnormal or significant findings are written in detail
  • Saves time but needs clear standards

7. Flow sheets and checklists

  • Graphic records for repeated observations – vital signs, intake–output, blood sugar, turning charts

8. Kardex

  • A card file with a quick summary of each patient's orders and care; used during handover

9. Computerised / electronic health records (EHR)

  • Records kept on computers – legible, quick to retrieve, can be shared among departments
  • Need password protection and data security; never share passwords

10. Case management and critical pathways

  • A multidisciplinary plan with expected outcomes for each day of hospital stay; variations are documented

(d) Legal guidelines for documentation – do's and don'ts (5 marks)

Do's

  1. Check the patient's identity – name and IP number on every page
  2. Write date and time for every entry; use the 24-hour clock
  3. Record promptly after giving care, in chronological order
  4. Write legibly in permanent blue or black ink
  5. Record facts objectively – what you see, hear, measure and do
  6. Use the patient's own words in quotes for subjective data
  7. Record every assessment, intervention, medication, teaching and the patient's response
  8. Record refusal of treatment or medicines and the reason, and inform the doctor
  9. Record changes in condition and the action taken, including the time the doctor was informed and his response
  10. Record verbal and telephone orders, read them back and get them countersigned within the time set by policy
  11. Use only approved abbreviations
  12. Sign every entry with name and designation
  13. Correct errors by drawing a single line, writing "mistaken entry", initials, date and time
  14. Draw lines through blank spaces
  15. Maintain confidentiality and keep records in a safe place

Don'ts

  1. Do not erase, overwrite, scratch, tear pages or use correction fluid
  2. Do not record in advance or record for someone else
  3. Do not use pencil or vague words such as "good", "normal", "fair", "slept well" without facts
  4. Do not write personal opinions, criticism of colleagues or blame
  5. Do not leave blank lines or spaces between entries
  6. Do not mention "incident report filed" in the patient's record
  7. Do not give records to unauthorised persons, take them home or photograph them
  8. Do not alter records after an incident or legal notice – this is a serious offence

Legal importance

  • In court, records are the main evidence; if care is not recorded, it is presumed not done
  • Records are kept for the period fixed by law and hospital policy; medico-legal records are preserved longer

Conclusion Records are permanent legal accounts of patient care and reports are exchanges of information among caregivers. Patient, ward, community and educational records are maintained by narrative, POMR (SOAP), PIE, focus (DAR), charting by exception and electronic methods. Following the legal do's and don'ts makes documentation accurate, complete and legally safe.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the confidentiality of patient records and the responsibilities of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Confidentiality is the duty to keep information about patients private and to share it only with authorised persons involved in their care or as required by law. It is an ethical principle, a legal duty and the basis of the patient's trust.

1. Importance

  • Builds trust – patients share full information only when they feel safe
  • Protects dignity and prevents stigma and discrimination (e.g. HIV, mental illness, termination of pregnancy)
  • It is a legal requirement

2. Legal and ethical basis

  • INC Code of Ethics – the nurse respects and maintains confidentiality
  • Right to privacy is a fundamental right (Supreme Court, 2017)
  • HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017 – protects confidentiality of HIV status
  • Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 – right to confidentiality
  • MTP Act – the identity of a woman whose pregnancy is terminated must not be revealed
  • PCPNDT Act – the sex of the fetus must not be disclosed
  • Information Technology Act, 2000 and Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 – protect electronic personal data

3. Exceptions – when information may be disclosed

  • With the patient's written consent
  • To other members of the health team for care
  • When required by law – court orders, medico-legal cases, notifiable diseases, birth and death registration
  • To protect others from serious harm, following legal procedures
  • In public health emergencies

4. Responsibilities of the nurse

  • Keep records in a safe place; do not leave case files open at the nursing station
  • Do not take records out of the ward without permission
  • Do not discuss patients in lifts, canteens or other public places, or on social media
  • Never photograph patients or records with a personal phone
  • Share information only with authorised persons; confirm the caller's identity before giving information on the telephone
  • Give information to relatives only with the patient's permission (except in emergencies or for minors, as per policy)
  • Protect passwords; log out of computers; do not share login details
  • Dispose of documents with patient details safely (shredding)
  • Students must remove identifying details from case studies

5. Consequences of a breach

  • Loss of trust, harm to the patient, legal action for damages, and disciplinary action by the nursing council

Conclusion Confidentiality protects the patient's privacy, dignity and trust and is required by ethics and law; the nurse shares information only with authorised persons and guards both paper and electronic records carefully.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain electronic health records – their advantages, disadvantages and the nurse's responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction An electronic health record (EHR) is a digital record of a patient's health information – history, diagnoses, medicines, allergies, investigation reports, images and notes – that is created, stored and shared electronically. An electronic medical record (EMR) usually refers to the record within one hospital, while an EHR can be shared across facilities. In India, the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) links records through the ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) number.

1. Components

  • Patient details and history
  • Doctor's orders entered directly into the computer
  • Electronic medication administration record, often with barcode scanning
  • Laboratory and radiology results
  • Nursing documentation – assessments, vital signs flow sheets, care plans, notes
  • Alerts for allergies and drug interactions; billing

2. Advantages

  • Legible, complete and well organised – no illegible handwriting
  • Quick access from anywhere in the hospital; no lost files
  • Fewer medication errors through alerts and barcode checks
  • Saves time and paper; avoids repeated tests
  • Continuity of care across departments and hospitals; supports telemedicine
  • Audit trail – records who accessed or changed the record and when
  • Data for research, quality improvement and planning

3. Disadvantages and challenges

  • High cost of hardware, software and maintenance
  • Need for training; resistance to change
  • Power and network failures
  • Privacy and cyber-security risks – hacking and data theft
  • Copy-paste errors and "alert fatigue"
  • Less eye contact with patients if the nurse focuses on the screen
  • Different systems may not communicate with each other

4. Responsibilities of the nurse

  • Use only your own login; protect your password; log off after use
  • Access only the records needed for the patient's care
  • Document accurately and in real time; avoid copying old notes
  • Correct errors as per policy – never delete entries
  • Maintain confidentiality; do not display screens to unauthorised persons
  • Follow downtime (paper backup) procedures during system failure
  • Report suspected data breaches
  • Keep updated through training

5. Digital health initiatives in India

  • Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission – ABHA number, health facility and health professional registries
  • e-Sanjeevani – national telemedicine service
  • Nikshay – online TB patient management
  • U-WIN – digital immunisation records
  • Hospital information systems in government and private hospitals

Conclusion Electronic health records make documentation legible, accessible and safer and support continuity of care, but bring challenges of cost, training and data security; nurses must use them accurately and protect patient confidentiality.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Convert 99.8 °F to °C.
answer_html:
Formula

  • °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9

Calculation

  • °C = (99.8 − 32) × 5/9
  • = 67.8 × 5/9
  • = 339 ÷ 9
  • = 37.7 °C (37.66 rounded off)

Answer: 99.8 °F = 37.7 °C – this is a mild rise above the normal oral temperature of 37 °C (98.6 °F).

Reverse formula: °F = (°C × 9/5) + 32.

  • Example: 38 °C = (38 × 9/5) + 32 = 68.4 + 32 = 100.4 °F

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Enumerate the methods of local heat application.
answer_html:
Introduction Heat may be applied locally in dry or moist form. Moist heat penetrates deeper and acts faster, but it can burn more easily.

A. Dry heat

  1. Hot water bottle (bag)
  2. Electric heating pad
  3. Aquathermia (K-pad) – circulating warm water pad
  4. Chemical hot packs
  5. Infrared lamp and heat cradle
  6. Diathermy (short-wave, by physiotherapists)

B. Moist heat

  1. Hot fomentation and hot compress
  2. Hot soaks (soaking a part in warm solution)
  3. Sitz bath (for the perineum)
  4. Steam inhalation
  5. Poultice
  6. Paraffin wax bath

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define pulse deficit and pulse pressure.
answer_html:
Pulse deficit

  • The difference between the apical heart rate and the radial pulse rate counted at the same time for one full minute
  • It is measured by two nurses – one counts the apical beat with a stethoscope and the other counts the radial pulse, starting together
  • Example: apical rate 110/min, radial 90/min → pulse deficit = 20 beats/min
  • Seen in atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias, when some heartbeats are too weak to reach the wrist

Pulse pressure

  • The difference between systolic and diastolic blood pressure
  • Example: BP 120/80 mmHg → pulse pressure = 40 mmHg (normal about 30–50 mmHg)
  • Wide pulse pressure – aortic regurgitation, arteriosclerosis, raised intracranial pressure; narrow – shock, cardiac tamponade, aortic stenosis

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Mention the normal values of vital signs in an adult.
answer_html:
Introduction Vital signs are measurements of the body's most basic functions and indicate the patient's general health.

Normal adult values

  1. Temperature – oral 37 °C (98.6 °F); normal range about 36.5–37.5 °C; rectal about 0.5 °C higher, axillary about 0.5 °C lower
  2. Pulse – 60–100 beats per minute, regular
  3. Respiration – 12–20 breaths per minute (often 16–20)
  4. Blood pressure – about 120/80 mmHg; less than 120/80 is normal
  5. Oxygen saturation (SpO2) – 95–100%
  6. Pain – often called the "fifth vital sign"; assessed on a scale of 0–10

Newborn: pulse 120–160/min, respiration 30–60/min.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the sites and characteristics of the pulse.

diagram.caption: Common pulse sites of the body

answer_html:
Introduction The pulse is the wave of blood created by contraction of the left ventricle, felt as a throbbing over an artery that lies near the surface and over a bone. It reflects the heart rate, rhythm and the condition of the arteries. Normal adult pulse is 60–100 beats per minute.

A. Sites of the pulse

  1. Temporal – over the temporal bone, in front of the ear; used in children
  2. Carotid – at the side of the neck, between the trachea and the sternocleidomastoid muscle; used in cardiac arrest and CPR (never press both sides together)
  3. Apical – at the apex of the heart, in the left 5th intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line, heard with a stethoscope; used for infants, irregular pulse and before giving digoxin
  4. Brachial – in the antecubital fossa, medial to the biceps tendon; used for BP measurement and for CPR in infants
  5. Radial – on the thumb side of the wrist; the most common site
  6. Ulnar – on the little-finger side of the wrist
  7. Femoral – in the groin, below the inguinal ligament; used in shock and cardiac arrest
  8. Popliteal – behind the knee
  9. Posterior tibial – behind the medial malleolus
  10. Dorsalis pedis – on the top of the foot; checks circulation to the feet (after leg surgery, in diabetics)

B. Characteristics of the pulse

1. Rate

  • Number of beats per minute
  • Tachycardia – above 100/min (fever, exercise, anxiety, shock, haemorrhage)
  • Bradycardia – below 60/min (athletes, sleep, raised intracranial pressure, heart block, digoxin toxicity)

2. Rhythm

  • The pattern of beats and the intervals between them – regular or irregular (arrhythmia)
  • An irregular pulse is counted for a full minute, and the apical rate is checked

3. Volume (amplitude, strength)

  • The force of blood felt with each beat
  • Bounding (full) – fever, hyperthyroidism, exercise
  • Weak, thready – shock, haemorrhage, heart failure

4. Tension

  • The force needed to obliterate the pulse; high in hypertension

5. Condition of the arterial wall

  • Normally soft and elastic; feels hard and cord-like in arteriosclerosis (elderly)

6. Equality

  • Pulses on both sides should be equal; inequality suggests arterial obstruction

Factors affecting the pulse: age, sex, exercise, emotions, fever, pain, haemorrhage, posture, drugs and disease.

Nursing points

  • Count with the pads of the index and middle fingers, never the thumb (the nurse's own pulse is felt in the thumb)
  • Patient should be at rest for 5 minutes; record rate, rhythm and volume

Conclusion The pulse can be felt at many superficial arteries, the radial being the most common; its rate, rhythm, volume, tension, arterial wall and equality give valuable information about the heart and circulation.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Describe the alterations in respiration.
answer_html:
Introduction Respiration is the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the atmosphere and the body cells. It includes ventilation (movement of air in and out of the lungs), diffusion in the alveoli and perfusion of the tissues. It is controlled by the respiratory centre in the medulla and pons. Normal adult rate is 12–20 breaths per minute, regular, quiet and effortless. The pulse–respiration ratio is about 4:1.

A. Alterations in rate

  1. Tachypnoea – rate above 20/min; fever, anxiety, pain, pneumonia, asthma, anaemia
  2. Bradypnoea – rate below 12/min; opioid (morphine) overdose, raised intracranial pressure, hypothermia
  3. Apnoea – temporary absence of breathing; sleep apnoea, cardiac arrest

B. Alterations in depth

  1. Hyperpnoea – increased depth; exercise, diabetic ketoacidosis
  2. Hypoventilation – shallow, slow breathing; drugs, anaesthesia, obesity → CO2 retention
  3. Hyperventilation – increased rate and depth; anxiety, panic, fever → loss of CO2, tingling and dizziness

C. Alterations in rhythm (abnormal breathing patterns)

  1. Cheyne–Stokes respiration – breathing gradually increases in depth, then decreases, followed by a period of apnoea, in a regular cycle; seen in heart failure, brain damage, and in dying patients
  2. Kussmaul's respiration – deep, rapid, laboured breathing; seen in diabetic ketoacidosis and renal failure (metabolic acidosis)
  3. Biot's respiration – irregular shallow breaths with irregular periods of apnoea; seen in brain injury and meningitis

D. Alterations in ease of breathing

  1. Dyspnoea – difficult, laboured breathing with use of accessory muscles, nasal flaring
  2. Orthopnoea – the patient can breathe comfortably only when sitting upright; seen in heart failure
  3. Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea – sudden breathlessness waking the patient at night (left heart failure)

E. Abnormal breath sounds

  1. Stridor – harsh, high-pitched sound on inspiration; upper airway obstruction (croup, foreign body)
  2. Wheeze – musical, whistling sound; asthma, COPD
  3. Stertorous breathing – snoring sound; unconscious patients, airway partly blocked by the tongue
  4. Crackles (rales) and rhonchi – heard with a stethoscope in pneumonia, pulmonary oedema and bronchitis
  5. Sighing – frequent deep breaths with a long expiration; anxiety

F. Related alterations

  • Cyanosis – bluish colour of lips and nails due to lack of oxygen
  • Low SpO2 (below 90–92%) – hypoxaemia

Nursing points

  • Count respiration without the patient's knowledge (while appearing to count the pulse), for a full minute
  • Observe rate, depth, rhythm, effort, sounds, chest movement, colour and SpO2
  • Report abnormal patterns immediately; position the patient upright, give oxygen as ordered

Conclusion Respiration may be altered in rate, depth, rhythm, ease and sounds; recognising patterns such as Cheyne–Stokes, Kussmaul's and orthopnoea helps the nurse detect serious conditions early.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the physiological effects of heat and cold applications and their contraindications.
answer_html:
Introduction Local application of heat and cold is a common nursing measure to relieve pain, reduce swelling, control temperature and promote healing. The nurse must know their effects, because wrong use can cause burns, frostbite or tissue damage.

A. Physiological effects of heat

  1. Vasodilation – increases blood flow to the part
  2. Increased tissue metabolism and oxygen supply
  3. Reduced blood viscosity and increased capillary permeability
  4. Muscle relaxation – relieves spasm and stiffness
  5. Pain relief – sedative effect on nerve endings
  6. Promotes suppuration – localises infection and helps pus formation
  7. Promotes healing by bringing nutrients and white blood cells

Uses of heat: muscle spasm, backache, joint stiffness, arthritis, abscess, thrombophlebitis, retention of urine (to promote voiding), menstrual cramps.

B. Physiological effects of cold

  1. Vasoconstriction – reduces blood flow
  2. Reduces oedema and inflammation
  3. Local anaesthetic effect – numbs nerve endings, reduces pain
  4. Reduces bleeding – vasoconstriction and increased blood viscosity help clotting
  5. Reduces metabolism and oxygen need of tissues
  6. Reduces body temperature (in fever) and muscle spasm

Uses of cold: sprains and injuries in the first 24–48 hours, epistaxis and minor bleeding, high fever (tepid sponging), tooth extraction, haemorrhoids, insect stings, post-operative swelling.

C. Rebound phenomenon

  • Maximum effect of heat or cold is reached in about 20–30 minutes; beyond this, the opposite effect occurs (heat causes vasoconstriction, cold causes vasodilation)
  • Therefore applications are limited to 15–30 minutes at a time

D. Contraindications of heat

  • First 24 hours after injury (increases swelling and bleeding)
  • Active bleeding, non-inflammatory oedema
  • Acute inflammation of unknown cause, e.g. abdominal pain that may be appendicitis (heat may cause rupture)
  • Over a malignant tumour, the testes, the abdomen of a pregnant woman
  • Impaired sensation (diabetic neuropathy, paralysis), unconscious patients, the very young and the elderly
  • Over metal implants (for diathermy)
  • Skin disorders with redness or blisters

E. Contraindications of cold

  • Open wounds (delays healing)
  • Impaired circulation – peripheral vascular disease, Raynaud's disease, diabetes
  • Allergy or hypersensitivity to cold
  • Shivering patients
  • Infants, the elderly and cardiac patients (vasoconstriction increases workload)

F. Nursing precautions

  • Check the temperature of the application (hot water bag about 46–52 °C for adults; lower for children and the elderly)
  • Cover hot water bags and ice bags with a cloth; never apply directly to skin
  • Inspect the skin every 5–10 minutes; stop if there is redness, pain, blistering, pallor or numbness
  • Record the time, method, duration and the patient's response

Conclusion Heat dilates vessels, relaxes muscles and promotes healing, while cold constricts vessels, reduces swelling, bleeding and pain; both must be used for limited periods with careful observation and avoided where contraindicated.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the types of fever and the nursing management of a patient with fever.
answer_html:
Introduction Fever (pyrexia) is an elevation of body temperature above the normal range (above about 37.5 °C oral) due to resetting of the hypothalamic thermostat by pyrogens – substances released by bacteria, viruses or damaged tissues. Hyperpyrexia is a temperature above 41 °C (105.8 °F), which is dangerous.

A. Stages of fever

  1. Onset (chill / cold stage) – the body raises its temperature to the new set point; the patient shivers, feels cold, skin is pale and cool, there is goose flesh
  2. Course (plateau / hot stage) – temperature remains high; skin is warm and flushed, the patient feels thirsty, has headache, body ache, rapid pulse and respiration, loss of appetite, and may be restless or delirious; children may have febrile convulsions
  3. Defervescence (sweating / flush stage) – the fever subsides; the patient sweats and feels comfortable
    • Crisis – sudden fall to normal
    • Lysis – gradual fall over several days

B. Types of fever

  1. Continuous (sustained) fever – remains above normal with daily variation of less than 1 °C; e.g. typhoid, lobar pneumonia
  2. Remittent fever – fluctuates by more than 1 °C but does not touch normal; e.g. infective endocarditis
  3. Intermittent fever – fever is present for some hours and returns to normal for the rest of the day; e.g. malaria:
    • quotidian – every day
    • tertian – every 48 hours (P. vivax)
    • quartan – every 72 hours (P. malariae)
  4. Relapsing fever – periods of fever alternate with fever-free days; e.g. relapsing fever caused by Borrelia
  5. Pel–Ebstein fever – fever for several days alternating with normal periods; seen in Hodgkin's lymphoma
  6. Septic (hectic) fever – wide swings with chills and sweating; seen in septicaemia and abscesses

C. Nursing management

  1. Monitor temperature every 4 hours (more often if very high), pulse, respiration and BP; record on the TPR chart
  2. Rest in a cool, well-ventilated room; light, loose cotton clothing
  3. During chills – give a light blanket, but remove extra covers once the chill stops
  4. Fluids – encourage 2.5–3 litres a day (water, juice, ORS, soups) unless restricted; maintain an intake–output chart
  5. Tepid sponging if temperature is above about 39 °C (102 °F) – water at about 30 °C; never use ice-cold water or alcohol
  6. Antipyretics – give paracetamol as prescribed; recheck temperature after 30–60 minutes
  7. Diet – high-calorie, high-protein, easily digestible, small frequent meals
  8. Oral care – frequent mouth washes; apply glycerine to dry lips
  9. Skin care – change damp clothes and linen after sweating; sponge bath
  10. Safety – watch for delirium and febrile convulsions in children; side rails
  11. Investigations – collect blood for malaria, blood culture and other tests as ordered
  12. Health education – complete the course of treatment, prevent mosquito bites, safe water

Conclusion Fever passes through chill, plateau and defervescence stages and may be continuous, remittent, intermittent or relapsing; nursing care focuses on monitoring, cooling, fluids, rest, nutrition, comfort and safety.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define vital signs. Explain the sites of temperature measurement, the factors affecting body temperature and the alterations in body temperature. (2 + 4 + 4 + 5)

diagram.caption: Stages of fever on a temperature graph

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Vital signs (cardinal signs) are the measurements of the body's most basic functions – temperature, pulse, respiration and blood pressure; oxygen saturation and pain are often added
  • They are indicators of the patient's health status and reflect changes in the body before other signs appear
  • Body temperature is the balance between heat produced and heat lost by the body; normal oral temperature is about 37 °C (98.6 °F), with a range of 36.5–37.5 °C

When to check vital signs: on admission, according to hospital routine or doctor's order, before and after surgery and invasive procedures, before and after giving drugs that affect them (e.g. antihypertensives), whenever the patient's condition changes or the patient feels unwell.

Regulation of temperature (in brief)

  • The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat
  • Heat production: metabolism, muscle activity, shivering, thyroxine and adrenaline
  • Heat loss: radiation, conduction, convection and evaporation (sweating)
  • When too hot – vasodilation and sweating; when too cold – vasoconstriction and shivering

(b) Sites of temperature measurement (4 marks)

Site Normal Advantages Disadvantages / contraindications
Oral (under the tongue, in the sublingual pocket) 37 °C (98.6 °F) easy, accessible, comfortable not for infants, unconscious, confused or uncooperative patients, mouth breathers, after oral surgery, patients with convulsions; wait 15–30 minutes after hot or cold drinks or smoking
Axillary (armpit) about 0.5 °C lower than oral (36.5 °C) safe, non-invasive, used for newborns and children takes longer; less accurate; affected by sweating and environment
Rectal about 0.5 °C higher than oral (37.5 °C) most reliable of the traditional sites (close to core temperature) uncomfortable, embarrassing; not for patients with diarrhoea, rectal surgery, haemorrhoids, cardiac patients (vagal stimulation), newborns (risk of perforation)
Tympanic (ear canal, infrared) close to core temperature very quick (seconds), easy affected by ear wax, otitis; needs correct technique (pull the pinna up and back in adults)
Temporal artery (forehead scanner) close to core quick, non-invasive affected by sweating and environment

Other sites: groin, oesophageal, bladder and pulmonary artery catheters (core temperature in ICU).

Equipment: digital thermometers (replacing mercury thermometers, which are being phased out because of mercury toxicity), infrared tympanic and forehead thermometers, disposable chemical-dot thermometers.

Technique points

  • Explain the procedure; use a clean thermometer with a disposable cover
  • Leave in place for the recommended time or until the digital thermometer beeps
  • Clean the thermometer after use; record and report abnormal readings

(c) Factors affecting body temperature (4 marks)

  1. Age – newborns and infants have unstable temperature control and lose heat quickly; the elderly often have lower temperatures and may not develop fever even in serious infection
  2. Diurnal (circadian) variation – temperature is lowest in the early morning (about 2–6 a.m.) and highest in the late afternoon and evening (about 4–8 p.m.); variation up to about 1 °C
  3. Exercise – muscle activity raises temperature
  4. Hormones – in women, progesterone raises temperature by about 0.3–0.6 °C after ovulation; menopause causes hot flushes; thyroxine increases metabolism
  5. Stress and emotions – the sympathetic system and adrenaline increase heat production
  6. Environment – hot or cold climate, clothing, room temperature
  7. Food and drinks – hot or cold drinks and smoking alter oral readings; digestion increases heat production
  8. Basal metabolic rate – higher BMR raises temperature
  9. Infection and illness – pyrogens raise the set point (fever); head injury may damage the hypothalamus
  10. Drugs – antipyretics lower temperature; some anaesthetics cause malignant hyperthermia
  11. Sleep – temperature falls during sleep
  12. Starvation and dehydration – affect temperature regulation

(d) Alterations in body temperature (5 marks)

1. Fever (pyrexia)

  • A rise in temperature due to resetting of the hypothalamic set point by pyrogens (infection, tissue damage, inflammation)
  • Low-grade (up to 38 °C), moderate (38–39 °C), high (39–40 °C), hyperpyrexia (above 41 °C)
  • Stages: chill (onset), plateau (course) and defervescence (crisis or lysis)
  • Types: continuous, remittent, intermittent, relapsing

2. Hyperthermia

  • A rise in temperature without change in the set point, when heat production or heat gain is more than heat loss (hot environment, heavy exercise)
  • (a) Heat cramps – painful muscle spasms due to loss of salt in sweat; give rest in a cool place and oral salt–water or ORS
  • (b) Heat exhaustion – excessive sweating, weakness, giddiness, nausea, pale moist skin, rapid weak pulse, normal or slightly raised temperature; move to a cool place, lie down with legs raised, give ORS
  • (c) Heat stroke – a medical emergency; temperature above 40 °C, hot, dry, flushed skin (sweating may stop), confusion, convulsions and coma; cool rapidly – move to shade, remove clothing, sponge with cool water and fan, ice packs to the neck, axillae and groin, and transfer to hospital
  • (d) Malignant hyperthermia – a rare inherited reaction to certain anaesthetics

3. Hypothermia

  • Core temperature below 35 °C (95 °F)
  • Causes: exposure to cold, cold water immersion, newborns (especially low-birth-weight babies), the elderly, malnutrition, alcohol intoxication, prolonged surgery
  • Stages: mild (32–35 °C) – shivering, cold pale skin, numbness; moderate (28–32 °C) – shivering stops, confusion, slow pulse and respiration; severe (below 28 °C) – unconsciousness, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest
  • Management: move to a warm place, remove wet clothing, cover with dry blankets (including the head), warm drinks if conscious, warm IV fluids in hospital, skin-to-skin contact (kangaroo mother care) for newborns; rewarm gradually
  • Frostbite – freezing of tissues, usually of fingers, toes, ears and nose, in very cold climates

Nursing responsibilities

  • Measure temperature accurately at the correct site and time
  • Record on the TPR chart and report abnormal values
  • Give cooling or warming measures, fluids and prescribed medicines
  • Educate families on the prevention of heat stroke (avoid outdoor work at noon in summer, drink water) and hypothermia (keep newborns warm, wrap the head)

Conclusion Vital signs are basic indicators of health. Temperature is measured at oral, axillary, rectal, tympanic and temporal sites, each with its own uses and limitations. It is affected by age, time of day, exercise, hormones, stress, environment and illness. Alterations include fever, hyperthermia (heat cramps, heat exhaustion, heat stroke) and hypothermia, each needing prompt nursing action.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define blood pressure. Explain the factors affecting blood pressure, the procedure of measurement, the common errors in measurement and the alterations in blood pressure. (2 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 3)

diagram.caption: Korotkoff sounds during deflation of the cuff

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Blood pressure (BP) is the force exerted by the blood against the walls of the arteries as it flows through them
  • Systolic pressure – the highest pressure, during contraction of the ventricles
  • Diastolic pressure – the lowest pressure, during relaxation of the ventricles
  • Pulse pressure – the difference between the two (normal about 40 mmHg)
  • Mean arterial pressure (MAP) = diastolic + one-third of pulse pressure (normal about 70–100 mmHg)
  • Measured in millimetres of mercury (mmHg) and written as systolic/diastolic, e.g. 120/80 mmHg

Physiology (in brief)

  • BP = cardiac output × peripheral resistance
  • It also depends on blood volume, viscosity of blood and elasticity of the arterial walls
  • It is regulated by baroreceptors (carotid sinus and aortic arch), the vasomotor centre, the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and the kidneys

(b) Factors affecting blood pressure (3 marks)

  1. Age – BP rises with age; children have lower BP
  2. Sex – men usually have higher BP than women until menopause
  3. Diurnal variation – lowest in the early morning hours during sleep, rises during the day
  4. Exercise and activity – raise BP temporarily
  5. Stress, anxiety, pain and anger – raise BP through the sympathetic system
  6. Posture – BP may fall on standing suddenly (postural hypotension)
  7. Obesity – increases BP
  8. Diet – high salt intake, alcohol and caffeine raise BP
  9. Smoking – nicotine causes vasoconstriction
  10. Medications – antihypertensives, diuretics and opioids lower BP; steroids, oral contraceptives and decongestants may raise it
  11. Race and heredity – family history of hypertension
  12. Disease – kidney disease, endocrine disorders, haemorrhage and shock, raised intracranial pressure
  13. Pregnancy – BP falls slightly in mid-pregnancy; pre-eclampsia raises it

(c) Procedure of measurement (auscultatory method) (4 marks)

Equipment

  • Sphygmomanometer – mercury (being phased out), aneroid or digital (electronic)
  • Cuff of correct size – the bladder width should be about 40% of the arm circumference and its length about 80%
  • Stethoscope

Preparation

  1. Explain the procedure; let the patient rest for at least 5 minutes
  2. Patient should not have exercised, smoked or taken coffee in the previous 30 minutes, and should have an empty bladder
  3. Patient seated with back supported, feet flat, legs uncrossed; or lying down
  4. Arm supported at the level of the heart, palm facing up, sleeve rolled up (not tight)

Steps

  1. Palpate the brachial artery
  2. Wrap the deflated cuff snugly, with its lower edge about 2.5 cm above the antecubital fossa and the centre of the bladder over the artery
  3. Palpatory method first: feel the radial pulse, inflate until it disappears, note this reading (approximate systolic), then deflate fully and wait 30–60 seconds
  4. Place the diaphragm of the stethoscope lightly over the brachial artery
  5. Inflate the cuff to about 30 mmHg above the palpated systolic level
  6. Deflate slowly at 2–3 mmHg per second
  7. Note the first clear tapping sound (Korotkoff phase I) – systolic pressure
  8. Note the point where the sounds disappear (phase V) – diastolic pressure in adults (in children and some adults where sounds continue to zero, phase IV – muffling – is recorded)
  9. Deflate completely; remove the cuff
  10. Wait 1–2 minutes before repeating; take readings on both arms at the first visit
  11. Record the reading, arm used, position and time; report abnormal values

Korotkoff sounds

  • Phase I – first clear tapping sound (systolic)
  • Phase II – swishing or murmuring sound
  • Phase III – crisp, louder sound
  • Phase IV – sound becomes muffled
  • Phase V – sound disappears (diastolic)
  • Auscultatory gap – a silent interval between phases I and II in some hypertensive patients; it causes underestimation of systolic pressure if the cuff is not inflated high enough – hence the palpatory method first

Other sites: the thigh (popliteal artery) with a wide cuff, when the arms cannot be used (bilateral arm injury, AV fistula, mastectomy side, IV infusion).

(d) Common errors in BP measurement (3 marks)

Error Effect
Cuff too narrow (small) falsely high reading
Cuff too wide (large) falsely low reading
Cuff wrapped too loosely or unevenly falsely high
Arm below heart level falsely high
Arm above heart level falsely low
Arm not supported (muscle contraction) falsely high
Deflating too fast systolic underestimated, diastolic overestimated
Deflating too slowly venous congestion, falsely high diastolic
Re-inflating without waiting falsely high (venous congestion)
Not checking palpatory systolic missing the auscultatory gap – systolic underestimated
Patient talking, anxious, in pain, after exercise, smoking or coffee, full bladder falsely high
Stethoscope pressed too hard falsely low diastolic
Eye not at the level of the mercury meniscus (parallax) wrong reading
Mercury not at zero, leaking bulb, faulty aneroid gauge inaccurate reading
Rounding off to 0 or 5 (digit preference) inaccurate record
"White-coat" anxiety falsely high in the clinic

(e) Alterations in blood pressure (3 marks)

1. Hypertension

  • BP persistently 140/90 mmHg or above (WHO and Indian guidelines); the American guidelines of 2017 use 130/80 mmHg
  • Confirmed by readings on at least two separate occasions
  • Primary (essential) – no known cause (most cases); secondary – due to kidney disease, endocrine disorders, pregnancy, drugs
  • Classification (JNC 7): normal below 120/80; prehypertension 120–139/80–89; stage 1 140–159/90–99; stage 2 160/100 or above
  • Hypertensive crisis – above 180/120 mmHg; an emergency
  • Risks: stroke, heart attack, heart failure, kidney failure, retinal damage
  • Signs – often none ("silent killer"); headache, giddiness, blurred vision, nosebleed

2. Hypotension

  • BP below 90/60 mmHg
  • Causes: haemorrhage, shock, dehydration, severe infection (septic shock), heart failure, drugs (antihypertensives, anaesthesia, opioids)
  • Signs: giddiness, fainting, cold clammy skin, rapid weak pulse, reduced urine output, confusion

3. Orthostatic (postural) hypotension

  • A fall in systolic BP of 20 mmHg or more (or diastolic of 10 mmHg or more) within 3 minutes of standing up
  • Seen in the elderly, after prolonged bed rest, dehydration, with antihypertensive drugs
  • Prevention: change position slowly – sit at the edge of the bed (dangling) before standing

Nursing responsibilities

  • Use correct technique and equipment; record and report abnormal readings promptly
  • Health education on salt reduction, weight control, exercise, avoiding tobacco and alcohol, and regular medication
  • Screening for hypertension in adults above 30 years under the national NCD programme

Conclusion Blood pressure is the force of blood on the arterial walls, determined by cardiac output and peripheral resistance and affected by age, activity, emotions, diet, drugs and disease. Accurate measurement needs the right cuff, correct position, the palpatory method and slow deflation; many errors can give false readings. Hypertension, hypotension and postural hypotension are important alterations that the nurse must detect and report.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain pulse oximetry.
answer_html:
Introduction Pulse oximetry is a non-invasive method of measuring the percentage of haemoglobin saturated with oxygen in arterial blood (SpO₂) and the pulse rate, using a sensor placed on a finger, toe, earlobe or forehead. It gives continuous, painless monitoring of oxygenation.

1. Principle

  • The sensor has two light sources – red and infrared – and a light detector on the opposite side
  • Oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin absorb these lights differently
  • The device analyses the pulsating (arterial) part of the signal and calculates the SpO₂

2. Normal values

  • 95–100% in healthy adults breathing room air
  • Below 90% – hypoxaemia; needs prompt action
  • In patients with chronic lung disease (COPD), a target of about 88–92% may be prescribed

3. Uses

  • Monitoring during anaesthesia, surgery and recovery
  • ICU, emergency and transport of patients
  • Respiratory diseases – pneumonia, asthma, COVID-19
  • Adjusting oxygen therapy; during sedation
  • Screening newborns for serious heart disease

4. Procedure

  1. Explain the procedure; perform hand hygiene
  2. Choose a site with good circulation; warm cold hands
  3. Remove nail polish or artificial nails
  4. Place the probe correctly – light source over the nail bed
  5. Keep the hand still and at heart level
  6. Wait for a steady reading and a good waveform; compare the displayed pulse with the palpated pulse
  7. Record SpO₂, site, and whether the patient is on room air or oxygen (litres per minute)

5. Factors affecting accuracy

  • Poor circulation – cold extremities, shock, low BP
  • Movement, shivering
  • Nail polish, artificial nails, bright light
  • Carbon monoxide poisoning – gives a falsely high reading
  • Severe anaemia; dark skin pigmentation may lead to overestimation
  • Wrong probe size, oedema

6. Nursing responsibilities

  • In continuous monitoring, change the site every 2–4 hours to prevent pressure injury and burns
  • Set alarm limits and respond to alarms
  • Correlate the reading with the patient's respiratory rate, colour and condition – treat the patient, not the number
  • Clean the probe between patients
  • Report low readings promptly

7. Limitations

  • Does not measure carbon dioxide or haemoglobin level; arterial blood gas analysis is more accurate

Conclusion Pulse oximetry measures SpO₂ painlessly using red and infrared light; normal values are 95–100%, and nurses must apply it correctly, know the factors affecting accuracy and interpret readings along with clinical signs.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the factors affecting respiration and the procedure of counting respiration.
answer_html:
Introduction Respiration is the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the atmosphere and the body cells. It is controlled by the respiratory centre in the brainstem, mainly in response to the level of carbon dioxide in the blood. The normal adult respiratory rate is about 12–20 breaths per minute.

A. Factors affecting respiration

  1. Age – faster in infants (about 30–50 per minute) and children; adult rate 12–20
  2. Exercise – increases rate and depth
