  3. Emotions – anxiety, fear and anger increase the rate
  4. Pain – acute pain increases the rate; chest or abdominal pain makes breathing shallow
  5. Fever – increases the rate (higher metabolism)
  6. High altitude – low oxygen increases the rate
  7. Position – slumping restricts breathing; sitting upright helps
  8. Medicines – opioids, sedatives and anaesthetics depress respiration
  9. Diseases – asthma, pneumonia, heart failure, anaemia; diabetic ketoacidosis (deep, rapid Kussmaul breathing); raised intracranial pressure (slow, irregular breathing)
  10. Smoking – chronic damage to the lungs
  11. Obesity, pregnancy and abdominal distension – restrict movement of the diaphragm
  12. Sleep – rate decreases

B. Procedure of counting respiration

  1. Hand hygiene; a watch with a seconds hand is needed
  2. The patient should be at rest and comfortable
  3. Count without the patient's knowledge – keep the fingers on the radial pulse after counting the pulse, because awareness changes breathing
  4. Watch the rise and fall of the chest or abdomen; one inspiration and one expiration count as one respiration
  5. Count for 30 seconds and multiply by 2 if regular; count for a full minute if irregular and in infants (watch abdominal movements)
  6. Observe:
    • depth – shallow, normal or deep
    • rhythm – regular or irregular
    • effort – use of accessory muscles, nasal flaring, retractions
    • sounds – wheeze, stridor, gurgling
    • colour – cyanosis; check SpO₂ if available
  7. Record the rate and character; report abnormal findings promptly (e.g. a rate below 10 or above 24 in an adult, laboured breathing or cyanosis)

C. Normal respiratory rates by age (approximate)

Age Breaths per minute
Newborn 30–60
Infant 30–50
Toddler and preschool child 20–30
School-age child 18–25
Adult 12–20

Conclusion Respiration is influenced by age, exercise, emotions, pain, fever, altitude, position, drugs and disease; it is counted unobtrusively for a full minute when irregular, noting rate, depth, rhythm, effort and colour.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define indent. Mention its types.
answer_html:
Definition An indent is a written requisition (request) for supplies and equipment sent by a ward or department to the main store, pharmacy, linen room or CSSD.

Types of indent

  1. Regular (routine, periodic) indent – sent on fixed days, weekly or monthly, for routine supplies
  2. Emergency indent – for urgent needs at any time
  3. Special (non-stock) indent – for items not usually kept in stock
  4. Supplementary indent – for additional quantities when the regular supply is not enough

Points: prepared by the ward in-charge in duplicate or triplicate, signed and countersigned by the nursing superintendent; items received are checked and entered in the stock register.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: List the types of hospital linen.
answer_html:
Introduction Linen includes all cloth articles used in the hospital for patients, staff and the environment.

Types of linen

  1. Bed linen – bedsheets, draw sheets, pillow covers, blankets, bedspreads
  2. Patient linen – patient gowns, pyjamas, towels, baby clothes and napkins
  3. Operation theatre linen – surgeons' gowns, drapes, caps, masks, leggings, towels, mackintosh covers
  4. Staff linen – uniforms, aprons
  5. Ward linen – screen curtains, window curtains, table covers, dusters, mops
  6. Special linen – abdominal binders, slings, bandages, cradle covers

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Differentiate between disposable and reusable articles with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Hospital articles are grouped according to whether they are used once or many times.

Disposable articles Reusable articles
used once and discarded used many times after cleaning, disinfection or sterilisation
no reprocessing; less risk of cross-infection need proper decontamination, cleaning and sterilisation
costly in the long run; produce more waste economical in the long run; need care and maintenance
e.g. syringes, needles, IV sets, gloves, urinary catheters, masks, urine bags, suction catheters e.g. surgical instruments, kidney trays, bowls, bedpans, glassware, linen, rubber hot water bags

Rule: a disposable item must never be reused.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the care and handling of hospital linen.
answer_html:
Introduction Linen is one of the costliest and most used items in a hospital. Proper care keeps the patient comfortable, prevents cross-infection and reduces the cost of replacement.

1. Collection of used linen

  • Remove soiled linen carefully without shaking it, to avoid spreading microorganisms into the air
  • Roll it inward with the soiled side inside and hold it away from the uniform
  • Never put linen on the floor or on another patient's bed or locker
  • Put it directly into the linen hamper or bag kept near the bed

2. Sorting and segregation

  • Separate ordinary soiled linen from linen soiled with blood or body fluids and linen from isolation (infected) rooms
  • Infected linen is put in separate, labelled, leak-proof bags and disinfected as per hospital policy before laundering; heavily soiled, non-reusable linen is disposed of as biomedical waste

3. Sending to the laundry

  • Count and record the articles in the linen register (laundry book) before sending
  • Remove pins, instruments and patients' belongings from pockets and folds

4. Laundering

  • Washed with detergent in hot water, rinsed, dried, ironed (ironing also helps disinfection)

5. Receiving clean linen

  • Count and check against the record; check for stains, tears and missing items
  • Report shortages and damage

6. Storage

  • Store in a clean, dry, closed cupboard, away from dust and moisture
  • Arrange in order of type; use "first in, first out" so that all linen is used evenly
  • Keep a fixed stock (par level) for each ward

7. Repair and condemnation

  • Send torn linen for mending; worn-out linen is condemned as per rules and replaced

8. Prevention of misuse and loss

  • Do not use linen as dusters, mops or for wrapping other articles
  • Mark linen with the hospital and ward name
  • Remove stains promptly – blood and other protein stains with cold water first

9. Inventory

  • Periodic stock-taking of all linen and maintenance of the linen register

Role of the nurse

  • Supervises the use, collection, counting and storage of linen; teaches support staff the correct handling of soiled and infected linen

Conclusion Careful collection, segregation, counting, laundering, storage, repair and inventory of linen ensure patient comfort, prevent infection and reduce hospital expenses.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain inventory and maintenance of ward equipment.
answer_html:
Introduction The ward has a large number of articles – instruments, linen, furniture, electrical equipment and consumables. The nurse in charge is responsible and accountable for them. Inventory and maintenance ensure that the right equipment is available, in working order, when needed.

A. Inventory

1. Meaning

  • An inventory is a complete list of all articles in a ward or department, with their quantity and condition
  • Stock-taking is the physical checking of the articles against the inventory list

2. When is it done?

  • At regular intervals (monthly, quarterly, annually)
  • When the in-charge changes (handing over and taking over charge)
  • When a loss is suspected

3. Registers maintained

  • Inventory (non-consumable) register – instruments, furniture, equipment
  • Stock register (consumables) – cotton, gauze, syringes, gloves, medicines
  • Linen register, breakage register, narcotic drugs register, equipment register with history cards

4. Purposes of inventory

  • Know what is available and in what condition
  • Plan indents – avoid overstocking and shortage
  • Prevent loss, pilferage and misuse; fix accountability
  • Identify damaged and outdated items for repair or condemnation
  • Check expiry dates of drugs and consumables

B. Maintenance

1. Meaning

  • Keeping equipment clean, safe and in good working condition

2. Types

  • Preventive maintenance – regular cleaning, checking, lubrication, servicing and calibration before a breakdown occurs; annual maintenance contracts (AMC) for costly equipment
  • Corrective (breakdown) maintenance – repair after a fault

3. Nursing responsibilities in maintenance

  • Clean and disinfect equipment after each use as per the manufacturer's instructions
  • Check daily – suction machine, oxygen cylinders, defibrillator, emergency (crash) cart, BP apparatus
  • Label faulty equipment "out of order", remove it from use, and report to the maintenance department; keep a repair record
  • Store equipment properly – dry, safe, dust-free, in a fixed place
  • Train staff in the correct use of equipment
  • Economy – prevent waste and misuse; use "first expiry, first out" for consumables

4. Condemnation

  • Articles beyond repair are condemned by a condemnation committee, recorded and replaced

Conclusion Inventory tells the nurse what is available and in what condition, while maintenance keeps equipment working safely; both ensure efficient patient care and accountability.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Classify the equipment used in a hospital ward. Explain the care of linen, rubber goods, glassware, metal articles and plastic articles, and the procedure of indent and inventory. (3 + 7 + 5)
answer_html:
(a) Classification of ward equipment (3 marks)

1. According to use (life of article)

  • Disposable (single-use) – syringes, needles, IV sets, gloves, masks, catheters, urine bags, suction catheters, dressings
  • Reusable – instruments, bowls, kidney trays, bedpans, glassware, linen, rubber goods

2. According to material

  • Linen – bed linen, patient gowns, towels, OT linen, curtains
  • Rubber goods – hot water bags, ice caps, air rings, rubber sheets (mackintosh), tubing, gloves
  • Glassware – bottles, measuring jars, specimen bottles, test tubes, glass syringes, thermometers
  • Metal articles – stainless steel instruments (forceps, scissors, artery forceps), kidney trays, bowls, gallipots, bedpans, urinals, sterilising drums
  • Plastic articles – jugs, mugs, bowls, mackintosh, catheters, tubing, IV bottles and bags
  • Enamelware – basins, bedpans, mugs (now mostly replaced by steel and plastic)
  • Furniture – beds, bedside lockers, over-bed tables, chairs, screens, stretchers, wheelchairs, trolleys, IV stands, cupboards
  • Electrical and electronic equipment – cardiac monitors, suction machines, nebulisers, oxygen concentrators, infusion pumps, ECG machines, defibrillators, glucometers
  • Paper and stationery – forms, charts, registers

3. According to cost and stock

  • Consumable (expendable) – used up: cotton, gauze, medicines
  • Non-consumable (permanent, capital) – remain for a long time: furniture, equipment

4. According to function

  • Diagnostic (BP apparatus, thermometer, ECG), therapeutic (nebuliser, suction), monitoring, comfort (air mattress, back rest), safety (side rails), transport (stretcher, wheelchair)

(b) Care of different articles (7 marks)

1. Linen

  • Remove soiled linen without shaking; roll inward and hold away from the uniform; never place on the floor
  • Segregate ordinary, soiled and infected linen into separate bags
  • Count and record in the linen register before sending to and on receiving from the laundry
  • Remove stains promptly (blood with cold water)
  • Store in clean, dry, closed cupboards; use "first in, first out"
  • Send torn linen for mending; condemn worn-out linen
  • Prevent misuse as dusters; mark with the hospital and ward name

2. Rubber goods

  • Rinse with cold water immediately after use and wash with soap and lukewarm water – hot water damages rubber
  • Dry thoroughly inside and outside
  • Disinfect with a suitable chemical disinfectant; avoid strong phenol, oil, grease and spirit, which damage rubber
  • Store away from heat, sunlight and sharp objects
  • Hot water bags: drain, dry upside down, then store with a little air inside and the stopper on, so that the sides do not stick together
  • Rubber sheets (mackintosh): wash, dry, and roll or hang – do not fold sharply or pin
  • Rubber tubing: flush, dry and hang straight; check for cracks
  • Dust with French chalk (talc) before storing to prevent sticking

3. Glassware

  • Handle carefully; avoid knocking glasses together
  • Rinse in cold water first (hot water coagulates protein and makes cleaning difficult), then wash with soap or detergent and warm water, using a bottle brush
  • Avoid sudden temperature changes – they crack glass; when boiling, place glassware in cold water and then bring it to the boil
  • Dry, and store upright in a closed cupboard
  • Check for chips and cracks; discard damaged items safely (blue container)
  • Clinical thermometers – clean with soap and cold water from the bulb towards the stem, disinfect as per policy, never in hot water

4. Metal articles and instruments

  • Rinse in cold water immediately after use to remove blood and organic matter
  • Decontaminate (e.g. soak in 0.5% chlorine solution for 10 minutes), then wash with detergent and a brush, opening the joints and hinges
  • Dry thoroughly to prevent rusting; lubricate hinges with instrument oil
  • Check for sharpness, alignment and rust; repair or replace faulty instruments
  • Protect sharp edges of scissors and blades; store sharp instruments separately
  • Pack and sterilise as per CSSD procedure (autoclave)
  • Bedpans and urinals – empty, rinse, wash, disinfect and dry; store in the sluice room
  • Enamelware – do not drop or knock; chipped enamel rusts and harbours germs

5. Plastic articles

  • Wash with cold or lukewarm water and soap; avoid hot water and heat, which deform plastic
  • Disinfect by chemical means (e.g. chlorine solution) as per policy
  • Avoid scratching with sharp objects or abrasives – scratches harbour germs
  • Disposable plastic items are never reused
  • Store away from heat and direct sunlight

6. Furniture

  • Damp dusting daily; clean and disinfect beds and lockers after each patient's discharge (terminal cleaning)
  • Oil wheels and check brakes of beds, stretchers and wheelchairs; report repairs

7. Electrical and electronic equipment

  • Follow the manufacturer's instructions; switch off and unplug before cleaning
  • Check daily (suction, defibrillator, monitor alarms); keep cords tidy and dry
  • Label faulty equipment "out of order" and report; keep maintenance records and AMC details

(c) Procedure of indent and inventory (5 marks)

A. Indent

  • Meaning: a written requisition for supplies from the ward to the store, pharmacy, linen room or CSSD
  • Types: regular (weekly or monthly), emergency, special (non-stock) and supplementary

Steps in preparing an indent

  1. Check the present stock (balance in hand) of each item
  2. Estimate the requirement – consider bed occupancy, consumption in the past period, special cases, expected admissions and buffer stock
  3. Fill the indent form (in duplicate or triplicate) – name of item, unit, quantity in stock, quantity required, remarks
  4. Sign it (ward in-charge) and get it countersigned by the nursing superintendent or authorised officer
  5. Send it on the scheduled day
  6. On receipt, check the items for quantity, quality, damage and expiry date against the indent
  7. Enter the items in the stock register
  8. Store properly, using FIFO (first in, first out) or FEFO (first expiry, first out)

Principles: indent only what is needed (economy), on time, legibly, through proper channels, and keep copies for records.

B. Inventory

  • Meaning: a complete list of all articles in the ward with their quantity and condition; stock-taking is physical verification against the list

Procedure

  1. Maintain separate registers – inventory register (non-consumables), stock register (consumables), linen, breakage, narcotics and equipment registers
  2. Conduct stock-taking at regular intervals and at change of charge, along with a witness or the incoming in-charge
  3. Count each article; note its condition – good, needs repair, unserviceable
  4. Compare with the register; explain shortages and excess
  5. Send repairable items for repair and unserviceable items for condemnation
  6. Record the findings, sign and submit to the authorities

Purposes

  • Ensures availability, prevents loss and pilferage, fixes accountability, helps planning and budgeting, identifies expired and damaged items

Role of the nurse

  • Uses equipment properly and economically, prevents waste, teaches staff, reports breakages promptly, keeps cupboards locked and records up to date, and ensures emergency equipment is always ready

Conclusion Ward equipment may be classified by use, material, cost and function. Linen, rubber, glass, metal and plastic articles each need specific care to prolong their life and prevent infection. A correct indent ensures adequate supplies, and regular inventory ensures accountability, economy and readiness of equipment for patient care.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: What is the central sterile supply department (CSSD)? State its functions.
answer_html:
Definition The central sterile supply department (CSSD) is a hospital department that receives, cleans, packs, sterilises, stores and distributes sterile instruments, linen and supplies to all wards, operation theatres and departments.

Zones (one-way flow)

  • Unclean (receiving and decontamination) → clean (inspection and packing) → sterile (sterilisation and storage) → dispatch

Functions

  1. Decontamination and cleaning of used items
  2. Inspection, assembly and packing of sets
  3. Sterilisation – autoclave (e.g. 121 °C for 15–20 minutes or 134 °C for 3–4 minutes), ethylene oxide or plasma for heat-sensitive items
  4. Quality control – chemical and biological indicators
  5. Storage and distribution; records and recall of faulty batches

Advantages: uniform standards, economy, saves nurses' time and reduces infection.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Introduction to Infection Control in Clinical Setting
question: Explain the safe handling of sharps.
answer_html:
Introduction Sharps (needles, blades, lancets, broken glass) can cause needle-stick injuries and transmit HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C.

Safe handling of sharps

  1. Never recap used needles; if unavoidable, use the one-handed scoop technique
  2. Do not bend, break or remove needles by hand
  3. Dispose immediately at the point of use into a puncture-proof, leak-proof white (translucent) container; use a needle destroyer or cutter
  4. Fill containers only up to three-quarters, then seal
  5. Pass sharps in a tray, never hand to hand
  6. Use safety-engineered devices when available
  7. Get hepatitis B vaccination
  8. After a needle-stick injury – wash with soap and running water (do not scrub or squeeze), report immediately, and start post-exposure prophylaxis as advised (for HIV, ideally within 2 hours and not later than 72 hours)

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Introduction to Infection Control in Clinical Setting
question: Differentiate between medical asepsis and surgical asepsis.
answer_html:
Introduction Asepsis means freedom from disease-causing microorganisms.

Medical asepsis Surgical asepsis
Clean technique Sterile technique
Reduces the number and spread of microorganisms Eliminates all microorganisms, including spores
An object is "clean" An object is "sterile"
Hand washing, clean gloves, cleaning, disinfection, isolation Surgical hand scrub, sterile gloves and gown, sterile field, sterilised instruments
Used in bathing, feeding, oral medicines, bed making, enemas Used in surgery, catheterisation, injections, IV cannulation, surgical dressings

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Introduction to Infection Control in Clinical Setting
question: Define health care-associated infection. Name common types.
answer_html:
Definition A health care-associated (nosocomial) infection is an infection that a patient acquires in a hospital or health care setting, which was not present or incubating at the time of admission. It usually appears 48 hours or more after admission, or within 30 days of surgery.

Common types

  1. Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) – the most common
  2. Surgical site infection (SSI)
  3. Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) and other hospital-acquired pneumonia
  4. Central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI)
  5. Infective diarrhoea (Clostridioides difficile)
  6. Infections due to resistant organisms – MRSA

Main cause: contaminated hands of health workers; hence hand hygiene is the most important preventive measure.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Introduction to Infection Control in Clinical Setting
question: List the steps of donning and doffing personal protective equipment.
answer_html:
Introduction Personal protective equipment (PPE) – gloves, gown, mask or respirator, goggles or face shield, cap and shoe covers – protects health workers from infection. It must be worn and removed in the correct order.

Donning (putting on) – after hand hygiene:

  1. Gown
  2. Mask or respirator (N95 for airborne infections) – check the fit
  3. Goggles or face shield
  4. Gloves – pulled over the cuffs of the gown

Doffing (removing) – at the doorway or anteroom:

  1. Gloves (most contaminated)
  2. Goggles or face shield
  3. Gown – rolled inside out
  4. Mask or respirator – handled by the straps only (after leaving the room)
  5. Hand hygiene – after removing all PPE (and whenever hands become contaminated)

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Introduction to Infection Control in Clinical Setting
question: Explain hand hygiene with the five moments of hand hygiene.

diagram.caption: WHO's five moments for hand hygiene around the patient zone

answer_html:
Introduction Hand hygiene is the single most important measure to prevent health care-associated infections. Hands of health workers carry germs from one patient to another. Hand hygiene means either hand washing with soap and water or hand rubbing with an alcohol-based hand rub.

A. WHO's five moments of hand hygiene (2009)

  1. Before touching a patient – to protect the patient from germs on your hands (e.g. before taking pulse, helping to move)
  2. Before a clean or aseptic procedure – to protect the patient from germs entering his body (e.g. before injection, catheterisation, dressing, oral care)
  3. After body fluid exposure risk – to protect yourself and the environment (e.g. after handling blood, urine, vomitus, removing gloves)
  4. After touching a patient – when leaving the patient (e.g. after bathing, examination)
  5. After touching patient surroundings – even if the patient was not touched (e.g. after changing bed linen, touching the bed rail or monitor)

B. Types of hand hygiene

  • Routine hand washing with soap and water – 40–60 seconds; when hands are visibly soiled, after using the toilet, and after caring for patients with diarrhoea (alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores)
  • Alcohol-based hand rub – 20–30 seconds; for routine decontamination when hands are not visibly soiled; quick and effective
  • Surgical hand scrub – before surgery, with antiseptic, for 3–5 minutes

C. Steps of hand washing (WHO)

  1. Wet hands with water; apply enough soap
  2. Rub palm to palm
  3. Right palm over left dorsum with interlaced fingers, and vice versa
  4. Palm to palm with fingers interlaced
  5. Backs of fingers to opposing palms with fingers interlocked
  6. Rotational rubbing of the thumb clasped in the opposite palm, and vice versa
  7. Rotational rubbing of fingertips in the opposite palm, and vice versa (and the wrists)
  8. Rinse with water; dry with a single-use towel; use the towel to turn off the tap

D. Points to remember

  • Keep nails short; no nail polish, artificial nails, rings or watches
  • Gloves do not replace hand hygiene
  • Apply moisturiser to prevent skin cracks

Conclusion Hand hygiene at the five moments – before patient contact, before aseptic tasks, after body fluid exposure, after patient contact and after touching surroundings – using correct technique, breaks the chain of infection and saves lives.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Introduction to Infection Control in Clinical Setting
question: Explain biomedical waste management.

diagram.caption: Colour coding of biomedical waste (BMW Management Rules, 2016)

answer_html:
Introduction Biomedical waste (BMW) is any waste generated during the diagnosis, treatment or immunisation of human beings or animals, or in research. About 10–25% of hospital waste is hazardous and can spread infection (HIV, hepatitis B and C), cause injuries and pollute the environment. In India, it is managed under the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 (amended in 2018 and 2019).

A. Steps of biomedical waste management

  1. Generation and segregation at source – the most important step
  2. Collection in colour-coded bags and containers
  3. Storage – in a separate, secure area; untreated waste is not stored beyond 48 hours
  4. Transportation – in covered trolleys within the hospital and in closed vehicles to the common bio-medical waste treatment facility (CBWTF)
  5. Treatment – incineration, autoclaving, microwaving, shredding, chemical disinfection
  6. Final disposal – secured landfill, recycling of treated plastics and metals

B. Colour coding and categories (BMW Rules, 2016)

Colour Waste Treatment
Yellow bag human and animal anatomical waste, soiled waste (dressings, cotton swabs, plaster casts, blood bags), expired and cytotoxic medicines, chemical waste, contaminated linen and mattresses, pre-treated laboratory waste incineration, plasma pyrolysis or deep burial (where permitted)
Red bag contaminated recyclable plastic – tubing, IV sets, catheters, urine bags, syringes without needles, gloves, vacutainers autoclaving or microwaving, then shredding and recycling
White (translucent) puncture-proof container sharps – needles, syringes with fixed needles, blades, scalpels, lancets autoclaving, shredding or encapsulation; sent to foundry or landfill
Blue puncture-proof box glassware – broken or discarded glass, medicine vials and ampoules, metallic body implants disinfection or autoclaving, then recycling
  • General (non-infectious) waste – paper, food, packaging – goes into the municipal waste stream (black or green bins as per local rules)
  • Bags must be non-chlorinated plastic, labelled with the biohazard symbol (cytotoxic symbol for cytotoxic waste) and bar-coded
  • Laboratory and microbiology waste and blood bags are pre-treated (sterilised or disinfected) on site before sending

C. Role of the nurse

  • Segregate waste at the point of generation; never mix categories
  • Fill bags only up to three-quarters; tie and label them
  • Handle sharps safely; use needle cutters
  • Wear PPE while handling waste; ensure hepatitis B vaccination of staff
  • Train and supervise support staff; maintain records
  • Report spills and injuries; follow the spill management protocol

Conclusion Biomedical waste management involves segregation at source, colour-coded collection, safe storage, transport, treatment and disposal as per the BMW Rules, 2016; careful segregation by nurses protects patients, staff, the community and the environment.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Introduction to Infection Control in Clinical Setting
question: Explain the standard precautions for infection control.
answer_html:
Introduction Standard precautions are the minimum infection-prevention practices applied to all patients, regardless of their diagnosis or infection status, in all health care settings. They are based on the principle that blood, all body fluids, secretions, excretions (except sweat), non-intact skin and mucous membranes may contain infectious agents.

Components of standard precautions

1. Hand hygiene

  • At the five moments; hand washing for visibly soiled hands, alcohol rub otherwise

2. Personal protective equipment (PPE) – chosen according to the risk

  • Gloves – when touching blood, body fluids, mucous membranes or non-intact skin; change between patients
  • Gown or apron – when clothing may be splashed
  • Mask, goggles or face shield – when splashes or sprays to the face are likely

3. Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette

  • Cover the mouth and nose while coughing or sneezing (tissue or elbow); dispose of tissues; hand hygiene; masks for coughing patients; keep a distance of about 1 metre

4. Safe injection practices

  • One needle, one syringe, one patient, one time; never reuse syringes; use single-dose vials when possible

5. Safe handling and disposal of sharps

  • Do not recap; dispose immediately in puncture-proof containers

6. Patient-care equipment

  • Clean, disinfect or sterilise reusable equipment before use on another patient

7. Environmental cleaning

  • Routine cleaning and disinfection of surfaces, especially frequently touched areas (bed rails, door handles)

8. Handling of linen

  • Handle soiled linen with minimal agitation; transport in closed bags

9. Waste management

  • Segregation of biomedical waste as per the BMW Rules

10. Patient placement

  • Single room for patients who may contaminate the environment or cannot maintain hygiene

11. Protection of health workers

  • Hepatitis B vaccination; reporting of exposures; post-exposure prophylaxis

Transmission-based precautions (in addition, for known or suspected infections)

  • Contact precautions – gloves and gown, dedicated equipment (MRSA, diarrhoea, scabies)
  • Droplet precautions – surgical mask within about 1 metre (influenza, diphtheria, mumps)
  • Airborne precautions – N95 respirator, single room with negative pressure or good ventilation, door closed (tuberculosis, measles, chickenpox)

Conclusion Standard precautions – hand hygiene, PPE, respiratory hygiene, safe injections, sharps safety, equipment and environmental cleaning, and safe waste disposal – are applied to every patient and are the foundation of infection control.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Introduction to Infection Control in Clinical Setting
question: Explain the stages of infection and the factors increasing susceptibility to infection.
answer_html:
Introduction Infection is the invasion and multiplication of microorganisms in body tissues, producing signs and symptoms and an immune response. An infection develops through definite stages, and some persons are more prone to infection than others.

A. Stages of infection

1. Incubation period

  • From the entry of the organism to the appearance of the first symptoms
  • Organisms multiply; varies with the disease (common cold 1–2 days; mumps about 16–18 days; hepatitis B about 6 weeks to 6 months)

2. Prodromal stage

  • From the onset of non-specific symptoms (malaise, mild fever, fatigue, headache) to the appearance of specific symptoms
  • The person is often highly infectious at this stage

3. Stage of illness (full stage)

  • Specific signs and symptoms of the disease appear – e.g. the rash of measles, swollen parotids in mumps
  • Local signs: redness, swelling, heat, pain, loss of function; systemic signs: fever, raised pulse, raised WBC count

4. Convalescence

  • Recovery period; symptoms disappear and the body returns to health; may take days to months

B. Factors increasing susceptibility to infection

  1. Age – newborns and infants (immature immunity) and the elderly (declining immunity)
  2. Nutritional status – malnutrition, protein and vitamin deficiencies reduce immunity
  3. Chronic diseases – diabetes mellitus, cancer, kidney failure, liver disease, HIV/AIDS
  4. Drugs – corticosteroids, chemotherapy, immunosuppressants after transplant; prolonged antibiotics disturb normal flora
  5. Breaks in the skin and mucous membranes – wounds, burns, surgery, pressure ulcers
  6. Invasive devices – urinary catheters, IV cannulas, central lines, endotracheal tubes, ventilators
  7. Stress – raises cortisol and lowers immunity
  8. Inadequate immunisation
  9. Heredity – inherited immune deficiency
  10. Prolonged hospitalisation – exposure to resistant hospital organisms
  11. Lifestyle – smoking, alcohol, drug abuse, poor hygiene, multiple sexual partners
  12. Environment – overcrowding, poor sanitation, unsafe water

C. Body defences (in brief)

  • First line – intact skin, mucous membranes, cilia, tears (lysozyme), stomach acid, normal flora, coughing and sneezing
  • Second line – inflammation (redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function), phagocytosis, fever, interferon
  • Third line – specific immune response: antibodies (B cells) and cell-mediated immunity (T cells)

Nursing importance

  • Identify high-risk patients and protect them – strict asepsis, early removal of catheters, good nutrition, skin care and immunisation

Conclusion Infection passes through incubation, prodromal, illness and convalescence stages; age, poor nutrition, chronic disease, drugs, wounds and invasive devices increase susceptibility, and nurses protect such patients by strict infection control.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Introduction to Infection Control in Clinical Setting
question: Define infection. Explain the chain of infection and the nursing measures to break the chain of infection. (2 + 6 + 7)

diagram.caption: The chain of infection with six links

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Infection is the invasion and multiplication of pathogenic microorganisms in body tissues, which produces signs and symptoms and an immune response
  • Colonisation – organisms are present and multiply but do not cause illness
  • Communicable (infectious) disease – an infection that can be transmitted from one person to another
  • Types of infection:
    • Local (a boil) and systemic (septicaemia)
    • Primary and secondary (a new infection on top of the first)
    • Acute and chronic
    • Exogenous (from outside) and endogenous (from the person's own flora)
    • Health care-associated (nosocomial) – acquired in hospital
    • Iatrogenic – caused by a diagnostic or therapeutic procedure
    • Opportunistic – in persons with low immunity

(b) The chain of infection (6 marks) Infection develops only when six links of a chain are connected. If any one link is broken, infection is prevented.

1. Infectious agent

  • The microorganism that causes infection – bacteria (Staphylococcus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis), viruses (HIV, hepatitis B, influenza), fungi (Candida), protozoa (Plasmodium), parasites
  • Its ability to cause disease depends on number (dose), virulence (disease-producing ability), ability to enter and survive in the host, and the host's resistance

2. Reservoir (source)

  • The place where organisms live and multiply
  • Humans – patients, carriers (persons who carry the organism without symptoms, e.g. typhoid carriers), health workers
  • Animals (rabies in dogs), insects, food and water, soil, and equipment and environment (sinks, wet mops, bed rails)

3. Portal of exit

  • The route by which organisms leave the reservoir
  • Respiratory tract (coughing, sneezing), gastrointestinal tract (faeces, vomitus), urinary tract, reproductive tract, skin and mucous membranes (wounds, pus), blood (injections, bleeding)

4. Mode of transmission

  • Contact – direct (touch, kissing, sexual contact) and indirect (through contaminated objects – fomites such as linen, instruments, thermometers, and contaminated hands)
  • Droplet – large droplets (more than 5 micrometres) from coughing, sneezing and talking, travelling about 1 metre; e.g. influenza, diphtheria
  • Airborne – tiny droplet nuclei (less than 5 micrometres) that stay suspended in air and travel long distances; e.g. tuberculosis, measles, chickenpox
  • Vehicle – contaminated food, water, blood, drugs and IV fluids; e.g. cholera, hepatitis A, hepatitis B through blood
  • Vector – insects and animals; e.g. mosquitoes (malaria, dengue), flies, fleas
  • The hands of health workers are the most common vehicle in hospitals

5. Portal of entry

  • The route by which organisms enter the new host – usually the same as the portal of exit
  • Respiratory tract, GI tract (mouth), urinary and reproductive tracts, broken skin, mucous membranes, and invasive devices (catheters, cannulas)

6. Susceptible host

  • A person who cannot resist the invading organism
  • Factors: extremes of age, malnutrition, chronic disease, immunosuppressive drugs, stress, wounds and burns, invasive devices, lack of immunisation

(c) Nursing measures to break the chain of infection (7 marks)

1. Against the infectious agent

  • Early identification and treatment of infection; send specimens for culture and give antibiotics as prescribed
  • Cleaning, disinfection and sterilisation of equipment – kill organisms before they reach a host
  • Use of antiseptics on skin before procedures

2. Against the reservoir

  • Hand hygiene; maintain personal hygiene of patients (bathing, oral care, perineal care)
  • Environmental cleanliness – damp dusting, mopping, disinfection of surfaces, dry environment (no stagnant water)
  • Change dressings, linen and drainage bags as required; empty drainage bottles and bedpans promptly
  • Proper storage of food, safe water
  • Control of insects and rodents
  • Treatment and screening of carriers

3. Against the portal of exit

  • Cover the mouth and nose while coughing or sneezing (cough etiquette); masks for coughing patients
  • Cover wounds with dressings
  • Safe handling and disposal of body fluids, excreta, secretions and soiled dressings
  • Wear gloves when handling body fluids

4. Against the mode of transmission

  • Hand hygiene at the five moments – the most effective measure
  • Standard precautions for all patients; PPE
  • Transmission-based precautions – contact, droplet and airborne isolation
  • Avoid shaking linen; carry articles away from the uniform
  • Use separate equipment (BP cuff, thermometer) for isolated patients
  • Safe injection practices and sharps disposal
  • Biomedical waste segregation and disposal
  • Proper food handling and safe water; vector control (mosquito nets)
  • Good ventilation of wards

5. Against the portal of entry

  • Maintain skin integrity – turning, skin care, prevention of pressure ulcers
  • Strict surgical asepsis in invasive procedures – catheterisation, injections, dressings, IV cannulation
  • Care of invasive devices – catheter care, closed drainage, cannula site care; remove devices as early as possible
  • Oral hygiene, especially for ventilated and unconscious patients
  • Keep drainage bags below the level of the bladder

6. Protecting the susceptible host

  • Adequate nutrition, fluids, rest and sleep
  • Immunisation of patients and staff (hepatitis B, influenza, tetanus)
  • Protective (reverse) isolation for immunocompromised patients (neutropenia, burns, transplant)
  • Reducing stress, early ambulation, deep breathing and coughing exercises
  • Health education of patients and families about hygiene and infection prevention

Cleaning, disinfection and sterilisation (Spaulding's approach)

  • Cleaning – removal of dirt and organic matter with water and detergent; always the first step
  • Disinfection – destroys most pathogens but not spores; e.g. 0.5–1% sodium hypochlorite for surfaces and spills, 70% alcohol for small surfaces, 2% glutaraldehyde for endoscopes, boiling for 20 minutes
  • Sterilisation – destroys all microorganisms including spores; e.g. autoclaving (steam under pressure, 121 °C for 15–20 minutes or 134 °C for 3–5 minutes), dry heat (hot air oven, 160 °C for 2 hours), ethylene oxide, plasma sterilisation
  • Critical items (enter sterile tissue – surgical instruments, catheters) must be sterile; semi-critical items (touch mucous membranes – endoscopes, thermometers) need high-level disinfection; non-critical items (touch intact skin – BP cuffs, bedpans) need cleaning and low-level disinfection

7. Organisational measures

  • Hospital infection control committee and infection control nurse
  • Surveillance of health care-associated infections, audits of hand hygiene
  • Training of staff; antibiotic stewardship

Summary table

Link Example Nursing measure
Infectious agent bacteria, virus sterilisation, antibiotics
Reservoir patient, carrier, wet surfaces hygiene, cleaning
Portal of exit cough, wound, faeces cover wounds, cough etiquette
Transmission hands, droplets, air hand hygiene, PPE, isolation
Portal of entry broken skin, catheters asepsis, device care
Susceptible host elderly, diabetic nutrition, immunisation, protective isolation

Conclusion Infection is the invasion and multiplication of pathogens in the body. It needs six links – agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry and susceptible host. Nurses break this chain at every link through hand hygiene, asepsis, cleaning and sterilisation, standard and transmission-based precautions, care of devices, waste management and protection of vulnerable patients.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Introduction to Infection Control in Clinical Setting
question: Differentiate between sterilisation and disinfection.
answer_html:
Introduction Both are methods of decontamination, but they differ in how completely they destroy microbes.

Sterilisation Disinfection
destroys all forms of microbial life, including spores destroys most disease-causing microbes, but not necessarily spores
absolute process relative process (high, intermediate or low level)
used for critical items that enter sterile tissue – surgical instruments, needles, catheters used for semi-critical and non-critical items – thermometers, bedpans, surfaces
methods: autoclave, hot air oven, ethylene oxide, radiation methods: boiling, alcohol, chlorine compounds, glutaraldehyde (short exposure)

Note: an antiseptic is a chemical used on living tissue (skin, wounds), e.g. povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Introduction to Infection Control in Clinical Setting
question: Explain the methods of sterilisation.
answer_html:
Introduction Sterilisation is the process of destroying all microorganisms, including spores, from an object. It is essential for instruments and supplies that enter sterile body tissues. Items must be thoroughly cleaned before sterilisation, because dirt and blood protect microbes.

A. Physical methods

1. Moist heat

  • Autoclave (steam under pressure) – the most reliable and widely used method
    • 121 °C at 15 lb/sq inch pressure for 15–20 minutes, or 134 °C for 3–4 minutes in high-speed autoclaves
    • Used for instruments, linen, dressings, glassware and some rubber goods
  • Boiling (100 °C for 10–20 minutes) only disinfects – spores may survive; it is not true sterilisation

2. Dry heat

  • Hot air oven – 160 °C for 2 hours (or 180 °C for 30 minutes); for glassware, powders, oils and sharp instruments
  • Incineration – burning of contaminated waste and soiled dressings
  • Flaming and red heat – in laboratories (inoculating loops)

3. Radiation

  • Gamma rays – "cold sterilisation" of disposable syringes, catheters, sutures and gloves by manufacturers
  • Ultraviolet rays – only disinfect air and surfaces (operation theatres, laboratories)

4. Filtration

  • Membrane filters remove bacteria from heat-sensitive fluids (vaccines, sera, some drugs)
  • HEPA filters clean the air in operation theatres and isolation rooms

B. Chemical methods

  • Ethylene oxide (ETO) gas – for heat-sensitive items (plastics, endoscope parts); items need aeration afterwards as the gas is toxic
  • Hydrogen peroxide gas plasma – low-temperature sterilisation
  • Glutaraldehyde 2% – high-level disinfection in about 20 minutes; sterilisation after prolonged immersion (about 10 hours); for endoscopes
  • Formaldehyde – fumigation of rooms

C. Monitoring of sterilisation

  • Physical – checking time, temperature and pressure gauges
  • Chemical indicators – autoclave tape and indicator strips that change colour; the Bowie–Dick test for air removal
  • Biological indicators – spores of heat-resistant bacteria; if they fail to grow, sterilisation was effective

D. Responsibilities of the nurse

  • Clean items thoroughly before sending them for sterilisation
  • Pack correctly; label with date, contents and expiry
  • Check indicators and package integrity before use; reject wet, torn or expired packs
  • Store sterile packs in a clean, dry, dust-free area
  • Never reuse single-use items
  • Handle sterile items with aseptic technique

Conclusion Sterilisation is done by moist heat (autoclave), dry heat, radiation, filtration or chemicals such as ethylene oxide; its effectiveness is checked by physical, chemical and biological indicators, and nurses ensure correct cleaning, packing, storage and use.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Introduction to Infection Control in Clinical Setting
question: Explain the body's defences against infection.
answer_html:
Introduction The human body has natural defences that protect it from infection. Infection occurs when microbes overcome these defences. They are described as three lines of defence.

A. First line of defence – external barriers (non-specific)

  • Intact skin – a tough, dry, acidic barrier; sebum contains fatty acids that kill bacteria; continual shedding of skin cells removes microbes
  • Mucous membranes – mucus traps microbes; cilia in the respiratory tract sweep them out
  • Secretions:
    • lysozyme in tears and saliva
    • hydrochloric acid in the stomach
    • acidic vaginal secretions
    • the flushing action and acidity of urine
  • Reflexes – coughing, sneezing, vomiting and diarrhoea expel microbes
  • Normal flora – harmless bacteria on the skin, gut and vagina compete with harmful ones

B. Second line of defence – internal non-specific defences

  • Phagocytes – neutrophils and macrophages engulf and destroy microbes
  • Inflammation – redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function; blood vessels dilate and white cells reach the site, localising the infection
  • Fever – slows the growth of microbes and boosts the immune response
  • Natural killer cells, the complement system and interferons

C. Third line of defence – specific immunity

  • Humoral immunity – B lymphocytes form antibodies
  • Cell-mediated immunity – T lymphocytes destroy infected cells
  • Has memory – the basis of immunisation

D. How health care can weaken these defences

  • Breaks in the skin – wounds, burns, IV lines, injections
  • Invasive devices – urinary catheters and endotracheal tubes bypass natural barriers
  • Reduced cough reflex – sedation, unconsciousness
  • Antibiotics disturb the normal flora → fungal infections, antibiotic-associated diarrhoea
  • Antacids reduce stomach acid
  • Malnutrition, steroids, chemotherapy and extremes of age

E. Nursing measures to support body defences

  • Skin care and prevention of pressure ulcers; hand hygiene
  • Oral hygiene; deep breathing and coughing exercises
  • Early ambulation; adequate nutrition and fluids
  • Immunisation of patients and staff
  • Use invasive devices only when necessary and remove them early
  • Rational use of antibiotics; rest and stress reduction

F. Signs of infection the nurse should observe

  • Local – redness, warmth, swelling, pain, pus, loss of function of the part
  • Systemic – fever, chills, fast pulse and breathing, tiredness, loss of appetite, raised white cell count
  • In the elderly and newborns – infection may show only as confusion, poor feeding, low temperature or lethargy

Conclusion The body is protected by external barriers, internal non-specific defences (phagocytes, inflammation, fever) and specific immunity; nurses protect and strengthen these defences to prevent infection.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Introduction to Infection Control in Clinical Setting
question: Define health care-associated infection. Explain its types, the risk factors, its prevention and the role of the infection control nurse. (2 + 4 + 5 + 4)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • A health care-associated infection (HAI), also called a nosocomial or hospital-acquired infection, is an infection acquired by a patient while receiving health care in a hospital or other facility, which was not present or incubating at the time of admission
  • It usually appears 48 hours or more after admission, or after discharge (e.g. a surgical site infection within 30 days of an operation)
  • Infections acquired by health workers at work are also included
  • Magnitude – WHO estimates that out of every 100 patients in acute-care hospitals, about 7 in high-income and 15 in low- and middle-income countries acquire at least one HAI; on average, about 1 in 10 affected patients dies from it
  • HAIs prolong hospital stay, increase costs, spread antimicrobial resistance and cause deaths

(b) Types of HAI (4 marks)

  1. Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) – one of the commonest HAIs
  2. Surgical site infection (SSI) – infection of the operation wound or deeper tissues
  3. Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) and other hospital-acquired pneumonias
  4. Central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI); phlebitis at peripheral IV sites
  5. Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (Clostridioides difficile) and outbreaks of gastroenteritis
  6. Infections with multidrug-resistant organisms – MRSA, carbapenem-resistant bacteria
  7. Blood-borne infections – hepatitis B and C, HIV (through unsafe injections, transfusion or needle-stick injury)
  8. Airborne and droplet infections – tuberculosis, influenza, COVID-19, chickenpox
  9. Neonatal sepsis in newborn units; infected pressure ulcers

Common organisms: Staphylococcus aureus, E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Enterococcus and Candida.

(c) Risk factors (5 marks)

1. Patient (host) factors

  • Extremes of age – newborns (especially preterm) and the elderly
  • Low immunity – cancer, chemotherapy, steroids, HIV, diabetes, malnutrition
  • Severe illness, burns, major surgery, ICU stay
  • Prolonged hospital stay

2. Invasive devices and procedures

  • Urinary catheters, IV cannulas and central lines, ventilators and endotracheal tubes, drains, dialysis
  • Surgical wounds; endoscopies

3. Practices of health workers

  • Poor hand hygiene – the most important route of spread
  • Breaks in aseptic technique
  • Improper cleaning, disinfection or sterilisation of equipment; reuse of single-use items
  • Unsafe injection practices

4. Environmental factors

  • Overcrowding, poor ventilation, lack of isolation rooms
  • Contaminated surfaces, equipment, water and food
  • Improper biomedical waste management

5. Antimicrobial misuse

  • Unnecessary or broad-spectrum antibiotics → resistant organisms and C. difficile infection

6. Other factors

  • Staff shortage and heavy workload; infected staff and visitors

(d) Prevention and role of the infection control nurse (4 marks)

A. Prevention

  • Standard precautions in all patients – hand hygiene at the five moments, PPE, safe injections, safe sharps handling, respiratory hygiene
  • Transmission-based precautions and isolation when needed
  • Care bundles – small sets of evidence-based practices that work best when done together:
    • CAUTI bundle – insert catheters only when indicated; aseptic insertion; closed drainage; bag below bladder level and off the floor; daily perineal care; daily review and early removal
    • CLABSI bundle – hand hygiene, maximal barrier precautions during insertion, chlorhexidine skin preparation, best site selection, scrubbing hubs before access, daily review and prompt removal
    • VAP bundle – head of bed elevated 30–45°, daily sedation breaks and assessment for weaning, oral care, suction with aseptic technique, avoiding unnecessary circuit changes
    • SSI bundle – preoperative bath, no shaving (clip if needed), prophylactic antibiotic within 60 minutes before incision, control of blood sugar and temperature, strict asepsis and wound care
  • Cleaning, disinfection and sterilisation of equipment and environment
  • Proper biomedical waste management
  • Antimicrobial stewardship – right antibiotic, right dose, right duration
  • Staff health – hepatitis B vaccination; post-exposure prophylaxis after needle-stick injury
  • Surveillance of infection rates

B. Role of the infection control nurse (ICN)

  • Member (often secretary) of the Hospital Infection Control Committee
  • Surveillance – daily ward rounds, collecting data and calculating rates (e.g. CAUTI per 1,000 catheter-days)
  • Early detection and investigation of outbreaks
  • Education and training of staff, students and housekeeping workers; hand hygiene campaigns
  • Audits – hand hygiene compliance, bundle compliance, sterilisation, cleaning and waste segregation
  • Policies and protocols – preparing and updating infection control manuals
  • Advising on isolation and use of PPE
  • Staff health – reporting of needle-stick injuries, vaccination records
  • Working with the microbiology laboratory on resistant organisms and with the antibiotic stewardship team
  • Reporting to hospital administration; supporting accreditation standards

Additional notes

Sources and modes of spread of HAI

  • Endogenous – from the patient's own normal flora (e.g. gut bacteria causing urinary infection after catheterisation)
  • Exogenous – from other patients, staff, visitors, equipment or the environment
  • Contact – mainly through the hands of health workers and shared equipment (thermometers, BP cuffs, stethoscopes)
  • Droplet and airborne spread – influenza, tuberculosis, COVID-19
  • Common vehicle – contaminated IV fluids, medicines, food or water
  • Vectors – flies, cockroaches, mosquitoes in poorly maintained wards

WHO five moments of hand hygiene

  1. Before touching a patient
  2. Before a clean or aseptic procedure
  3. After body fluid exposure risk
  4. After touching a patient
  5. After touching the patient's surroundings

Early detection by the ward nurse – signs to report

  • New fever, chills or unexplained rise in pulse
  • Redness, swelling, pain or pus at wound, IV or catheter sites
  • Cloudy, foul-smelling urine; burning on urination
  • New cough, purulent secretions or increasing oxygen need in ventilated patients
  • Diarrhoea in patients on antibiotics

Isolation and cohorting

  • Patients with multidrug-resistant organisms are placed in single rooms or cohorted (grouped) with dedicated equipment and staff where possible

Measuring HAI – an example

  • CAUTI rate = (number of CAUTI cases ÷ number of catheter-days) × 1,000
  • Rates are compared month by month to judge whether prevention measures are working

Impact of HAI

  • Longer hospital stay and higher costs for the family
  • Disability and death
  • Spread of antimicrobial resistance in the hospital and community
  • Loss of public trust and legal consequences for the hospital

Role of the ward nurse in preventing HAI

  • Follow aseptic technique for every invasive procedure – catheterisation, IV cannulation, dressings, suctioning
  • Catheter care – keep the drainage closed and the bag below bladder level; perineal hygiene; remind the doctor daily about removal
  • IV site care – label cannulas with the date, inspect the site every shift, change sets and cannulas as per policy, scrub the hub before each access
  • Wound care – clean technique or sterile dressings as needed; watch for signs of infection
  • Oral care and head elevation in ventilated and unconscious patients
  • Educate patients and visitors about hand hygiene, cough etiquette and limiting visitors
  • Supervise cleaning, linen handling and waste segregation in the ward
  • Document device insertion dates and report suspected infections promptly

Conclusion Health care-associated infections – mainly CAUTI, SSI, VAP and CLABSI – arise from patient factors, invasive devices, poor practices, the environment and antibiotic misuse. They are largely preventable through hand hygiene, standard precautions, care bundles, sterilisation, waste management and surveillance, and the infection control nurse leads these efforts.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: List the comfort devices.
answer_html:
Introduction Comfort devices are articles used to support the body, maintain good alignment, relieve pressure and make the patient comfortable in bed.

Comfort devices

  1. Pillows – support the head, limbs and back
  2. Back rest – supports the patient in a sitting (Fowler's) position
  3. Cardiac (over-bed) table – for leaning forward in breathlessness, and for meals
  4. Bed cradle – keeps the weight of bedclothes off injured legs, burns or fresh plaster
  5. Foot board / foot rest – prevents foot drop
  6. Sandbags and trochanter rolls – prevent external rotation of the hip
  7. Hand rolls – keep the fingers in a functional position
  8. Knee rest – prevents sliding down in bed
  9. Air, water, alternating-pressure and foam (egg-crate) mattresses – prevent pressure ulcers
  10. Air cushions and heel and elbow protectors
  11. Bed blocks – raise the foot or head end of the bed
  12. Overhead trapeze (monkey bar) and side rails

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Name the types of beds.
answer_html:
Introduction Beds are made in different ways depending on the patient's condition, and special beds are used for particular needs.

A. Types of bed making

  1. Closed bed – an unoccupied bed made ready for a new patient
  2. Open bed – top linen folded back, ready for an ambulatory patient
  3. Occupied bed – made with the patient in it
  4. Admission bed – prepared for a patient being admitted
  5. Post-operative (anaesthetic) bed – for a patient returning from surgery
  6. Cardiac bed, fracture bed, amputation bed and burns bed – for special conditions

B. Special beds

  • Fowler's bed (backrest adjustable), hi-low and electric beds, ICU beds, air-fluidised and low air-loss beds, water beds, kinetic (rotating) beds, Stryker frame (for spinal injury), delivery bed, paediatric cot with side rails

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Describe the stages of sleep.
answer_html:
Introduction Sleep is a natural, recurring state of reduced consciousness. It occurs in cycles of about 90 minutes; an adult has 4–6 cycles each night.

A. NREM (non-rapid eye movement) sleep – about 75% of sleep

  1. Stage N1 – lightest sleep; drowsiness; easily awakened; lasts a few minutes
  2. Stage N2 – light sleep; heart rate and temperature fall; about half of total sleep
  3. Stage N3 – deep (slow-wave, delta) sleep; hardest to wake; growth hormone is released; body tissues are repaired

B. REM (rapid eye movement) sleep – about 20–25% of sleep

  • Dreaming occurs; eyes move rapidly; brain is active; muscles are relaxed (paralysed); pulse and respiration irregular
  • Important for memory, learning and emotional balance

Control: the reticular activating system in the brainstem and melatonin from the pineal gland regulate the sleep–wake cycle (circadian rhythm).

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the gate control theory of pain.
answer_html:
Introduction The gate control theory was proposed by Melzack and Wall (1965). It explains why pain can be reduced by rubbing, massage, distraction and emotional support.

Key points

  1. A "gate" in the substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn of the spinal cord controls the passage of pain impulses to the brain
  2. Small nerve fibres (A-delta and C) carry pain impulses and open the gate
  3. Large nerve fibres (A-beta) carry touch and pressure; their stimulation closes the gate – so rubbing, massage, heat, cold and TENS reduce pain
  4. Messages from the brain (attention, emotions, past experience) can also open or close the gate – anxiety increases pain; distraction, relaxation and endorphins reduce it

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Describe the therapeutic positions and their uses.
answer_html:
Introduction Positioning means placing the patient in a posture that promotes comfort, maintains body alignment, prevents complications and facilitates examinations and procedures. Positions should be changed at least every 2 hours for bed-bound patients.

1. Fowler's position – sitting up in bed

  • High Fowler's (60–90°), semi-Fowler's (30–45°), low Fowler's (15–30°)
  • Uses: breathlessness, heart failure, after abdominal and thyroid surgery, feeding, nasogastric tube feeding, preventing aspiration, raised intracranial pressure (semi-Fowler's)

2. Supine (dorsal) position – lying flat on the back

  • Uses: rest, physical examination, after spinal anaesthesia (as ordered), spinal injury

3. Dorsal recumbent position – on the back with knees flexed and feet flat on the bed

  • Uses: vaginal examination, perineal care, catheterisation of female patients

4. Prone position – lying on the abdomen with the head turned to one side

  • Uses: examination and treatment of the back, after some spinal surgery, preventing hip and knee flexion contractures; improves oxygenation in severe respiratory distress (ARDS)

5. Lateral (side-lying) position

  • Uses: rest, relief of pressure on the back and sacrum, giving back care, unconscious patients

6. Sims' (semi-prone) position – on the left side with the right knee and thigh drawn up and the left arm behind

  • Uses: enema, rectal examination, insertion of suppositories, unconscious patients (drainage of secretions)

7. Lithotomy position – on the back with hips and knees flexed and legs supported in stirrups

  • Uses: delivery, vaginal examination and surgery, perineal and rectal procedures

8. Trendelenburg position – head end of the bed lowered, feet raised

  • Uses: some pelvic surgery; in the past for shock (now legs-up position with head flat is preferred)

9. Reverse Trendelenburg – head end raised, feet lowered

  • Uses: hiatus hernia, after some neck and head surgery

10. Knee-chest (genupectoral) position – kneeling with chest and head resting on the bed

  • Uses: rectal and sigmoid examination; relieving pressure on a prolapsed cord

11. Orthopnoeic position – sitting up and leaning forward on a cardiac table with pillows

  • Uses: severe breathlessness, asthma, heart failure

Nursing principles

  • Explain, ensure privacy, use pillows and comfort devices for support, maintain alignment, protect bony prominences, and record the position and the patient's response

Conclusion Therapeutic positions such as Fowler's, supine, prone, lateral, Sims', lithotomy and Trendelenburg promote comfort, breathing and safety, prevent complications and help in examinations and treatment.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the purposes and principles of bed making.
answer_html:
Introduction Bed making is the preparation of a bed in a way that provides comfort, cleanliness and safety for the patient. Since a sick person spends most of the time in bed, a well-made bed is an important part of nursing care.

A. Purposes of bed making

  1. To provide a clean, comfortable and safe bed
  2. To prevent pressure ulcers – wrinkles, crumbs and damp linen damage the skin
  3. To prevent cross-infection by removing soiled linen
  4. To make the bed ready for a specific need – admission, post-operative, fracture or cardiac patients
  5. To provide rest and sleep
  6. To give an opportunity to observe the patient's skin and condition
  7. To keep the ward neat and tidy
  8. To economise time, energy and linen

B. Principles of bed making

1. Preparation

  • Perform hand hygiene; collect all articles in the order of use before starting – saves time and energy
  • Ensure privacy for occupied beds; explain the procedure to the patient

2. Infection control

  • Do not shake linen – it spreads microorganisms and dust
  • Hold soiled linen away from the uniform; never put linen on the floor or on another patient's bed
  • Put soiled linen directly into the linen bag; handle infected linen as per policy
  • Use clean linen for each patient

3. Body mechanics

  • Raise the bed to a comfortable working height; lock the wheels
  • Keep the back straight, bend at the knees, avoid twisting; work on one side completely, then the other

4. Comfort and safety of the patient

  • Make the bed smooth and wrinkle-free; tuck linen firmly
  • Make mitred corners for neatness and firmness
  • Make a toe pleat in the top sheet to allow free movement of the feet and prevent foot drop
  • Raise side rails for occupied beds of restless, elderly or sedated patients; keep the call bell within reach
  • Keep the patient covered and warm during an occupied bed change

5. Economy

  • Use linen economically; avoid tearing or misusing linen

6. Order and aesthetics

  • Follow the hospital's standard method so that all beds look uniform; keep the bedside locker tidy

7. After care

  • Lower the bed to the lowest position; place belongings within reach; perform hand hygiene and record

Conclusion Bed making provides comfort, cleanliness and safety, prevents pressure ulcers and infection, and saves time when principles of preparation, asepsis, body mechanics, patient safety and economy are followed.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the factors affecting sleep and the nursing measures to promote sleep.
answer_html:
Introduction Sleep is a natural, periodic state of rest in which consciousness and responsiveness to the environment are reduced. Rest is a state of calmness and relaxation without emotional stress. Sleep restores energy, repairs tissues, supports immunity and consolidates memory. Hospitalised patients often have poor sleep.

Sleep needs by age: newborn 14–17 hours; school child 9–11 hours; adolescent 8–10 hours; adult 7–9 hours; the elderly sleep about 7–8 hours, with more frequent waking.

A. Factors affecting sleep

  1. Age – the elderly have lighter, interrupted sleep
  2. Physical illness – pain, breathlessness, cough, fever, nausea, itching, nocturia (frequent urination at night)
  3. Drugs – diuretics, steroids, bronchodilators, caffeine, alcohol (disturbs REM sleep), withdrawal of sleeping tablets
  4. Environment – noise, bright light, uncomfortable temperature, unfamiliar bed, shared ward, monitors and alarms
  5. Emotional stress – anxiety about illness, family, finances; depression
  6. Lifestyle – night shifts, irregular routines, jet lag
  7. Diet – heavy meals, tea or coffee late in the evening, hunger
  8. Exercise and fatigue – moderate exercise helps; exercise just before bed or extreme fatigue disturbs sleep
  9. Smoking – nicotine is a stimulant
  10. Hospital routines – waking patients for vital signs, medicines and procedures

B. Nursing measures to promote sleep

  1. Comfortable environment – reduce noise (soft voices, silent footwear, lower alarm volumes), dim the lights at night, maintain a comfortable temperature and ventilation
  2. Comfort measures – a clean, wrinkle-free bed; comfortable position; back massage; warm bath or wash
  3. Relieve pain and discomfort – give analgesics on time; treat cough and breathlessness
  4. Bedtime routine – follow the patient's usual habits (prayer, reading, warm milk)
  5. Empty the bladder before sleep; limit fluids late in the evening if nocturia is a problem
  6. Avoid stimulants – tea, coffee and smoking in the evening; avoid heavy meals at night
  7. Cluster nursing activities so that the patient is not repeatedly disturbed
  8. Reduce anxiety – listen, explain, reassure
  9. Relaxation techniques – deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, soft music
  10. Regular sleep–wake schedule and limited daytime naps; activity during the day
  11. Sleeping tablets only as prescribed and as a last resort; observe for side effects and falls

Conclusion Sleep is affected by age, illness, drugs, environment, emotions and routines; a quiet, comfortable environment, pain relief, bedtime routines and reduced disturbance help patients sleep well.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Describe the common sleep disorders.
answer_html:
Introduction Sleep disorders are conditions that disturb the quantity, quality or timing of sleep, causing daytime problems. They are common in hospital patients, shift workers and the elderly.

1. Insomnia

  • Difficulty in falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early, with daytime tiredness
  • Causes: stress, anxiety, depression, pain, caffeine, irregular routines, drugs
  • Management: sleep hygiene, relaxation, treat the cause, cognitive behaviour therapy, hypnotics for a short period only

2. Hypersomnia

  • Excessive sleep or daytime sleepiness; seen in depression, hypothyroidism, sleep deprivation

3. Narcolepsy

  • Sudden, uncontrollable attacks of sleep during the day; may have cataplexy (sudden muscle weakness with emotion); risky while driving

4. Sleep apnoea

  • Repeated pauses in breathing (10 seconds or more) during sleep
  • Obstructive sleep apnoea – airway blocked by relaxed throat tissues; common in obese persons; loud snoring, gasping, morning headache, daytime sleepiness
  • Central sleep apnoea – the brain fails to send signals to breathe
  • Management: weight loss, avoid alcohol and sedatives, side sleeping, CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure)

5. Parasomnias – abnormal behaviour during sleep

  • Somnambulism (sleepwalking) – safety measures needed
  • Night terrors – sudden screaming and fear in children during deep sleep, with no memory of it next morning
  • Nightmares – frightening dreams during REM sleep; the person remembers them
  • Nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting) – after the age of 5 years
  • Bruxism – grinding of teeth

6. Restless legs syndrome

  • Uncomfortable sensations in the legs with an urge to move them, mainly at night

7. Circadian rhythm disorders

  • Shift-work sleep disorder and jet lag – mismatch between the body clock and the sleep schedule

8. Sleep deprivation

  • Lack of adequate sleep – common in ICU patients and night-shift workers
  • Effects: irritability, poor concentration, confusion, reduced immunity, accidents

Nursing role

  • Assess sleep pattern (sleep diary), teach sleep hygiene, ensure safety (sleepwalkers, narcolepsy), report snoring with breath pauses, and reduce disturbance in hospital

Conclusion Insomnia, hypersomnia, narcolepsy, sleep apnoea, parasomnias and circadian disorders impair health and safety; nurses identify them early and promote healthy sleep habits.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the non-pharmacological methods of pain relief.
answer_html:
Introduction Non-pharmacological methods relieve pain without drugs. They work by closing the pain "gate" (gate control theory), releasing endorphins, reducing anxiety and muscle tension, and distracting attention. They are safe, cheap and can be combined with analgesics; many can be taught to patients and families.

A. Physical (cutaneous) methods

  1. Positioning and comfort measures – supporting the painful part with pillows, splinting the abdominal wound with a pillow while coughing, a comfortable bed
  2. Heat application – hot water bag, warm compress for muscle spasm and joint pain
  3. Cold application – ice packs for sprains, injuries and post-operative swelling in the first 24–48 hours
  4. Massage – back massage relaxes muscles and stimulates large fibres
  5. TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation) – mild electrical current through skin electrodes
  6. Acupressure and acupuncture
  7. Immobilisation – splints and slings for fractures and inflamed joints
  8. Exercise and physiotherapy – for chronic back and joint pain

B. Cognitive and behavioural methods

  1. Distraction – focusing attention away from pain: talking, music, television, reading, games for children
  2. Relaxation techniques – slow deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, yoga and meditation
  3. Guided imagery – imagining a pleasant, peaceful scene
  4. Music therapy
  5. Patient education and preparatory information – explaining what to expect before a procedure reduces fear and pain
  6. Biofeedback and hypnosis (by trained persons)

C. Emotional and spiritual support

  • The presence of the nurse or family, listening, reassurance, prayer and spiritual practices

D. Complementary therapies

  • Aromatherapy, reflexology, therapeutic touch

E. Environmental measures

  • Quiet, dim and comfortable surroundings; adequate rest and sleep

Nursing points

  • Choose methods that suit the patient's age, culture and preference
  • Teach and practise them before pain becomes severe
  • Assess pain before and after each method and record the response

Conclusion Positioning, heat and cold, massage, TENS, distraction, relaxation, guided imagery, music and emotional support relieve pain safely and enhance the effect of analgesics.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define pain. Explain the types of pain, the assessment of pain, and the pharmacological and non-pharmacological management of pain. (2 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 3)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP, 2020): pain is "an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage"
  • Margo McCaffery: "Pain is whatever the experiencing person says it is, existing whenever he says it does" – the nurse must believe the patient's report
  • Pain is a protective mechanism that warns of harm, and it is often called the fifth vital sign

Physiology of pain (nociception) in brief

  1. Transduction – a harmful stimulus (heat, pressure, chemicals such as prostaglandins, bradykinin and histamine) activates nociceptors (pain receptors)
  2. Transmission – impulses travel along A-delta fibres (fast, sharp, well-localised pain) and C fibres (slow, dull, burning, poorly localised pain) to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, then through the spinothalamic tract to the thalamus and the cerebral cortex
  3. Perception – the person becomes aware of pain in the cortex
  4. Modulation – the body reduces pain by releasing endorphins and enkephalins (natural opioids); the gate control theory explains how touch, emotions and attention change pain

(b) Types of pain (3 marks)

1. According to duration

Acute pain Chronic pain
sudden onset, less than 3 months lasts 3–6 months or more
identifiable cause (injury, surgery) cause may not be clear
subsides with healing persists beyond healing
signs of sympathetic response – raised pulse and BP, sweating, dilated pupils sympathetic signs usually absent; fatigue, depression, sleep problems
e.g. post-operative pain, fracture, appendicitis e.g. arthritis, low backache, cancer pain

2. According to origin

  • Cutaneous (superficial) – from skin and subcutaneous tissue; sharp, well localised (cut, burn)
  • Deep somatic – from bones, muscles, ligaments and joints; dull, diffuse (sprain, fracture)
  • Visceral – from internal organs; poorly localised, cramping, with nausea and sweating (intestinal colic, renal colic)

3. According to spread

  • Localised – confined to one site
  • Radiating – spreads from the origin to nearby areas (sciatica down the leg)
  • Referred – felt at a site away from the organ involved: heart pain felt in the left arm and jaw; gall bladder pain in the right shoulder; appendix pain first felt around the umbilicus

4. According to mechanism

  • Nociceptive – due to tissue damage
  • Neuropathic – due to damage of nerves; burning, shooting, tingling (diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, sciatica)
  • Psychogenic – psychological factors play a major role

5. Special types

  • Phantom limb pain – pain felt in an amputated limb
  • Intractable pain – severe pain that does not respond to usual treatment
  • Breakthrough pain – a sudden flare of pain in a patient on regular analgesics (common in cancer)

(c) Assessment of pain (4 marks)

1. Pain history – PQRST

  • P – Provoking / palliating factors – what makes it worse or better
  • Q – Quality – sharp, dull, burning, throbbing, stabbing, cramping
  • R – Region / radiation – where it is and where it spreads
  • S – Severity – intensity on a pain scale
  • T – Timing – onset, duration, frequency, constant or intermittent
  • Also ask about associated symptoms (nausea, sweating), the effect on daily life and sleep, previous pain experiences and what relieves it

2. Pain rating scales

  • Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) – 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst possible pain); mild 1–3, moderate 4–6, severe 7–10
  • Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) – a 10 cm line from "no pain" to "worst pain"; the patient marks a point
  • Verbal Descriptor Scale – no pain, mild, moderate, severe, very severe
  • Wong–Baker FACES scale – faces from smiling to crying; for children (about 3 years and above) and patients with language barriers
  • FLACC scale – Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability; for infants, young children and non-verbal patients
  • Behavioural scales for unconscious and ventilated patients, and the PAINAD scale for patients with dementia

3. Observation

  • Physiological signs (mainly in acute pain) – raised pulse, BP and respiration, sweating, pallor, dilated pupils, nausea
  • Behavioural signs – grimacing, frowning, crying, moaning, clenching teeth, guarding the painful part, restlessness or lying very still, rubbing, withdrawal

4. Factors affecting pain experience

  • Age (children may not express pain; the elderly may under-report), culture (some cultures expect silent endurance), past experience, anxiety and fear, attention, the meaning of pain (labour pain vs cancer pain), fatigue, and family support

5. Documentation

  • Record the pain score, site and character on the chart, and re-assess after interventions

(d) Pharmacological management (3 marks)

1. WHO analgesic ladder

  • Step 1 – mild pain: non-opioids – paracetamol, NSAIDs (ibuprofen, diclofenac) ± adjuvants
  • Step 2 – moderate pain: weak opioids – tramadol, codeine ± non-opioid ± adjuvants
  • Step 3 – severe pain: strong opioids – morphine, fentanyl ± non-opioid ± adjuvants
  • Principles: "by the mouth" (oral route when possible), "by the clock" (regular doses, not only on demand), "by the ladder", "for the individual" and "attention to detail"

2. Adjuvant drugs

  • Antidepressants (amitriptyline) and anticonvulsants (gabapentin, pregabalin, carbamazepine) for neuropathic pain; corticosteroids for swelling and bone pain; muscle relaxants

3. Local and regional anaesthesia

  • Local anaesthetics (lignocaine), nerve blocks, epidural analgesia (post-operative and labour pain)
