4. Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA)

  • A programmed pump lets the patient give himself small doses of an opioid within safe limits

Nursing responsibilities

  • Give analgesics on time, before pain becomes severe; give before painful procedures and physiotherapy
  • Re-assess pain about 30 minutes after an injection and 60 minutes after an oral dose
  • Opioids: watch for respiratory depression (check respiratory rate and sedation level), constipation, nausea, drowsiness and urinary retention; keep naloxone available; follow narcotic register rules
  • NSAIDs: give after food; watch for gastric irritation, bleeding and kidney problems
  • Dispel myths – appropriate opioid use for pain rarely causes addiction

(e) Non-pharmacological management (3 marks)

  • Physical: comfortable positioning, splinting the wound with a pillow when coughing, heat and cold applications, massage, TENS, immobilisation of fractures, exercise and physiotherapy, acupressure
  • Cognitive–behavioural: distraction (music, conversation, TV, play for children), relaxation (deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation), guided imagery, yoga and meditation, biofeedback
  • Patient education: explaining procedures and what sensations to expect reduces fear and pain
  • Emotional and spiritual support: presence, listening, reassurance, prayer, family support
  • Environment: quiet, comfortable surroundings, adequate rest and sleep

Role of the nurse in pain management (summary)

  • Believe the patient's report of pain
  • Assess regularly with a suitable scale
  • Plan combined pharmacological and non-pharmacological care
  • Give analgesics safely and on time
  • Evaluate relief and side effects
  • Document and communicate with the team
  • Educate the patient and family

Conclusion Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience linked with tissue damage, and it is whatever the patient says it is. It may be acute or chronic; cutaneous, somatic or visceral; localised, radiating or referred; nociceptive or neuropathic. Systematic assessment using PQRST and pain scales, analgesics given according to the WHO ladder, and non-drug methods such as positioning, heat and cold, massage, distraction and relaxation together give effective pain relief.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: List the functions of sleep.
answer_html:
Introduction Sleep is a natural, recurring state of reduced consciousness and activity. It is essential for health.

Functions of sleep

  1. Restoration and repair – growth hormone is released during deep sleep; tissues are repaired and proteins built
  2. Conservation of energy – metabolism slows
  3. Memory and learning – the brain consolidates memories
  4. Emotional balance – reduces stress and irritability; maintains mood
  5. Immunity – strengthens the body's defences
  6. Hormonal and metabolic balance – regulation of appetite and blood sugar
  7. Growth and development in children
  8. Clearance of waste products from the brain

Sleep needs (approximate): newborns 14–17 hours, school-age children 9–11 hours, adults 7–9 hours a day.

Nursing: patients in hospital need sleep for recovery – reduce noise, light and interruptions at night.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define pain threshold and pain tolerance.
answer_html:
Pain threshold

  • The lowest intensity of a stimulus at which a person first feels it as painful
  • It is fairly similar among most people

Pain tolerance

  • The maximum intensity or duration of pain a person is willing or able to bear before seeking relief or reacting
  • It varies widely between people

Factors affecting pain tolerance

  • Increase – distraction, strong motivation, beliefs, alcohol, analgesics, adequate rest
  • Decrease – anxiety, fear, fatigue, sleep deprivation, repeated pain, depression
  • Culture, age, sex and past experience also influence it

Nursing importance

  • Accept the patient's report of pain – "pain is whatever the person says it is" (Margo McCaffery)
  • Do not judge pain by how much the patient tolerates; assess with a pain scale and treat early

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the procedure of making an occupied bed.
answer_html:
Introduction An occupied bed is a bed made while the patient remains in it. It is done when the patient cannot get out of bed – strict bed rest, unconsciousness, traction, severe illness or weakness.

Purposes

  • Comfort of the patient; clean, dry, wrinkle-free linen to prevent pressure ulcers
  • Minimum exertion for the patient
  • Opportunity to observe the skin and the patient's condition
  • Hygiene and a tidy unit

Articles

  • Clean bottom sheet, mackintosh (if needed), draw sheet, top sheet, pillow covers, blanket or bedspread
  • Linen hamper (soiled linen bag), gloves if linen is soiled, screens

Procedure

A. Preparation

  1. Check the patient's condition and any restrictions on movement
  2. Explain the procedure; provide privacy with screens; close windows and switch off fans
  3. Hand hygiene; arrange articles in order of use
  4. Get a helper if the patient is heavy or very ill
  5. Adjust the bed to working height; lower the side rail on the working side and keep the other raised

B. Removing and replacing the bottom linen

  1. Loosen the top linen; remove and fold the blanket; keep the patient covered with the top sheet
  2. Remove extra pillows; turn the patient to the far side, facing away (log roll if spinal injury), with the rail up
  3. Roll the soiled bottom linen towards the patient's back
  4. Clean and dry the mattress if needed
  5. Place the clean bottom sheet with its centre fold at the centre of the bed; tuck it at the head, mitre the corners and tuck the side; fan-fold the remaining half against the patient's back
  6. Place the clean mackintosh and draw sheet, tuck them in and fan-fold the remainder
  7. Help the patient roll over the folds onto the clean side; raise the rail
  8. Go to the other side; remove the soiled linen by rolling it inwards and put it directly into the hamper – never on the floor, never shaken, held away from the uniform
  9. Pull the clean linen through; tighten, tuck and mitre the corners so there are no wrinkles

C. Completing the bed

  1. Turn the patient onto the back or into a comfortable position; change the pillow covers and replace the pillows
  2. Spread the clean top sheet over the patient and remove the used one from underneath without exposing him
  3. Place the blanket; make a toe pleat (to allow foot movement and prevent foot drop); mitre the bottom corners; fold the top edge back neatly

D. After care

  1. Lower the bed, raise side rails, keep the call bell within reach
  2. Tidy the unit; send linen to the laundry; hand hygiene
  3. Record and report skin condition and how the patient tolerated the procedure

Points to remember

  • Keep the patient covered; talk to him throughout
  • Protect tubes, drains and IV lines
  • Use good body mechanics; work from head to foot
  • Watch for pain, breathlessness or distress

Conclusion An occupied bed is made without getting the patient out of bed, changing one half of the bed at a time; it keeps the patient clean, comfortable and safe from pressure ulcers with minimum effort for him.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Promoting Safety in Health Care Environment
question: List the safety devices used in hospitals.
answer_html:
Introduction Safety devices protect patients from falls, injuries and accidents in the hospital.

Safety devices

  1. Side rails on beds and stretchers
  2. Low beds and bed and chair alarms
  3. Grab bars in bathrooms and toilets
  4. Call bells (nurse call system) within reach
  5. Non-skid slippers and non-slip floor mats
  6. Wheel locks (brakes) on beds, wheelchairs and trolleys
  7. Walking aids – walkers, canes, crutches
  8. Restraints – used only when necessary, as a last resort
  9. Identification wristbands and allergy bands
  10. Night lights and good lighting
  11. Fire extinguishers, smoke detectors and alarms
  12. Safety belts on stretchers and wheelchairs

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Promoting Safety in Health Care Environment
question: Explain RACE and PASS in fire safety.
answer_html:
Introduction Two simple acronyms help hospital staff respond quickly to a fire.

RACE – the response to a fire

  1. R – Rescue patients and people in immediate danger
  2. A – Alarm – activate the fire alarm and inform the fire control room or fire brigade
  3. C – Contain (confine) the fire – close doors and windows; shut off oxygen supply to the area if safe
  4. E – Extinguish a small fire, or Evacuate the area

PASS – using a fire extinguisher

  1. P – Pull the safety pin
  2. A – Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire
  3. S – Squeeze the handle
  4. S – Sweep from side to side

Remember: do not use lifts during a fire; never use water on electrical or oil fires.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Promoting Safety in Health Care Environment
question: Explain fall risk assessment and the prevention of falls in hospital.
answer_html:
Introduction A fall is an unplanned descent to the floor, with or without injury. Falls are among the most common incidents in hospitals and may cause fractures (especially hip fracture in the elderly), head injury, longer stay and even death. Most falls can be prevented by risk assessment and preventive measures.

A. Risk factors for falls

  • Age above 65 years, history of previous falls
  • Impaired mobility, weakness, poor balance, unsteady gait
  • Confusion, dementia, delirium, sedation
  • Medicines – sedatives, sleeping pills, antihypertensives, diuretics, insulin and oral hypoglycaemics, opioids
  • Postural hypotension, giddiness
  • Urinary urgency, frequency, nocturia – hurrying to the toilet
  • Visual impairment
  • IV lines, catheters and drains
  • Environmental hazards – wet or slippery floors, poor lighting, clutter, high beds, unlocked wheels, poor footwear, unfamiliar surroundings

B. Fall risk assessment

  • Assess on admission, after any change in condition, after a fall, on transfer and at regular intervals
  • Morse Fall Scale – the most widely used tool:
Item Score
History of falling no 0, yes 25
Secondary diagnosis no 0, yes 15
Ambulatory aid none / bed rest / nurse assists 0; crutches, cane or walker 15; holds on to furniture 30
IV line or heparin lock no 0, yes 20
Gait normal / bed rest / wheelchair 0; weak 10; impaired 20
Mental status knows own limits 0; forgets limitations 15
  • A score of 45 or more is commonly taken as high risk (cut-off values vary by hospital)
  • Other tools: Hendrich II fall risk model, paediatric fall scales (Humpty Dumpty)

C. Prevention of falls

  1. Identify high-risk patients – a fall-risk band, sign on the bed
  2. Orient the patient to the room, toilet and call bell
  3. Keep the bed at its lowest position with wheels locked; raise side rails as per policy
  4. Keep the call bell, water, spectacles and personal articles within reach
  5. Regular toileting rounds; bedpan or commode at night for patients with frequency
  6. Non-skid footwear; avoid long, loose clothing
  7. Good lighting, night lights; keep floors dry and clutter-free; put up "wet floor" signs
  8. Grab bars in toilets and bathrooms
  9. Teach patients to change position slowly – sit, dangle legs, then stand (to prevent postural hypotension)
  10. Assist with ambulation; provide walking aids
  11. Review medicines that increase fall risk with the doctor
  12. Frequent observation of confused patients; place them near the nurses' station; involve family members
  13. Use bed alarms; avoid restraints, which may increase injury

D. After a fall

  • Do not lift the patient immediately; assess for injury, check vital signs, inform the doctor, help back to bed safely, observe, fill an incident report and review the risk plan

Conclusion Fall prevention depends on identifying risk factors, assessing risk with tools such as the Morse Fall Scale and applying preventive measures in the environment, care routines and patient education.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Promoting Safety in Health Care Environment
question: Explain the control of the physical environment for patient safety and comfort.
answer_html:
Introduction The physical environment of the ward – temperature, humidity, ventilation, light, noise, odour and cleanliness – directly affects the patient's comfort, rest, safety and recovery. Florence Nightingale stressed that the nurse must manage the environment to help the patient heal.

1. Temperature

  • A comfortable room temperature of about 20–25 °C for most patients
  • Warmer rooms for newborns, the elderly and post-operative patients; cooler rooms for febrile patients
  • Avoid draughts; use fans, coolers, heaters and blankets as needed

2. Humidity

  • Relative humidity of about 40–60%
  • Very dry air irritates the airway; very humid air causes discomfort, sweating and growth of moulds

3. Ventilation

  • Fresh air removes odours, heat, moisture and airborne microorganisms
  • Cross-ventilation through windows; exhaust fans; air-conditioning with filters
  • Isolation rooms for airborne infections (tuberculosis) need negative pressure and frequent air changes; operation theatres need filtered, positive-pressure air

4. Lighting

  • Adequate natural light during the day improves mood and helps the body clock
  • Good artificial light for procedures; night lights to prevent falls; avoid glare in the patient's eyes

5. Noise control

  • Noise disturbs sleep and rest, raises BP and increases stress
  • Speak softly, wear silent footwear, attend to alarms and phones promptly, oil squeaky trolleys, close doors gently, limit visitors, and keep the ward quiet at night
  • The WHO recommends very low noise levels in patient rooms, especially at night

6. Odour control

  • Remove bedpans, vomit bowls, soiled dressings and linen promptly
  • Good ventilation; keep bins covered; maintain toilets; use deodorisers when needed

7. Cleanliness and pest control

  • Daily damp dusting and mopping; terminal cleaning after discharge
  • Pest control – rodents, cockroaches, flies, mosquitoes and bed bugs spread infection and disturb patients; use wire mesh on windows, covered food and waste, regular pest-control treatment

8. Space and layout

  • Adequate space between beds for infection control and privacy; screens or curtains for privacy

9. Reduction of physical hazards

  • Fire safety – no smoking, safe use of oxygen, electrical safety, extinguishers, clear fire exits
  • Electrical safety – check wires and plugs, do not overload sockets, keep fluids away from equipment
  • Chemical safety – label and store disinfectants and drugs safely
  • Radiation safety – shields and limited exposure

Role of the nurse

  • Assesses and adjusts the environment for each patient's needs, supervises cleaning staff and reports hazards

Conclusion Proper control of temperature, humidity, ventilation, lighting, noise, odour, cleanliness and pests, along with removal of hazards, creates a safe, comfortable healing environment.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Promoting Safety in Health Care Environment
question: Define restraint. Explain the types, purposes, indications, legal implications and the guidelines for application of restraints, with nursing care of a restrained patient. (2 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 5)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • A restraint is any method – physical, mechanical or chemical – that restricts a person's freedom of movement, physical activity or normal access to his body
  • Restraints are used only to protect the patient or others from harm, when other measures have failed, and never as punishment or for the convenience of staff
  • Seclusion – keeping a patient alone in a room from which he cannot leave – is also a form of restraint

(b) Types of restraints (3 marks)

1. Physical (mechanical) restraints

  • Wrist and ankle restraints (limb holders) – padded cloth or leather straps; prevent pulling out of tubes and lines
  • Mitten restraints – cover the hands; prevent scratching (eczema, burns) and pulling tubes, while allowing arm movement
  • Elbow restraints – used in infants and children to prevent bending of the elbow and touching the face, IV site or cleft lip repair
  • Jacket (vest) restraint – keeps a confused patient in bed or chair; risk of strangulation if wrongly applied
  • Belt (waist) restraint – on stretchers and wheelchairs
  • Mummy restraint – wrapping an infant in a sheet for short procedures (venepuncture, gastric lavage, eye examination)
  • Clove-hitch restraint – a figure-of-eight knot of bandage around a wrist or ankle
  • Crib nets and crib tops – for children
  • Side rails – act as restraints when used to stop a patient who wants to get out of bed
  • Chairs with locked trays

2. Chemical restraints

  • Drugs – sedatives or antipsychotics – given mainly to control behaviour, not as standard treatment of a condition

3. Environmental restraints

  • Seclusion rooms, locked doors and closed wards

(c) Purposes and indications (2 marks)

Purposes

  • To protect the patient from injury – falls, self-harm
  • To protect others from a violent patient
  • To prevent interference with treatment – pulling out IV lines, catheters, nasogastric tubes, endotracheal tubes, drains, dressings
  • To immobilise a part or a child for examination or a procedure

Indications

  • Confused, disoriented or delirious patients (elderly, post-anaesthesia, head injury, alcohol withdrawal)
  • Violent or aggressive patients who are a danger to themselves or others
  • Restless or semi-conscious patients with tubes and lines
  • Infants and young children during procedures or after surgery (cleft lip, eye surgery)
  • Patients at high risk of falls – only when alternatives have failed

(d) Legal implications and consent (3 marks)

  • Restraint restricts a person's freedom; using it without a valid reason, order or consent may amount to false imprisonment, assault or battery, and can lead to legal action for negligence if the patient is injured
  • Physician's order – restraints (except in an emergency) are used on a written order stating the type, reason and duration; in an emergency the nurse may apply a restraint and obtain the order as soon as possible, as per hospital policy; orders are time-limited and renewed only after re-assessment
  • Informed consent – explain the reason to the patient and the family and obtain consent as per policy; when the patient is not competent, consent is taken from the legal guardian or relatives
  • Least restrictive method for the shortest possible time
  • Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (India) – physical restraint of a person with mental illness may be used only when it is the only means to prevent imminent and immediate harm, must be authorised by the psychiatrist in charge, used no longer than absolutely necessary, recorded in the medical notes, and the nominated representative must be informed within 24 hours; it must never be used as punishment or because of staff shortage; chaining is prohibited; seclusion and solitary confinement are not allowed
  • Documentation is the nurse's main legal protection – reasons, alternatives tried, order, consent, type, time of application and removal, observations and the patient's response
  • The patient's dignity and rights must be respected at all times

(e) Guidelines for application and nursing care of a restrained patient (5 marks)

Before applying

  1. Try alternatives first – frequent observation, family member at the bedside, reorientation, diversion, pain relief, toileting schedule, low bed, bed alarm, hiding tubes under clothing or bandage, moving the patient near the nurses' station
  2. Assess the patient's condition, the reason for restraint and the risk of injury
  3. Obtain the doctor's order and consent as per policy
  4. Explain the reason to the patient (even if confused) and the family in a calm, simple way
  5. Select the correct type and size of restraint

During application

  1. Ensure privacy; have enough staff for violent patients
  2. Pad bony prominences (wrists, ankles) to prevent friction and pressure injury
  3. Place the patient in good body alignment, with the head of the bed slightly raised to prevent aspiration
  4. Apply the restraint snugly but not tightly – allow two fingers between the restraint and the skin
  5. Tie with a quick-release knot (bow or clove hitch) to the bed frame, not to the side rails (moving the rail can injure the patient)
  6. Never restrain a patient face down or tie a jacket restraint so that it can tighten across the chest or neck

Care while the restraint is in place

  1. Observe every 15–30 minutes – circulation (colour, warmth, capillary refill, pulse distal to the restraint), sensation, movement and skin condition
  2. Release the restraint at least every 2 hours (one limb at a time for violent patients) to give range-of-motion exercises, change position, give skin care and check the skin
  3. Meet basic needs – fluids, food, toileting, hygiene, comfort and sleep
  4. Keep the call bell within reach and speak to the patient often; never leave a restrained patient unattended for long
  5. Watch for complications – skin abrasions, pressure ulcers, impaired circulation, nerve damage, fractures, dehydration, constipation, incontinence, aspiration, contractures, strangulation or asphyxia, increased agitation, fear, humiliation and depression
  6. Re-assess the need for restraint regularly and remove it as soon as possible
  7. Provide emotional support and maintain dignity; allow family visits

Documentation

  1. Record the behaviour that required restraint, alternatives tried, doctor's order and consent, type of restraint, time applied and removed, observations every 15–30 minutes, care given, the patient's response and family information

Conclusion A restraint is any method that limits a patient's freedom of movement, used only to prevent harm when other measures fail. Physical, chemical and environmental restraints have definite purposes and indications but also serious risks and legal implications. With a valid order, consent, the least restrictive method, correct application, frequent observation, regular release, attention to basic needs and complete documentation, the nurse keeps the restrained patient safe and protects his dignity and rights.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Promoting Safety in Health Care Environment
question: Name the classes of fire and the extinguishers used for each.
answer_html:
Introduction Fires are classified by the material that is burning, because each needs a suitable extinguisher.

Class Burning material Extinguisher
A ordinary solids – wood, paper, cloth, linen, plastics water, foam, ABC dry powder
B flammable liquids – petrol, oil, spirit, alcohol-based hand rub, paint foam, CO₂, dry powder – never a water jet
C flammable gases – LPG, piped gas dry powder; shut off the gas supply
D burning metals – magnesium, sodium special dry powder
Electrical electrical equipment and wiring CO₂ or dry powder; switch off the power; never water

Note: ABC (multipurpose) dry powder extinguishers are common in hospitals; CO₂ extinguishers are preferred near electrical and electronic equipment (ICU, OT). Kitchen oil fires need wet chemical extinguishers or a fire blanket.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Promoting Safety in Health Care Environment
question: What are the International Patient Safety Goals?
answer_html:
Introduction The International Patient Safety Goals (IPSGs), set by the Joint Commission International and followed in accreditation standards, address the commonest causes of harm to patients.

The six goals

  1. Identify patients correctly – use two identifiers (name and hospital number or date of birth), never the bed number
  2. Improve effective communication – read back verbal and telephone orders and critical results; structured handover (SBAR)
  3. Improve the safety of high-alert medications – concentrated potassium chloride, insulin, heparin; care with look-alike, sound-alike drugs
  4. Ensure safe surgery – correct patient, correct procedure, correct site; site marking, "time-out", surgical safety checklist
  5. Reduce the risk of health care-associated infections – hand hygiene
  6. Reduce the risk of harm from falls – fall risk assessment and prevention

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
unit_title: Promoting Safety in Health Care Environment
question: Explain fire safety in hospitals and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Hospitals have a high risk of fire – oxygen, flammable liquids, electrical equipment, kitchens and linen are present, and many patients cannot move by themselves. A fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen (the fire triangle); oxygen-rich areas such as ICUs burn especially fiercely. Fires in hospital newborn units and ICUs in India, including the one at the Bhandara District Hospital in January 2021, have shown the need for strict fire safety.

A. Common causes of hospital fires

  • Electrical short circuits, overloaded sockets and extension boards, faulty equipment
  • Oxygen leaks and use of oxygen near heat or sparks
  • Smoking, spirit lamps, heaters, kitchen fires
  • Flammable chemicals stored carelessly

B. Prevention

  • Regular electrical safety checks; avoid overloading sockets; switch off unused equipment; report sparking and damaged cables
  • Oxygen safety – "No Smoking" signs; check for leaks; store cylinders upright and chained, away from heat; keep oil and grease away from regulators; turn off oxygen when not in use
  • Store spirit and alcohol in small quantities in a cool place
  • Keep corridors and exits clear; dispose of waste promptly
  • Fire detection and fighting systems – smoke detectors, alarms, sprinklers, extinguishers and hose reels, regularly checked and refilled
  • Exit signs, emergency lighting and a displayed evacuation plan
  • Fire safety audits, fire department clearance, staff training and regular mock drills
  • Every nurse should know where the extinguishers, alarms, exits and oxygen zone valves are

C. Role of the nurse during a fire

  • Follow RACE – Rescue patients in immediate danger, raise the Alarm, Contain the fire by closing doors and windows, Extinguish a small fire or Evacuate
  • Use extinguishers by PASS – Pull the pin, Aim at the base, Squeeze the handle, Sweep side to side
  • Evacuation:
    • move patients horizontally first (to a safe area on the same floor beyond fire doors), then vertically by stairs if needed
    • patients in immediate danger first; then walking patients (guided), then wheelchair patients, then bed-bound patients
    • never use lifts
    • turn off the oxygen zone valve when instructed, ensuring patients on oxygen have portable cylinders
    • crawl low under smoke; cover the nose and mouth with a wet cloth
  • Account for all patients using the census; take essential records and medicines if safe
  • Stay calm and reassure patients and relatives

D. After the fire

  • Head count; care of the injured; report and document; review causes and improve safety

Conclusion Fire safety in hospitals depends on preventing electrical and oxygen hazards, maintaining detection and fighting equipment, training staff and practising drills; during a fire the nurse follows RACE and PASS and evacuates patients safely.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: What is LAMA? State the nurse's responsibilities.
answer_html:
Definition LAMA (Leave Against Medical Advice), also called DAMA (Discharge Against Medical Advice), is when a patient (or his guardian) leaves the hospital before the doctor advises discharge, against medical advice.

Nurse's responsibilities

  1. Inform the doctor and the nursing in-charge immediately
  2. Find out the reason (cost, fear, dissatisfaction, family problems) and try to solve it
  3. The doctor explains the risks of leaving; the nurse supports this
  4. Get the LAMA form signed by the patient or relative, with a witness
  5. Do not detain the patient by force – that would be illegal
  6. Give a discharge summary, return belongings and remove IV lines
  7. Record the details in the nursing notes and register; inform the police if it is a medico-legal case

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: What is absconding? List the actions to be taken.
answer_html:
Definition Absconding is when a patient leaves the hospital without informing anyone and without permission, before discharge.

Actions to be taken

  1. Search the ward, toilets and hospital premises
  2. Inform the nursing in-charge, the doctor and the hospital security immediately
  3. Inform the relatives
  4. Inform the police if the patient is a medico-legal case, a psychiatric patient, a minor or a prisoner
  5. List and keep the patient's belongings safely
  6. Write the time last seen, the description of the patient and all actions taken in the nursing notes and the incident report

Prevention: regular observation and head counts, especially of confused, psychiatric and medico-legal patients.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: List the medico-legal issues related to admission and discharge.
answer_html:
Introduction Some aspects of admission and discharge have legal importance, and the nurse must handle them carefully.

Medico-legal issues

  1. Informed consent for admission, treatment and procedures
  2. Medico-legal cases (MLC) – road accidents, burns, poisoning, assault, suspected crime – must be registered and the police informed
  3. Correct identification of the patient – identity band
  4. Patient's valuables – listed, signed and safely kept or handed over to relatives
  5. Confidentiality of records
  6. LAMA (DAMA) – signed consent and documentation
  7. Absconding – reporting to the authorities
  8. Death – death certificate, handing over the body, post-mortem in MLC
  9. Accurate documentation of all events and times

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the role of the nurse in the admission of a patient.
answer_html:
Introduction Admission is the entry of a patient into a hospital for observation, investigation, treatment or care. Admission can be frightening – a strange place, strange people and worry about illness. The way the nurse receives the patient forms his first impression of the hospital and builds trust.

Types of admission

  • Emergency, routine (planned or elective), day-care, transfer from another unit or hospital, and medico-legal admissions

Role of the nurse

1. Preparation of the unit before arrival

  • Prepare an admission bed and a clean, well-equipped unit
  • Keep ready: thermometer, BP apparatus, stethoscope, weighing scale, admission forms and case file, identity band, hospital gown, bedpan or urinal, kidney tray, water jug and glass
  • Arrange special equipment according to the condition – oxygen, suction, IV stand, monitor

2. Receiving the patient

  • Greet the patient and family warmly by name, introduce yourself and make the patient comfortable
  • Check the admission order and papers; put on the identity band
  • Attend first to emergency needs – airway, breathing, bleeding, pain

3. Orientation

  • Show the patient the bed, locker, toilet and bathroom, call bell and nurses' station
  • Explain ward routines – meal times, doctors' rounds, visiting hours, rules about smoking and food from outside
  • Introduce the patient to staff and neighbouring patients
  • Explain the patient's rights and responsibilities

4. Care of belongings and valuables

  • List valuables (jewellery, money, mobile phone) in the presence of a witness; hand them to relatives or keep them in safe custody with a receipt; record and sign

5. Assessment

  • Record vital signs, height and weight
  • Take a nursing history and do a physical assessment; note allergies, current medicines and special needs
  • Collect specimens as ordered (urine, blood)

6. Communication and documentation

  • Inform the doctor about the admission; start the prescribed treatment
  • Complete the admission register, case sheet, TPR chart and census
  • Obtain consent for treatment as per policy

7. Psychological support

  • Reduce anxiety by explaining procedures and answering questions; respect privacy and culture
  • Allow a relative to stay if needed (children, elderly, critically ill)

8. Medico-legal admissions

  • Register the case as MLC, inform the police, preserve evidence (clothes, poison containers, vomitus) and record accurately

9. Care planning

  • Prepare an initial nursing care plan based on the assessment

Conclusion By preparing the unit, receiving the patient warmly, orienting him, caring for valuables, assessing, documenting, supporting emotionally and handling legal aspects, the nurse makes admission safe and reassuring.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the types of discharge.
answer_html:
Introduction Discharge is the formal release of a patient from the hospital after treatment, or when he leaves care for other reasons. The type of discharge decides the procedure and the legal documents needed.

1. Planned (routine) discharge

  • The doctor decides that the patient has recovered sufficiently to go home
  • Discharge planning starts from admission; the patient and family are prepared and taught home care
  • A discharge summary, prescriptions and follow-up date are given

2. Discharge against medical advice (LAMA / DAMA)

  • The patient insists on leaving before the doctor advises discharge
  • The risks are explained; a LAMA form is signed by the patient or relative with a witness; the event is recorded
  • The patient is not detained by force; the police are informed in medico-legal cases

3. Absconding

  • The patient leaves without informing or without permission
  • The ward and premises are searched; the in-charge, doctor, relatives and (when required) police are informed; belongings are listed and an incident report is written

4. Transfer

  • Internal transfer – from one ward or unit to another in the same hospital (e.g. from ICU to ward, from medicine to surgery)
  • External transfer – to another hospital for specialised care or at the family's request
  • A transfer report goes with the patient; the receiving unit is informed in advance; the patient is escorted with records and medicines

5. Referral

  • The patient is sent to another hospital, specialist or service for further investigation or treatment (e.g. from PHC to district hospital)
  • A referral slip with diagnosis, treatment given and reason for referral is sent; transport and escort are arranged for serious patients

6. Discharge on request

  • The patient or family requests early discharge and the doctor agrees after assessing the condition

7. Discharge to another facility

  • To a rehabilitation centre, nursing home, hospice or old-age home

8. Discharge on death

  • After death, the body is handed over to the relatives (or the police in MLC) after the death certificate and procedures

Role of the nurse in all types

  • Verify the order, inform and prepare the patient and family, complete documents, return belongings, give instructions and record all details

Conclusion Discharge may be planned, against medical advice, by absconding, by transfer, by referral, on request, to another facility or on death; each type has its own procedure and legal requirements that the nurse must follow.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain discharge planning.
answer_html:
Introduction Discharge planning is the systematic process of preparing a patient and family to move from the hospital to home or another care setting, so that care continues safely and readmission is prevented. It begins on admission and involves the whole health team.

Purposes

  • Continuity of care after discharge
  • Prepare the patient and family for self-care
  • Prevent complications and readmission
  • Reduce the length of hospital stay
  • Make the best use of community resources

Steps of discharge planning

1. Assessment (from admission)

  • The patient's self-care ability, mobility, mental status and learning needs
  • Home environment – stairs, toilet, cleanliness, distance from the hospital
  • Family support and caregiver availability; financial situation
  • Need for equipment (walker, oxygen, glucometer) and services (physiotherapy, dressing, home nursing)

2. Planning

  • Set goals with the patient and family; involve doctors, dietitian, physiotherapist and social worker
  • Decide the likely date of discharge and the teaching needed

3. Patient and family education (memory aid "M-E-T-H-O-D")

  • M – Medications: names, dose, time, route, side effects, importance of not stopping suddenly
  • E – Environment and Exercise: safe home, activity limits, exercises
  • T – Treatment: wound care, catheter or stoma care, insulin injection – with demonstration and return demonstration
  • H – Health teaching: warning signs to report (fever, bleeding, wound discharge, breathlessness), hygiene, lifestyle
  • O – Out-patient follow-up: date, place, investigations to bring
  • D – Diet: special diet, fluids

4. Arranging resources

  • Referral to community health workers, home-care services, rehabilitation centres, support groups
  • Arranging equipment and transport; information on government schemes

5. Implementation on the day of discharge

  • Discharge summary, prescriptions and certificates; handing over medicines; final assessment

6. Evaluation and follow-up

  • Check understanding before discharge; follow-up phone calls or home visits where possible

Conclusion Discharge planning, starting at admission, assesses needs, educates the patient and family, arranges resources and ensures continuity of care, preventing complications and readmission.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define admission and discharge. Describe the admission procedure and the discharge procedure, including the role of the nurse and the care of the unit after discharge. (2 + 6 + 7)
answer_html:
(a) Definitions (2 marks)

  • Admission: the entry of a patient into a hospital (or any health care facility) for observation, investigation, diagnosis, treatment or care, for a period of stay
  • Discharge: the formal release of a patient from the hospital after treatment, or when he leaves care for other reasons (against advice, transfer, referral, death)
  • Types of admission: emergency, routine (planned or elective), day-care, transfer and medico-legal
  • Types of discharge: planned, LAMA (DAMA), absconding, transfer, referral, on request, to another facility, and on death

(b) Admission procedure with the role of the nurse (6 marks)

1. Preparation of the unit

  • Clean the unit; make an admission bed (top linen fan-folded for easy entry)
  • Keep ready the admission tray: thermometer, BP apparatus, stethoscope, watch, weighing machine, measuring tape, torch
  • Forms: admission form, case sheet, TPR chart, nursing assessment sheet, intake–output chart, consent forms
  • Patient articles: hospital gown, identity band, bedpan or urinal, kidney tray, jug and glass, towel
  • Special equipment as per diagnosis – oxygen, suction, IV stand, monitor, cardiac table

2. Receiving the patient

  • Greet the patient and relatives courteously, call him by name and introduce yourself
  • Check the admission order, OPD papers and identity; apply the identity band (name, age, IP number)
  • Help the patient to bed; ensure privacy and comfort; attend first to urgent needs

3. Orientation to the ward

  • Bed, locker, call bell, light switches, toilet and bathroom, nurses' station
  • Ward routines – meal times, doctors' rounds, visiting hours, rules, fire exits
  • Introduction to staff and neighbouring patients
  • Patients' rights and responsibilities

4. Changing clothes and care of belongings

  • Help the patient change into a hospital gown (as per policy)
  • Valuables – list them in the presence of the patient, relative and a witness; hand them over to relatives or keep in safe custody with a receipt; record and sign in the valuables register
  • Label and store clothing

5. Initial assessment

  • Vital signs, height, weight, general condition, level of consciousness, pain
  • Nursing history – present illness, past history, allergies, current medicines, habits, family history
  • Physical examination (head-to-toe), risk assessments (falls, pressure ulcers)
  • Collect specimens – urine, blood – as ordered

6. Informing the doctor and starting treatment

  • Inform the doctor; carry out orders; arrange investigations

7. Consent

  • Obtain general consent for treatment; special consents later for procedures and surgery

8. Documentation

  • Admission register, census, case sheet, TPR chart, nursing notes, diet sheet; inform the dietary department

9. Psychological support and health teaching

  • Explain the illness and procedures in simple words, answer questions, reduce fear; allow an attendant as per policy

10. Medico-legal admission

  • Register as MLC, inform the police, preserve evidence (clothes, weapons, poison containers, vomitus, gastric lavage samples), record findings carefully, and keep the patient under observation

11. Initial care plan

  • Identify nursing problems and plan care

Patients' rights to be respected during admission and discharge

  • The Charter of Patients' Rights (National Human Rights Commission, 2018) includes the right to information about illness and costs, records and reports, emergency care, informed consent, confidentiality, dignity and privacy, non-discrimination, a second opinion, safety and quality care, proper referral and transfer, and the right to take discharge or receive the body of a deceased relative without being detained for disputed dues
  • The nurse explains these rights and responsibilities in simple words and protects them at every step

Common problems at admission and how the nurse helps

  • Fear and anxiety – a calm, friendly welcome and clear explanation
  • Language barrier – an interpreter or a staff member who speaks the patient's language
  • Financial worry – information about insurance and government schemes; referral to the medical social worker
  • Separation from family – flexible visiting, an attendant for children and the elderly

(c) Discharge procedure with the role of the nurse (7 marks)

1. Discharge planning (begins on admission)

  • Assess self-care needs, home environment and family support; teach throughout the stay

2. Verify the discharge order

  • Check the written discharge order of the doctor

3. Inform the patient and family in advance

  • Give time to arrange transport and settle formalities

4. Health education (M-E-T-H-O-D)

  • Medicines – name, dose, time, route, side effects; exercise and activity; treatment at home (wound care, insulin); health teaching on hygiene, warning signs and lifestyle; out-patient follow-up date; diet
  • Use demonstration and return demonstration; give written instructions in the patient's language

5. Documents

  • Discharge summary (diagnosis, treatment, investigations, condition at discharge, advice, follow-up), prescription, medical certificates, investigation reports and X-rays
  • Settlement of bills and discharge clearance as per hospital policy; insurance papers

6. Physical preparation

  • Record final vital signs and assess the condition; inform the doctor if there is any change
  • Remove IV cannula and other devices as ordered; give a final dressing if needed
  • Help the patient to dress

7. Return of belongings

  • Return valuables and belongings against the list; get the patient's or relative's signature

8. Medicines

  • Hand over medicines with instructions; return unused ward medicines to the pharmacy

9. Escorting the patient

  • Take the patient to the vehicle in a wheelchair or on a stretcher, with an attendant; say goodbye courteously

10. Recording and informing

  • Record the discharge in the nursing notes, discharge register and census; inform the dietary, accounts and records departments; send the case file to the medical records department

11. Special discharges

  • LAMA – signed form with witness; absconding – search, inform, incident report; transfer and referral – transfer report, escort; death – last offices, death certificate, handing over the body

(d) Care of the unit after discharge

  • Remove all linen; send it to the laundry (infected linen separately as per policy)
  • Clean and disinfect the mattress, pillow (with protective covers), bed frame, locker, over-bed table, call bell and equipment; air the mattress and pillow in sunlight where possible
  • Clean, disinfect or sterilise reusable articles (bedpan, kidney tray, jug); discard disposables
  • Terminal disinfection of the room after an infectious patient
  • Make a closed bed; replenish supplies; keep the unit ready for the next admission
  • Inform the admission desk that the bed is available

Conclusion Admission is the entry of a patient into hospital and discharge is his formal release. A well-organised admission – preparation, warm reception, orientation, care of valuables, assessment, documentation and support – builds trust, while planned discharge with health education, documents, return of belongings and proper records ensures continuity of care. Careful cleaning of the unit after discharge prevents cross-infection.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: What is informed consent? List its essential elements.
answer_html:
Definition Informed consent is the voluntary agreement given by a competent person (or legal guardian) to undergo a procedure, treatment or research, after being given adequate information about its nature, purpose, benefits, risks, alternatives and the consequences of refusal, in a language he understands.

Essential elements

  1. Capacity (competence) – adult of sound mind; a guardian consents for minors and those unable to decide
  2. Disclosure of adequate information
  3. Understanding by the patient
  4. Voluntariness – no force or pressure
  5. Documentation – written consent signed by the patient, doctor and a witness for major procedures

Types: implied (e.g. holding out the arm for BP) and expressed (verbal or written). In a life-threatening emergency, treatment may be given without consent.

Nurse's role: the doctor explains and obtains consent; the nurse may witness the signature, ensures the patient understood and was not sedated while signing, informs the doctor of any doubts and checks the consent form before surgery.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define body mechanics.
answer_html:
Definition Body mechanics is the efficient, coordinated and safe use of the body (muscles, bones, joints and nervous system) to maintain balance, posture and body alignment while moving, lifting, bending and carrying out daily activities.

Elements

  1. Body alignment (posture) – correct position of body parts in relation to each other
  2. Balance – a stable centre of gravity over a wide base of support
  3. Coordinated body movement

Importance: prevents back injuries in nurses, reduces fatigue, conserves energy and ensures the safety of patients during moving and lifting.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Mention the types of exercise.
answer_html:
Introduction Exercise maintains muscle strength, joint mobility and circulation, especially in bedridden patients.

A. Range-of-motion (ROM) exercises

  1. Active ROM – done by the patient himself
  2. Active-assisted ROM – the patient moves the joint with help from the nurse
  3. Passive ROM – the nurse moves each joint through its full range when the patient cannot

B. Other types

  1. Isotonic – muscle shortens and the joint moves (walking, lifting legs)
  2. Isometric – muscle contracts without joint movement (tightening the thigh muscles in bed – quadriceps setting)
  3. Isokinetic (resistive) – movement against resistance (exercise machines)
  4. Aerobic – walking, cycling, swimming; anaerobic – weight lifting
  5. Breathing exercises – deep breathing, incentive spirometry

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: List the hazards of immobility.
answer_html:
Introduction Prolonged bed rest affects almost every system of the body.

Hazards of immobility

  1. Musculoskeletal – muscle wasting, contractures (foot drop), joint stiffness, osteoporosis
  2. Cardiovascular – postural hypotension, increased heart workload, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism
  3. Respiratory – poor chest expansion, pooling of secretions, hypostatic pneumonia, atelectasis
  4. Skin – pressure ulcers
  5. Gastrointestinal – loss of appetite, constipation
  6. Urinary – urinary stasis, renal stones, urinary infection
  7. Metabolic – loss of protein (negative nitrogen balance), slow healing
  8. Psychological – boredom, depression, disorientation, dependency

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the principles of body mechanics.
answer_html:
Introduction Body mechanics is the coordinated, efficient use of the body to maintain balance, posture and alignment during movement. Nurses lift, turn, move and transfer patients many times a day; back injury is one of the most common occupational problems in nursing. Following the principles of body mechanics protects both the nurse and the patient.

Key terms

  • Centre of gravity – the point where the body's weight is concentrated (at about the level of the second sacral vertebra in standing adults)
  • Line of gravity – an imaginary vertical line through the centre of gravity
  • Base of support – the area on which the body rests (the feet)

Principles of body mechanics

1. Wide base of support

  • Stand with feet apart (about shoulder width), one foot slightly forward – increases stability

2. Lower the centre of gravity

  • Bend at the hips and knees (squat), not at the waist, when lifting or moving low objects – increases stability and uses the legs

3. Keep the line of gravity within the base of support

  • Keep the back straight and the body balanced

4. Keep the load close to the body

  • Hold the patient or object close to your centre of gravity – reduces strain on the back

5. Use the large, strong muscles

  • Use the muscles of the legs, thighs and arms rather than the back

6. Avoid twisting

  • Face the direction of movement; turn by pivoting the feet, not by twisting the spine

7. Push, pull, roll or slide instead of lifting

  • Moving an object on a level surface by pulling or rolling takes less effort; use slide sheets and turning sheets to reduce friction

8. Use your body weight as a counterweight

  • Rock backwards or forwards to add force

9. Tighten the abdominal and gluteal muscles (internal girdle) before moving

10. Work at a comfortable height

  • Raise the bed to waist level before giving care; lower it afterwards for safety

11. Get help and use mechanical aids

  • Do not lift heavy patients alone; use mechanical lifts, transfer boards and trolleys
  • Coordinate with helpers – count "one, two, three" and move together

12. Smooth, rhythmic movements

  • Avoid jerky movements; alternate periods of rest and activity

13. Explain to the patient and encourage him to help as much as possible

Benefits

  • Prevents back strain and injury in nurses
  • Reduces fatigue and conserves energy
  • Ensures the comfort and safety of patients

Conclusion A wide base, low centre of gravity, straight back, load close to the body, use of leg muscles, avoiding twisting, pulling or rolling instead of lifting, and teamwork form the basis of safe body mechanics.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the nursing interventions for impaired body alignment and mobility.
answer_html:
Introduction Body alignment is the correct position of body parts in relation to one another, which reduces strain on muscles and joints. Impaired mobility is a limitation in independent, purposeful movement of the body. It occurs in paralysis, fractures, arthritis, pain, weakness, unconsciousness and after surgery. Nursing interventions aim to maintain alignment, prevent complications and restore mobility.

1. Assessment

  • Posture, gait, range of motion of joints, muscle strength, balance, activity tolerance and ability to perform daily activities
  • Risk of falls and pressure ulcers (Morse, Braden scales); use of aids

2. Positioning and maintaining alignment

  • Change position at least every 2 hours; use a turning schedule
  • Comfort devices: pillows to support limbs; trochanter rolls to prevent external rotation of the hips; foot board or splints to prevent foot drop; hand rolls to keep fingers in a functional position; small pillow under the head; avoid a pillow under the knees for long periods (risk of flexion contracture and DVT)
  • Use positions such as supine, lateral, prone, semi-prone (Sims') and Fowler's in rotation

3. Range-of-motion exercises

  • Passive ROM for unconscious and paralysed patients; active-assisted and active ROM as the patient improves
  • Move each joint through its full range 2–3 times a day, 5–10 times each, gently, without causing pain

4. Muscle-strengthening exercises

  • Isometric exercises – quadriceps and gluteal setting in bed
  • Exercises with weights or resistance bands as advised by the physiotherapist

5. Moving and transferring the patient

  • Use body mechanics, turning sheets and slide sheets; transfer from bed to chair or stretcher safely with wheel locks applied; use mechanical lifts when needed

6. Early ambulation and assisting with walking

  • Dangle the legs at the bedside before standing (prevents postural hypotension)
  • Use a gait belt; stand on the patient's weak side; start with short distances
  • Teach the correct use of walking aids – cane (held on the strong side), walker, crutches

7. Prevention of complications

  • Skin care and pressure relief; deep breathing and coughing; leg exercises and compression stockings for DVT prevention; fluids and fibre to prevent constipation

8. Self-care and independence

  • Encourage the patient to do as much as possible himself; provide adaptive devices

9. Psychological support and education

  • Encourage, motivate, involve the family, and teach home exercises

Conclusion Correct positioning with comfort devices, regular turning, ROM and strengthening exercises, safe transfers, early ambulation with aids and prevention of complications maintain alignment and restore mobility.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the Braden and Norton scales for pressure ulcer risk assessment.
answer_html:
Introduction A pressure ulcer (bed sore, decubitus ulcer, pressure injury) is a localised injury to the skin and underlying tissue, usually over a bony prominence, caused by pressure, shear and friction. Risk assessment scales help the nurse identify patients at risk early so that preventive measures start in time. Assessment is done on admission and regularly thereafter.

A. Braden scale (Bergstrom and Braden) The most widely used scale. It has six sub-scales:

Sub-scale What is assessed Score
Sensory perception ability to respond to pressure-related discomfort 1–4
Moisture degree to which skin is exposed to moisture (sweat, urine, faeces) 1–4
Activity degree of physical activity (bedfast to walks frequently) 1–4
Mobility ability to change and control body position 1–4
Nutrition usual food intake pattern 1–4
Friction and shear sliding in bed, need for help in moving 1–3
  • Total score: 6–23; a lower score means higher risk
  • Risk levels: 15–18 mild risk; 13–14 moderate risk; 10–12 high risk; 9 or below – very high risk
  • A score of 18 or less generally indicates the patient is at risk

B. Norton scale (Doreen Norton, 1962) The first pressure ulcer risk scale. It has five parameters, each scored 1–4:

Parameter 4 3 2 1
Physical condition good fair poor very bad
Mental condition alert apathetic confused stuporous
Activity ambulant walks with help chair-bound bed-bound
Mobility full slightly limited very limited immobile
Incontinence none occasional usually urine double (urine and faeces)
  • Total score: 5–20; a score of 14 or less indicates risk, and below 12 indicates high risk

C. Comparison

Point Braden Norton
Items 6 5
Score range 6–23 5–20
At risk 18 or less 14 or less
Special features includes nutrition, friction and shear includes mental condition and incontinence

D. Nursing use

  • Score on admission and at regular intervals (e.g. daily or each shift in ICU) and whenever the condition changes
  • For at-risk patients: reposition every 2 hours, pressure-relieving mattresses, keep skin clean and dry, manage incontinence, good nutrition and fluids, avoid friction and shear (lift, do not drag), protect heels and elbows, inspect the skin daily
  • Record the score and the preventive plan

Conclusion The Braden (6 items, 6–23) and Norton (5 items, 5–20) scales help nurses identify patients at risk of pressure ulcers; low scores call for intensive preventive care.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the nursing care of a patient with a plaster cast.
answer_html:
Introduction A cast is a rigid external device made of plaster of Paris (POP) or synthetic material (fibreglass) applied to immobilise a fractured bone or injured part, maintain alignment and allow healing. A splint is a less rigid support (plaster slab, Thomas splint, cock-up splint, air splint) used to immobilise a part temporarily or long term. Careful nursing care prevents serious complications such as compartment syndrome.

1. Care of a fresh (wet) cast

  • A POP cast takes about 24–48 hours to dry completely; fibreglass dries within about 30 minutes
  • Leave the cast uncovered to dry; do not use heaters or hair dryers (they cause burns and uneven drying)
  • Handle the wet cast with the palms, not the fingertips (fingertip dents cause pressure points)
  • Support it on pillows without pressure; turn the patient every 2 hours to allow even drying

2. Elevation

  • Elevate the limb on pillows above the level of the heart for the first 24–48 hours to reduce swelling

3. Neurovascular assessment (most important)

  • Check the fingers or toes every hour for the first 24 hours, then every 4 hours
  • The 5 Ps: pain (especially pain out of proportion or on passive stretching), pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia (tingling, numbness), paralysis; also coldness, swelling and slow capillary refill (more than 2–3 seconds)
  • Report immediately – these may indicate compartment syndrome, which needs urgent splitting or removal of the cast

4. Skin care

  • Keep the edges smooth – petal the rough edges with tape; inspect the skin around the edges for redness and irritation
  • Never insert objects (pencils, sticks) to scratch under the cast; itching may be relieved by cool air from a fan

5. Observation for complications

  • Pressure sores under the cast – burning pain, a "hot spot", foul smell
  • Infection – fever, foul odour, discharge staining the cast
  • Bleeding – mark the stained area on the cast with the time and watch for spreading
  • Cast syndrome (with body casts) – nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension
  • Joint stiffness and muscle wasting

6. Keep the cast clean and dry

  • Cover with plastic during bathing; protect from urine and faeces (hip spica) with waterproof material

7. Exercise and mobility

  • Isometric exercises of muscles inside the cast; ROM exercises of joints not in the cast
  • Teach crutch walking or the use of a walker; use slings for arm casts

8. Patient education

  • Keep the limb elevated, move fingers and toes, report warning signs (pain, numbness, colour change, foul smell), do not wet or break the cast, keep follow-up appointments

9. Care after cast removal

  • Wash the skin gently, apply moisturiser, do not scrub off dead skin; continue exercises; support the limb until strength returns

Conclusion Care of a patient in a cast centres on proper drying, elevation, frequent neurovascular checks for the 5 Ps, skin care, observation for complications, exercises and patient education.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the hazards (effects) of immobility on the various body systems and the nursing care of an immobilised patient. (7 + 8)
answer_html:
Introduction Immobility is the inability to move about freely and independently. It may be prescribed (bed rest after surgery, fractures, traction) or due to illness (paralysis, unconsciousness, severe weakness, pain, depression). Although bed rest has benefits – it reduces oxygen needs, pain and strain on injured parts – prolonged immobility affects every system of the body.

(a) Hazards of immobility on the body systems (7 marks)

1. Musculoskeletal system

  • Muscle atrophy and weakness – muscles can lose about 10–15% of their strength each week of complete bed rest ("disuse atrophy")
  • Contractures – permanent shortening of muscles and tendons, fixing joints in abnormal positions: foot drop (plantar flexion), wrist drop, hip and knee flexion contractures
  • Joint stiffness and ankylosis
  • Disuse osteoporosis – loss of calcium from bones makes them weak and prone to fracture
  • Reduced endurance and poor coordination

2. Cardiovascular system

  • Orthostatic (postural) hypotension – a fall in BP on sitting or standing, causing dizziness and fainting
  • Increased cardiac workload – the heart works harder in the lying position
  • Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) – due to Virchow's triad: venous stasis, hypercoagulability and injury to the vessel wall; signs are pain, swelling, warmth and redness of the calf
  • Pulmonary embolism – a clot breaks off and blocks a pulmonary artery; can be fatal
  • Dependent oedema of the sacrum and legs

3. Respiratory system

  • Decreased chest expansion and shallow breathing
  • Stasis (pooling) of secretions in the lungs; weak cough
  • Hypostatic pneumonia and atelectasis (collapse of alveoli)
  • Reduced oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange

4. Integumentary system (skin)

  • Pressure ulcers over bony prominences – sacrum, heels, hips (greater trochanter), elbows, shoulder blades, occiput, ears
  • Due to pressure, shear, friction, moisture and poor nutrition

5. Gastrointestinal system

  • Loss of appetite, indigestion, flatulence
  • Constipation and faecal impaction – reduced peristalsis, weak abdominal muscles, difficulty using a bedpan, lack of privacy, low fibre and fluid intake

6. Urinary system

  • Urinary stasis – difficult to empty the bladder completely while lying down
  • Renal calculi (stones) – calcium released from bones (hypercalciuria) plus stasis
  • Urinary tract infection, retention and incontinence

7. Metabolic system

  • Decreased metabolic rate
  • Negative nitrogen balance – breakdown of body protein; delayed wound healing
  • Calcium imbalance (raised blood and urine calcium)
  • Fluid and electrolyte imbalance; impaired temperature regulation

8. Nervous system and psychosocial effects

  • Sensory deprivation, boredom, disorientation, confusion (especially in the elderly)
  • Anxiety, depression, frustration, anger, sleep disturbance
  • Loss of self-esteem, dependency, changes in roles and body image, social isolation
  • In children – delayed development

Summary

System Main hazards
Musculoskeletal atrophy, contractures, foot drop, osteoporosis
Cardiovascular postural hypotension, DVT, embolism
Respiratory hypostatic pneumonia, atelectasis
Skin pressure ulcers
GI anorexia, constipation
Urinary stasis, stones, infection
Metabolic negative nitrogen balance, poor healing
Psychological depression, disorientation, dependency

(b) Nursing care of an immobilised patient (8 marks)

1. Assessment

  • Level of mobility, muscle strength, ROM, skin condition, breathing, bowel and bladder pattern, nutrition, mental state
  • Risk scores – Braden or Norton (pressure ulcers), Morse (falls), DVT risk

2. Musculoskeletal care

  • Change position every 2 hours; maintain good body alignment with pillows, trochanter rolls, hand rolls and a foot board (prevents foot drop)
  • ROM exercises – passive, active-assisted or active, 2–3 times a day
  • Isometric exercises – quadriceps and gluteal setting
  • Early ambulation as soon as permitted; physiotherapy referral
  • Avoid prolonged knee flexion with pillows under the knees

3. Cardiovascular care

  • Leg exercises – ankle pumping, foot circles, leg raising every hour while awake
  • Graduated compression stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression as ordered
  • Adequate fluids to prevent blood viscosity; anticoagulants (heparin) as prescribed
  • Do not massage the legs (may dislodge a clot); avoid crossing legs and tight bands
  • Observe daily for calf pain, swelling, warmth and redness; report signs of pulmonary embolism (sudden breathlessness, chest pain)
  • Prevent postural hypotension – raise the head end gradually, dangle the legs before standing, change position slowly

4. Respiratory care

  • Deep breathing and coughing exercises every 1–2 hours; incentive spirometry
  • Change position frequently; semi-Fowler's position
  • Chest physiotherapy, postural drainage and suctioning when needed
  • Adequate fluids to keep secretions thin; avoid tight bedclothes
  • Observe for fever, cough, abnormal breath sounds

5. Skin care and prevention of pressure ulcers

  • Inspect the skin over bony prominences at least once a day
  • Reposition every 2 hours; use air or alternating-pressure mattresses, pillows between knees and under heels
  • Keep the skin clean and dry; manage incontinence promptly; use barrier creams
  • Avoid friction and shear – lift with a sheet, do not drag; keep the head end at or below 30° when possible
  • Keep linen dry, clean and wrinkle-free
  • Good nutrition and hydration

6. Nutrition and elimination

  • High-protein, high-calorie diet with vitamins (especially vitamin C) and minerals for tissue repair
  • Fluids 2–3 litres a day (unless restricted)
  • High-fibre diet, fruits, vegetables and a regular bowel routine; privacy and a comfortable position for the bedpan; laxatives as ordered
  • Encourage voiding in a natural position when possible; catheter care if catheterised; maintain an intake–output chart; observe urine for cloudiness, blood and odour

7. Psychosocial care

  • Talk to the patient, explain care, encourage expression of feelings
  • Diversion – radio, newspapers, books, television, hobbies, visitors
  • Encourage self-care and decision-making to maintain independence and self-esteem
  • Keep the patient oriented – clock, calendar, window view
  • Involve the family; occupational therapy; refer for counselling if depressed

8. Safety

  • Side rails, call bell within reach, safe transfers using body mechanics, fall prevention

9. Patient and family education

  • Teach exercises, positioning, skin care, signs of complications and home care before discharge

10. Documentation

  • Record position changes (turning chart), exercises, skin condition, intake–output, bowel movements and the patient's response

Conclusion Prolonged immobility causes muscle wasting and contractures, postural hypotension and DVT, pneumonia, pressure ulcers, constipation, urinary stones and infection, metabolic changes and depression. Regular position changes, alignment, exercises, early ambulation, breathing exercises, skin care, good nutrition and fluids, bowel and bladder care, psychological support and education prevent these hazards and restore function.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain crutch walking – measurement, gaits and the nurse's responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction Crutches are walking aids that transfer body weight from the legs to the arms and shoulders. They are used after fractures, sprains, amputation, surgery or in weakness of the legs. Types include axillary (underarm), forearm (elbow) and platform crutches.

A. Measurement of axillary crutches

  • With the patient standing, the crutch tip is placed about 15 cm to the side and 15 cm in front of the foot
  • The top of the crutch should be 2–3 finger-widths below the armpit
  • The hand grip is adjusted so that the elbow is slightly bent (20–30°)
  • Weight must be taken on the hands, not the armpits – pressure in the armpit can damage the nerves (crutch palsy)

B. Preparation

  • Assess arm strength and balance; teach arm-strengthening exercises (pushing up in bed, squeezing a ball)
  • Check rubber tips, pads and screws
  • Well-fitting, non-slip, low-heeled shoes
  • Teach the tripod position – the basic standing position, with crutches 15 cm in front of and to the side of the feet, forming a triangle

C. Crutch gaits

  1. Four-point gait – right crutch → left foot → left crutch → right foot
    • slow and very stable; three points always on the ground; for patients who can bear some weight on both legs
  2. Three-point gait – both crutches and the affected leg move forward together, then the unaffected leg
    • for patients who cannot bear weight, or can bear only partial weight, on one leg (e.g. fracture of one leg)
  3. Two-point gait – right crutch with left foot, then left crutch with right foot
    • faster; like normal walking; needs partial weight-bearing on both legs
  4. Swing-to gait – both crutches forward, then both legs swing up to the crutches
    • for paralysis of both legs (with braces)
  5. Swing-through gait – both crutches forward, then the legs swing beyond the crutches
    • fastest; needs good strength and balance

D. Stairs and sitting

  • Going up: the unaffected (good) leg first, then the crutches and affected leg
  • Going down: the crutches and affected leg first, then the good leg
  • Memory aid: "Up with the good, down with the bad"
  • Sitting down: back up to the chair, hold both crutches in the hand on the affected side, reach for the armrest with the other hand and lower slowly

E. Nurse's responsibilities

  • Remove hazards – wet floors, loose mats, clutter
  • Walk beside the patient on the affected side at first; use a gait belt
  • Teach the patient to look ahead, not at the feet, and to take small steps at first
  • Watch for fatigue, dizziness and pain; allow rest
  • Inspect the armpits and hands for pressure
  • Teach the family; progress gradually as advised by the doctor or physiotherapist

Conclusion Correctly measured crutches, the right gait (four-point, three-point, two-point, swing-to or swing-through) and safe techniques on stairs allow patients to walk independently and safely, under the nurse's guidance.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the techniques of moving, lifting and transferring a patient.
answer_html:
Introduction Moving and transferring means changing a patient's position in bed or moving him from one surface to another – bed to chair, bed to stretcher. It is needed for comfort, care and prevention of complications, and must be done safely to protect both the patient and the nurse (back injuries are common among nurses).

A. General principles

  • Assess the patient – weight, strength, ability to help, pain, tubes and drains
  • Plan – get enough helpers and aids (slide sheets, transfer boards, hoists)
  • Explain and encourage the patient to help
  • Lock the wheels of bed, chair or stretcher; adjust bed height
  • Use good body mechanics – wide base of support, bend the knees, not the back, keep the load close, avoid twisting, slide or pull rather than lift
  • Work together on a count ("one, two, three")

B. Common techniques

1. Moving a patient up in bed (two nurses)

  • Bed flat; pillow against the headboard
  • Patient bends knees with feet flat, chin on chest, arms folded
  • Nurses on either side hold a draw sheet or slide sheet, face the head of the bed and, on the count, shift their weight forward while the patient pushes with his feet

2. Turning to the side and log rolling

  • For ordinary turning, move the patient to one side of the bed first, then turn him towards you
  • Log rolling for spinal injury – three or more persons turn the patient as one unit, keeping the head, neck and spine in line; a pillow between the legs

3. Helping the patient sit at the edge of the bed (dangling)

  • Raise the head of the bed; support the shoulders and knees; pivot the patient so the legs hang over the side
  • Let him sit for a few minutes; watch for dizziness (postural hypotension) and check the pulse

4. Bed to chair or wheelchair

  • Place the chair at an angle beside the bed on the patient's stronger side; lock the wheels; raise the footrests
  • Patient wears non-slip footwear; use a gait belt
  • Stand facing the patient, brace his weak knee with yours; on the count, he stands, pivots on the strong leg and sits down slowly

5. Bed to stretcher

  • Bed and stretcher at the same height, side by side, wheels locked
  • Three or four persons use a slide sheet, transfer board or draw sheet to slide the patient across on the count
  • Secure with straps and side rails

6. Mechanical hoist – for heavy or fully dependent patients

C. Safety and nursing responsibilities

  • Protect tubes, drains and IV lines
  • Maintain privacy and dignity
  • Never pull on the patient's arms – risk of shoulder injury, especially in stroke
  • Watch for pain, dizziness or change in colour
  • Document how the patient tolerated the move; teach caregivers safe techniques

Conclusion Patients are moved and transferred safely by assessment, planning, enough helpers and aids, good body mechanics and coordinated techniques such as the draw-sheet lift, log roll, pivot transfer and slide-sheet transfer.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define patient education. Mention its domains.
answer_html:
Definition Patient education is a planned process of teaching that helps patients and their families gain the knowledge, attitudes and skills needed to maintain or improve health, cope with illness and take part in decisions about care.

Domains of learning (Bloom)

  1. Cognitive – knowledge and understanding (e.g. knowing the signs of hypoglycaemia)
  2. Affective – attitudes, values and feelings (e.g. accepting the need for lifelong insulin)
  3. Psychomotor – practical skills (e.g. giving an insulin injection, checking blood sugar)

Key point: teaching is complete only when the patient understands and can do what was taught – checked by teach-back or return demonstration.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: List the barriers to patient teaching.
answer_html:
Introduction Barriers are factors that prevent effective learning.

A. Patient-related

  1. Pain, fatigue, nausea, breathlessness
  2. Anxiety, fear, denial, depression
  3. Low literacy, language differences
  4. Hearing and visual impairment, memory problems
  5. Cultural beliefs and lack of motivation

B. Nurse-related

  1. Lack of time and heavy workload
  2. Poor teaching or communication skills; use of jargon

C. Environmental and organisational

  1. Noise, lack of privacy, interruptions
  2. Lack of teaching materials; early discharge

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the purposes and importance of patient teaching.
answer_html:
Introduction Patient teaching is one of the most important independent functions of the nurse. The nurse spends the most time with patients and families, so she is in the best position to teach them how to stay healthy, manage illness and prevent complications. Every patient also has the right to information about his health.

A. Purposes of patient teaching

1. Promotion of health

  • Teaching healthy habits – balanced diet, exercise, personal hygiene, avoiding tobacco and alcohol, stress management

2. Prevention of illness

  • Immunisation, hand washing, safe water, breast self-examination, screening, prevention of injuries

3. Restoration of health

  • Understanding the illness and treatment – medicines, diet, wound care, exercises – so that recovery is faster

4. Coping with impaired function

  • Helping patients with chronic illness or disability adapt – e.g. a patient with a colostomy, diabetes, stroke or amputation learns new ways of daily living

5. Self-care and independence

  • Teaching skills such as insulin injection, blood sugar monitoring, BP measurement, catheter care and inhaler use

6. Informed decision-making

  • Giving enough information so that the patient can give informed consent and choose among treatment options

B. Importance of patient teaching

  1. Improves compliance with medicines, diet and follow-up
  2. Reduces anxiety before surgery and procedures – a patient who knows what to expect is calmer
  3. Prevents complications and readmissions – e.g. teaching foot care to diabetics prevents ulcers and amputation
  4. Shortens hospital stay and reduces the cost of treatment
  5. Involves the family in care at home
  6. Improves patient satisfaction and trust in the health team
  7. Legal and ethical duty – patients have a right to information; teaching given must be documented
  8. Promotes community health – educated patients spread correct health messages to others

C. Who and when to teach

  • Patients, family members and caregivers
  • Teaching starts on admission, continues throughout the stay (planned and incidental teaching at every procedure) and is completed before discharge

Conclusion Patient teaching promotes health, prevents illness, restores health and helps patients cope with disability; it improves compliance, reduces anxiety, complications and costs, and is a legal and ethical responsibility of the nurse.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the principles of patient teaching.
answer_html:
Introduction Principles of teaching are basic rules that make learning easy, effective and lasting. Following them helps the nurse teach patients and families of all ages, backgrounds and levels of education.

1. Readiness of the learner

  • Teach when the patient is physically and emotionally ready – not when he is in pain, very tired, sedated or has just received bad news
  • Readiness is seen when he asks questions or shows interest

2. Motivation

  • Link teaching with what matters to the patient – "If you take your tablets regularly, you can go back to work"

3. Individualised teaching

  • Plan according to the patient's age, education, language, culture, occupation and learning style

4. Active participation

  • The patient learns better by doing – discussion, questions, practice and return demonstration

5. Proceed from known to unknown, simple to complex, concrete to abstract

  • Start with what the patient already knows; build up step by step

6. Small amounts at a time

  • Short sessions of about 15–20 minutes; three or four key points per session

7. Repetition and reinforcement
