  • Repeat important points; praise correct answers and performance

8. Use of multiple senses and teaching aids

  • Charts, models, pictures, pamphlets, videos and real equipment – "I hear and I forget; I see and I remember; I do and I understand"

9. Simple language

  • Use the patient's mother tongue, simple words and local examples; avoid medical jargon

10. Suitable environment and timing

  • Quiet, comfortable, private place; avoid meal and rest times

11. Involve the family

  • Especially for children, the elderly and patients needing home care

12. Feedback and evaluation

  • Use the teach-back method ("Tell me how you will take this medicine") and return demonstration; reteach if needed

13. Cultural sensitivity

  • Respect beliefs and food habits; adapt advice accordingly

14. Written instructions

  • Give printed or written instructions, in large letters for the elderly, to take home

Conclusion Effective patient teaching follows principles of readiness, motivation, individualisation, active participation, simple-to-complex sequence, small amounts, repetition, teaching aids, simple language, family involvement and evaluation.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define patient education. Explain the purposes, principles and process of patient teaching, integrating the nursing process. (2 + 3 + 4 + 6)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Patient education is the planned, organised process of teaching by which patients and families acquire the knowledge, attitudes and skills needed to promote health, prevent illness, manage illness and cope with its effects
  • Health education (WHO): any combination of learning experiences designed to help individuals and communities improve their health by increasing knowledge or influencing attitudes
  • Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour resulting from experience
  • Patient education is a right of the patient and an independent responsibility of the nurse

Domains of learning (Bloom)

  • Cognitive – knowledge (what to eat in diabetes)
  • Affective – attitudes and feelings (willingness to change diet)
  • Psychomotor – skills (checking blood sugar with a glucometer)

(b) Purposes of patient teaching (3 marks)

  1. Promotion of health – healthy lifestyle, nutrition, exercise, hygiene
  2. Prevention of illness and injury – immunisation, screening, safety at home
  3. Restoration of health – understanding illness, treatment and medicines
  4. Coping with impaired function – adapting to chronic illness and disability
  5. Self-care and independence – learning skills for home care
  6. Informed decision-making and informed consent
  7. Improving compliance and reducing complications and readmissions
  8. Reducing anxiety and hospital stay
  9. Involving and preparing the family for home care

(c) Principles of patient teaching (4 marks)

  1. Readiness – physical (no severe pain or fatigue) and emotional (anxiety controlled, illness accepted)
  2. Motivation – relate teaching to the patient's own goals
  3. Individualisation – according to age, education, culture, language and learning style
  4. Active participation – discussion, practice and return demonstration
  5. Known to unknown, simple to complex, concrete to abstract
  6. Small amounts in short sessions; important points first
  7. Repetition and reinforcement; praise progress
  8. Multiple senses – use audio-visual aids, models and real equipment
  9. Simple language in the patient's mother tongue; avoid jargon
  10. Conducive environment – quiet, private, comfortable, at a suitable time
  11. Family involvement
  12. Evaluation and feedback – teach-back and return demonstration
  13. Consistency – all team members give the same message

(d) Process of patient teaching – integrating the nursing process (6 marks) The teaching process follows the same steps as the nursing process – assessment, nursing diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation.

Step 1: Assessment of learning needs

  • What the patient already knows and what he needs to know about the illness, medicines, diet, activity and warning signs
  • Readiness to learn
    • Physical – pain, fatigue, breathlessness, sedation, sensory deficits
    • Emotional – anxiety, fear, denial, depression
    • Experiential – past experiences of illness and learning
  • Ability to learn – age, developmental stage, literacy, language, memory, vision, hearing
  • Learning style – learns by seeing, hearing or doing
  • Motivation, cultural beliefs and health practices
  • Support system – family members who will help at home
  • Resources – finances, equipment, distance from the hospital

Step 2: Nursing diagnosis

  • Examples:
    • Deficient knowledge related to a new diagnosis of diabetes mellitus
    • Readiness for enhanced knowledge of infant care
    • Ineffective health management related to complexity of the medication schedule
    • Anxiety related to lack of information about surgery

Step 3: Planning

  • Set priorities – first what the patient must know for safety (e.g. recognising and treating hypoglycaemia), then what is useful to know
  • Write learning objectives that are SMART – specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound, covering all three domains
    • Example: "By the end of the second session, the patient will demonstrate correct self-injection of insulin" (psychomotor)
    • "The patient will list three signs of low blood sugar" (cognitive)
  • Decide the content – arranged from simple to complex
  • Select teaching methods – explanation, discussion, demonstration, role play, group teaching, video
  • Select teaching aids – flip charts, posters, models, pamphlets in the local language, real equipment (insulin pen, glucometer, inhaler)
  • Plan time, place and participants – short sessions, include family members
  • Coordinate with the doctor, dietitian and physiotherapist so that messages are consistent

Step 4: Implementation

  • Create a comfortable, private environment; build rapport
  • State the purpose of the session
  • Teach in small, logical steps; use simple language and local examples
  • Demonstrate skills step by step, then allow practice and return demonstration
  • Encourage questions; repeat key points; praise correct performance
  • Give written or pictorial instructions to take home
  • Use incidental teaching – explain while giving care (e.g. explaining the medicine while giving it)

Step 5: Evaluation

  • Check whether the objectives have been achieved:
    • Teach-back method – the patient explains in his own words what he has learnt
    • Return demonstration of skills
    • Oral questions and observation of behaviour change (correct diet choices, regular medication)
    • Follow-up results – blood sugar, BP, wound healing, readmission
  • Reteach or change the method if learning is incomplete

Step 6: Documentation

  • Record what was taught, to whom, the methods and materials used, the patient's response and understanding, and further teaching needed
  • Documentation is legal proof that teaching was given and ensures continuity among staff

Example: teaching a newly diagnosed diabetic patient

Nursing process step Teaching action
Assessment knows little about diabetes; reads Marathi; wife cooks at home
Diagnosis deficient knowledge related to new diagnosis of diabetes
Planning objectives on diet, insulin, hypoglycaemia; pictures and glucometer; include wife
Implementation three short sessions; demonstration of insulin injection; diet chart in Marathi
Evaluation patient injects insulin correctly; wife explains the diet plan (teach-back)

Role of the nurse as a teacher

  • Identifies learning needs, plans and gives teaching, uses every contact as a teaching opportunity, involves the family, evaluates learning and documents it

Conclusion Patient education is a planned process of helping patients and families gain the knowledge, attitudes and skills needed for health. It serves to promote health, prevent illness, restore health and help patients cope. Following the principles of readiness, individualisation, participation and repetition, and using the nursing process – assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation – makes patient teaching systematic, effective and measurable.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: What is health literacy?
answer_html:
Definition Health literacy is the degree to which a person can obtain, understand, judge and use health information and services to make appropriate health decisions. Even educated people may have low health literacy about medical matters.

Effects of low health literacy

  • Taking medicines wrongly; missed follow-up visits
  • Poor control of chronic diseases; more hospital admissions

Warning signs

  • Incomplete forms, "I forgot my glasses", not asking questions, inability to explain one's own medicines

Role of the nurse

  1. Use simple words in the patient's own language; avoid medical jargon
  2. Use pictures, models and demonstrations
  3. Teach two or three key points at a time
  4. Check understanding by the teach-back method
  5. Give written instructions in large print; involve the family

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the methods of patient teaching.
answer_html:
Introduction A teaching method is the way information or a skill is presented so that the patient learns. The nurse chooses the method according to the type of learning (knowledge, attitude or skill), the patient's age, literacy, language and condition, the number of learners and the resources available.

Methods

1. Explanation and discussion (one-to-one teaching)

  • The commonest method in hospitals; individualised, private and allows questions
  • Example: explaining diet to a diabetic patient

2. Lecture (health talk)

  • Gives information to a group in a short time; little participation
  • Example: talk on tuberculosis in the out-patient waiting area

3. Demonstration and return demonstration

  • Best for skills (psychomotor learning)
  • The nurse shows the skill step by step; the patient then practises and repeats it under supervision
  • Examples: insulin injection, breastfeeding positions, colostomy care, crutch walking, oral rehydration solution

4. Group discussion and group teaching

  • Patients with similar problems share experiences and support each other – helps change attitudes
  • Examples: antenatal classes, diabetic and cardiac rehabilitation groups

5. Role play and simulation

  • Practising real situations – e.g. an adolescent practising refusing tobacco

6. Printed and self-learning material

  • Pamphlets, booklets, flip books, discharge instruction sheets
  • Videos, mobile messages and apps

7. Audio-visual aids

  • Posters, charts, flash cards, models, real objects (food models), puppets for children

8. Storytelling, songs and puppet shows

  • Effective with children and rural communities

9. Community methods

  • Exhibitions, street plays, health camps, radio and television, social media campaigns

10. Telephone and tele-teaching

  • Follow-up calls and teleconsultation after discharge

Choosing a method

Learning domain Suitable methods
Knowledge (cognitive) explanation, lecture, pamphlets, videos
Attitude (affective) group discussion, role play, sharing experiences
Skill (psychomotor) demonstration and return demonstration

Points for effective teaching

  • Combine methods; involve the family
  • Use the patient's own language; keep sessions short
  • Check learning by return demonstration and teach-back

Example – a simple teaching plan

  • Topic – insulin self-injection for a newly diagnosed diabetic patient
  • Objective – the patient will give his own insulin injection correctly before discharge
  • Method – explanation followed by demonstration and return demonstration
  • Aids – insulin pen or syringe, injection-site chart, pamphlet in Marathi
  • Evaluation – the patient demonstrates the full procedure without help on two occasions

Conclusion Patient teaching uses explanation, lecture, demonstration, group discussion, role play, printed and audio-visual materials and community methods; the nurse chooses and combines them to suit the patient and the type of learning.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: State the golden rules of first aid.
answer_html:
Definition First aid is the immediate and temporary care given to a person who is injured or suddenly taken ill, using the materials available, until medical help arrives or the person reaches hospital.

Golden rules

  1. Ensure safety of yourself, the casualty and bystanders first
  2. Do first things first – quickly, quietly and without panic
  3. Check and maintain Airway, Breathing and Circulation; start CPR if needed
  4. Stop bleeding and treat shock
  5. Do not move the casualty unnecessarily, especially if a spinal injury is suspected
  6. Reassure the casualty; keep the crowd away
  7. Do not give anything by mouth to an unconscious person
  8. Keep the casualty warm and comfortable
  9. Call for help – ambulance 108 / 112 – and arrange transport to hospital
  10. Do no further harm; hand over with a clear account of what happened

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: State the first aid for external haemorrhage.
answer_html:
Introduction Haemorrhage is the escape of blood from blood vessels. Severe bleeding can cause shock and death within minutes.

First aid

  1. Wear gloves if available; reassure the casualty
  2. Apply direct, firm pressure on the wound with a clean pad or cloth for at least 10 minutes – do not keep lifting it to check
  3. Raise the injured part above the level of the heart (if no fracture)
  4. Lay the casualty down to reduce shock
  5. If blood soaks through, add more pads on top; do not remove the first pad
  6. Do not remove embedded objects – press around them
  7. For life-threatening limb bleeding not controlled by pressure, a tourniquet may be applied 5–7 cm above the wound by a trained person; note the time
  8. Bandage firmly, treat for shock and transfer to hospital

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: State the first aid for snake bite.
answer_html:
Introduction In India, most deaths are due to the "Big Four" – common cobra, common krait, Russell's viper and saw-scaled viper. The national protocol uses the memory aid "Do it R.I.G.H.T."

First aid – R.I.G.H.T.

  1. R – Reassure the victim; most bites are not fatal, and fear increases the spread
  2. I – Immobilise the bitten limb like a fracture with a splint; keep the person still and lying down
  3. G.H. – Get to Hospital immediately (call 108); anti-snake venom (ASV) is the only specific treatment
  4. T – Tell the doctor about symptoms such as drooping eyelids, bleeding or difficulty in breathing

Don'ts

  • Do not tie a tight tourniquet, cut or suck the wound, apply ice, or use herbal remedies
  • Do not try to catch or kill the snake
  • Remove rings, bangles and tight clothing from the bitten limb

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Describe the first aid for choking in an adult.
answer_html:
Introduction Choking is blockage of the airway by a foreign body (often food). Signs: the person clutches the throat, cannot speak, cough or breathe, and turns blue.

First aid for a conscious adult

  1. Ask, "Are you choking?" If he can cough, encourage coughing
  2. If he cannot cough or breathe – give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand while he leans forward
  3. If unsuccessful, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre) – stand behind, place a fist above the navel and below the breastbone, grasp it with the other hand and pull sharply inwards and upwards
  4. Repeat back blows and abdominal thrusts until the object comes out
  5. For pregnant or obese persons, use chest thrusts
  6. If he becomes unconscious, lower him to the ground, call 108 and start CPR; look in the mouth before giving breaths

Infants: 5 back blows (face down on the forearm) and 5 chest thrusts with two fingers – no abdominal thrusts.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the rule of nines in burns.

diagram.caption: Rule of nines for estimating burnt body surface area in adults

answer_html:
Introduction The rule of nines (Wallace) is a quick method to estimate the percentage of total body surface area (TBSA) burnt in adults. It helps decide fluid needs and referral.

Rule of nines – adult

  1. Head and neck – 9%
  2. Each upper limb – 9% (both = 18%)
  3. Front of the trunk – 18%
  4. Back of the trunk – 18%
  5. Each lower limb – 18% (both = 36%)
  6. Perineum and genitals – 1% - Total = 100%

Other points

  • The patient's palm with fingers is about 1% of TBSA – useful for small, scattered burns
  • In children, the head is relatively larger and the legs smaller, so the Lund and Browder chart is preferred

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Mention the types and uses of bandages.
answer_html:
Introduction A bandage is a strip of material used to hold dressings and splints in place, give support, apply pressure and immobilise a part.

Types and uses

  1. Roller bandage – a long rolled strip (gauze, crepe, cotton); holds dressings, gives support and pressure
    • Turns: circular, spiral, reverse spiral, figure-of-eight, recurrent (for head and stumps), spica (shoulder, hip, thumb)
  2. Triangular bandage – used as an arm sling, a head bandage, a pad, or folded as broad or narrow bandages for splints
  3. Crepe (elastic) bandage – for sprains and to give compression
  4. Tubular bandage – for fingers and limbs
  5. Adhesive bandage – for small wounds

Principles: bandage from distal to proximal, firmly but not tightly, cover the dressing completely, leave fingers and toes exposed and check circulation.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the steps of first aid for a wound.
answer_html:
Introduction A wound is a break in the continuity of the skin, mucous membrane or underlying tissues. First aid for wounds aims to stop bleeding, prevent infection and promote healing.

Types of wounds

  • Closed – bruise (contusion), haematoma
  • Open – abrasion (graze), incised (clean cut by a sharp object), lacerated (torn, irregular edges), puncture (nail, needle), penetrating (stab, gunshot), avulsion (skin torn off), crush wounds and bites

Steps of first aid for a wound

1. Ensure safety and protect yourself

  • Make the scene safe; wash hands and wear gloves if available

2. Reassure and position the casualty

  • Make the casualty sit or lie down comfortably; reassure him

3. Control bleeding

  • Apply direct pressure with a clean pad
  • Elevate the injured part if no fracture is suspected

4. Expose and examine the wound

  • Remove or cut away clothing gently; check the size, depth and any foreign body

5. Clean the wound (for minor wounds)

  • Wash with clean running water or normal saline to remove dirt
  • Clean from the centre outwards
  • Remove loose dirt and gravel gently; do not remove deeply embedded objects – pad around them

6. Apply an antiseptic (for minor wounds) – e.g. povidone-iodine – if available

7. Cover the wound

  • Apply a sterile or clean, non-fluffy dressing that covers the wound completely, with a margin

8. Bandage

  • Bandage firmly but not too tightly; check circulation beyond the bandage (colour, warmth, sensation of fingers or toes)

9. Immobilise the injured part with a sling or splint if the wound is large or near a joint

10. Treat for shock if bleeding is severe

11. Prevent tetanus

  • Advise tetanus toxoid (Td) as per immunisation status

12. Refer to hospital

  • For deep, gaping or dirty wounds, wounds needing stitches, wounds of the face, hands or joints, embedded objects, animal bites and signs of infection

Special wounds

  • Dog bite – wash immediately with soap and running water for 15 minutes, apply an antiseptic, do not bandage tightly or suture immediately, and send for anti-rabies vaccination (and immunoglobulin when indicated)
  • Abdominal wound with protruding intestines – do not push them back; cover with a moist sterile dressing; nothing by mouth
  • Chest wound (sucking wound) – cover to stop air entry; half-sitting position

Signs of infection to watch for: increasing pain, redness, swelling, warmth, pus and fever.

Conclusion First aid for a wound involves safety, reassurance, control of bleeding, cleaning, covering with a sterile dressing, bandaging, immobilisation, treatment of shock, tetanus prevention and referral when needed.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the first aid management of burns.
answer_html:
Introduction A burn is an injury to the skin and deeper tissues caused by heat, chemicals, electricity, radiation or friction. A scald is a burn caused by moist heat – hot water, steam, hot oil. Burns are common in Indian homes (kitchen fires, kerosene stoves, firecrackers).

Classification by depth

  • Superficial (first degree) – epidermis only; red, painful, no blisters (sunburn)
  • Partial thickness (second degree) – epidermis and part of the dermis; blisters, red, very painful
  • Full thickness (third degree) – all skin layers; white, leathery or charred; painless because nerve endings are destroyed
  • Fourth degree – reaching muscle and bone

Extent: the rule of nines (adult); the patient's palm is about 1%.

General first aid for thermal burns

  1. Stop the burning process
    • If clothes catch fire – "Stop, Drop and Roll"; smother flames with a blanket or thick cloth (not nylon); do not run
    • Remove the person from the source of heat
  2. Check Airway, Breathing and Circulation; call 108
  3. Cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible
    • Do not use ice, ice-cold water, toothpaste, oil, ghee, butter, ink or turmeric
  4. Remove rings, bangles, watches, belts and tight clothing before swelling starts; do not pull off clothing stuck to the burn
  5. Cover the burn loosely with a clean, non-fluffy cloth, sterile dressing or cling film
  6. Do not break blisters
  7. Keep the person warm – cover unburnt areas; cooling large areas can cause hypothermia
  8. Treat for shock – lay down, raise legs if no other injury
  9. For large burns, transfer urgently to hospital (IV fluids are needed); small sips of oral fluids only as advised
  10. Reassure and monitor breathing, especially after burns in closed rooms (smoke inhalation)

Chemical burns

  • Brush off dry chemicals, then flush with plenty of running water for at least 20 minutes; remove contaminated clothing (with gloves)
  • Eye – irrigate continuously for 15–20 minutes, holding the eyelids open

Electrical burns

  • Switch off the current or separate the person using a dry, non-conducting object (wooden stick, plastic chair); never touch him directly
  • Check breathing and start CPR if needed; look for entry and exit wounds
  • Always refer – internal damage and heart rhythm problems may occur

Refer to hospital

  • Burns of more than 10% of the body in adults (smaller in children and the elderly), full-thickness burns, burns of the face, hands, feet, genitals, perineum and major joints, circumferential burns, inhalation injury, electrical and chemical burns

Conclusion First aid for burns is: stop the burning, check ABC, cool with running water for 20 minutes, remove constricting items, cover with a clean dressing, keep warm, treat shock and refer – while avoiding harmful home remedies.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain basic cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) in an adult.
answer_html:
Introduction Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is an emergency procedure of chest compressions and rescue breaths to maintain blood flow to the brain and heart in a person whose heart has stopped (cardiac arrest). Brain damage begins within 4–6 minutes without oxygen, so CPR must start immediately. The modern sequence is C-A-B: Compressions, Airway, Breathing.

Steps of adult CPR

1. Check the scene for safety

  • Make sure there is no danger to you or the casualty (traffic, fire, electricity)

2. Check responsiveness

  • Tap the shoulders and shout, "Are you all right?"

3. Call for help

  • Shout for help; call 108 / 112; ask someone to bring an AED (automated external defibrillator)

4. Check breathing (and pulse, for health workers)

  • Look at the chest for normal breathing for not more than 10 seconds; health workers also feel the carotid pulse
  • Gasping is not normal breathing – start CPR

5. Chest compressions (C)

  • Place the casualty flat on his back on a firm surface
  • Kneel beside him; place the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest (lower half of the breastbone), the other hand on top, fingers interlocked
  • Keep arms straight, shoulders directly above the hands
  • Push hard: depth at least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm
  • Push fast: 100–120 compressions per minute
  • Allow full chest recoil after each compression; minimise interruptions

6. Open the airway (A)

  • Head tilt–chin lift; use jaw thrust if a neck injury is suspected

7. Rescue breaths (B)

  • Pinch the nose, seal your mouth over his mouth (use a face shield or bag-mask if available) and give 2 breaths, each over 1 second, enough to make the chest rise

8. Continue cycles of 30 compressions to 2 breaths

  • Ratio 30:2; change the person giving compressions every 2 minutes to avoid fatigue
  • Compression-only CPR is acceptable for untrained bystanders

9. Use the AED as soon as it arrives

  • Switch on and follow the voice prompts; attach pads; ensure no one touches the casualty during analysis and shock; resume CPR immediately after the shock

10. Continue until

  • Professional help takes over, the casualty starts breathing normally, or the rescuer is exhausted or the scene becomes unsafe

11. Recovery position

  • If breathing returns and there is no spinal injury, place him in the recovery position and monitor until help arrives

Children and infants (in brief)

  • Compression depth about one-third of the chest depth – about 5 cm in children and 4 cm in infants
  • Infants – two fingers (single rescuer) or two thumbs encircling the chest; ratio 30:2 for one rescuer and 15:2 for two health workers

Signs of effective CPR: chest rises with each breath; a pulse can be felt with each compression; skin colour improves.

Conclusion Adult CPR is: safety, response, call 108 and get an AED, check breathing, 30 hard and fast compressions (5–6 cm, 100–120/min) and 2 breaths, AED use as early as possible, and continuation until help arrives.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the first aid management of poisoning.
answer_html:
Introduction A poison is any substance that, when it enters the body in sufficient quantity, damages health or causes death. Poisons enter by swallowing, inhaling, injection (bites, stings) or absorption through the skin and eyes. In rural Maharashtra and other agricultural areas, organophosphorus (OP) insecticide poisoning is very common, along with rat poison (aluminium or zinc phosphide), kerosene, drug overdose, corrosive acids, snake bite and scorpion sting.

General signs of poisoning

  • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea; burns around the mouth (corrosives); abnormal smell of breath (kerosene); drowsiness, confusion, convulsions, unconsciousness; breathing difficulty
  • OP poisoning: excessive salivation, sweating, tears, pinpoint pupils, vomiting, diarrhoea, muscle twitching, breathlessness, smell of insecticide

General first aid

  1. Ensure safety – wear gloves; ventilate the room in gas poisoning; avoid contact with the poison
  2. Remove the person from the source – take to fresh air in gas or smoke poisoning
  3. Call for help – 108, and the nearest poison information centre if available
  4. Check Airway, Breathing and Circulation; start CPR if needed (use a face shield or bag-mask – avoid mouth-to-mouth in OP and cyanide poisoning)
  5. Unconscious but breathing – place in the recovery position to prevent aspiration of vomit
  6. Do not induce vomiting – especially in corrosive (acid, alkali) and kerosene or petrol poisoning, and in drowsy patients (risk of aspiration and further burns)
  7. Do not give anything by mouth unless advised by a doctor or poison centre
  8. Skin contamination (e.g. OP sprayed on the body) – remove contaminated clothing and wash the skin with soap and plenty of water
  9. Eye contamination – irrigate with clean running water for 15–20 minutes
  10. Identify the poison – keep the container, label, remaining tablets or plants and vomitus and send them with the patient
  11. Note the time of poisoning, amount and symptoms
  12. Reassure, keep warm and transport urgently to hospital; monitor breathing on the way

Specific points

  • Food poisoning – oral rehydration solution (ORS) for vomiting and diarrhoea; refer if severe
  • Scorpion sting – wash the site, apply a cold pack, keep the limb still, reassure and take to hospital urgently (especially children)
  • Dog bite – wash with soap and running water for 15 minutes and send for anti-rabies treatment
  • Suicidal poisoning – never leave the person alone; treat with respect; it is a medico-legal case

Hospital treatment (for knowledge): gastric lavage when indicated, activated charcoal, antidotes such as atropine and pralidoxime (OP), naloxone (opioids), ASV (snake bite).

Conclusion First aid for poisoning is: safety, remove from source, call 108, maintain ABC, recovery position, no induced vomiting, decontaminate skin and eyes, keep the poison container and transfer urgently to hospital.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Describe the methods of transportation of an injured person.
answer_html:
Introduction After first aid, the casualty often needs to be moved to safety or to hospital. Wrong handling can worsen injuries, especially of the spine. The method depends on the nature of the injury, the condition of the casualty, the number of helpers, the distance and the route.

Principles of transportation

  • Do not move the casualty unless there is danger (fire, traffic, collapse) or he must be taken to hospital
  • Give first aid first – ABC, control bleeding, immobilise fractures
  • Suspected spinal injury – keep head, neck and body in a straight line; move only with a spinal board and trained helpers (log roll)
  • Move gently, smoothly and steadily; use proper body mechanics
  • Keep the casualty warm, reassure him and observe continuously
  • One person gives clear commands so that helpers move together
  • On a stretcher, the casualty is usually carried feet first; the head end is kept higher when going up stairs or uphill

A. One-rescuer methods

  1. Human crutch – for a conscious casualty with a minor leg injury who can walk with support; the rescuer stands on the injured side and supports him around the waist
  2. Cradle method – for children and light adults; carried in the arms
  3. Pick-a-back (piggyback) – for a conscious casualty who can hold on
  4. Fireman's lift – for an unconscious or helpless casualty who is not too heavy (not for spinal, chest or abdominal injuries)
  5. Drag methods – clothes drag, blanket drag or shoulder drag – to pull a casualty quickly out of danger along the ground, keeping the head supported

B. Two-rescuer methods

  1. Two-handed seat – for a casualty who cannot use his arms; rescuers form a seat with their hands and support his back with the other arms
  2. Three-handed seat – leaves one hand free to support an injured leg
  3. Four-handed seat – for a conscious casualty who can put his arms around the rescuers' shoulders; each rescuer grasps his own wrist and the partner's other wrist to form a seat
  4. Fore-and-aft carry – one rescuer holds under the armpits from behind and the other holds under the knees
  5. Chair method – the casualty sits on a chair carried by two rescuers; useful on stairs and in narrow passages

C. Stretchers

  1. Standard stretcher – for serious injuries, unconscious casualties and long distances
  2. Improvised stretchers – a blanket or two coats with two poles; a door or wooden plank
  3. Scoop stretcher and spinal (long) board – for spinal injuries
  4. Wheeled stretcher (trolley) and ambulance – the ambulance (108) is the best means for serious casualties

Loading a stretcher: test it first; lift the casualty with four or more helpers using the blanket lift or log roll, keeping the body in line; secure him with straps.

Conclusion Transportation must be safe, gentle and suited to the injury; one-rescuer methods (human crutch, cradle, pick-a-back, fireman's lift, drags), two-rescuer methods (hand seats, fore-and-aft, chair) and stretchers are chosen according to the casualty's condition and the help available.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define first aid. Explain the principles of first aid and the first aid management of wounds, haemorrhage and shock. (2 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 3)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • First aid is the immediate and temporary care given to a person who is injured or suddenly taken ill, using the facilities and materials available at the time, until medical help arrives or the person reaches hospital
  • First aider – a trained person who gives first aid
  • Aims of first aid (the 3 Ps):
    • Preserve life
    • Prevent the condition from becoming worse
    • Promote recovery

Qualities of a good first aider

  • Observant, tactful, resourceful (uses what is available), dextrous (skilful with hands), explicit (clear instructions), discriminating (decides priorities), persevering and sympathetic

(b) Principles (golden rules) of first aid (3 marks)

  1. Ensure safety – of yourself, the casualty and bystanders; wear gloves if available
  2. Assess the situation quickly and calmly – what happened, how many are injured, what help is available
  3. Primary survey – DR ABC: Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, Circulation (and CPR if needed)
  4. Treat life-threatening conditions first – airway obstruction, stopped breathing, severe bleeding, shock (priority or triage)
  5. Call for help early – 108 / 112
  6. Do not move the casualty unnecessarily, especially with suspected spinal injury
  7. Reassure the casualty and keep the crowd away
  8. Do not remove clothes unnecessarily; loosen tight clothing
  9. Nothing by mouth to unconscious casualties or those who may need surgery
  10. Keep the casualty warm and comfortable
  11. Do only what is necessary – do no further harm; do not try to be a doctor
  12. Arrange safe transport and hand over with a full report of the history and first aid given

(c) First aid management of wounds (3 marks) Wound: a break in the continuity of the skin, mucous membrane or underlying tissues.

Types: closed (bruise, haematoma) and open – abrasion, incised, lacerated, puncture, penetrating, avulsion, crush and bite wounds.

First aid

  1. Safety and gloves; reassure; position comfortably
  2. Control bleeding – direct pressure and elevation
  3. Clean minor wounds with clean running water or saline, from the centre outwards
  4. Do not remove embedded objects – pad around them
  5. Cover with a sterile or clean, non-fluffy dressing; bandage firmly, not tightly; check circulation
  6. Immobilise large wounds; treat shock
  7. Advise tetanus protection; refer deep, dirty and gaping wounds and bites
  8. Dog bite – wash with soap and running water for 15 minutes; anti-rabies vaccine

(d) First aid management of haemorrhage (4 marks) Haemorrhage: the escape of blood from a ruptured blood vessel.

Types of haemorrhage

  • According to the vessel:
    • Arterial – bright red, spurts with each heartbeat; most dangerous
    • Venous – dark red, flows steadily
    • Capillary – oozes from the whole surface; usually minor
  • According to the site:
    • External – visible on the body surface
    • Internal – inside the body; concealed (into the abdomen or chest, e.g. ruptured spleen, ectopic pregnancy) or revealed through openings – epistaxis (nose), haemoptysis (coughed blood), haematemesis (vomited blood), melaena (black stools), haematuria (blood in urine)
  • According to time:
    • Primary – at the time of injury
    • Reactionary – within 24 hours (e.g. slipping of a ligature as BP rises)
    • Secondary – after about 7–14 days, due to infection

Signs of severe blood loss

  • Pale, cold, clammy skin; rapid, weak pulse; falling BP; rapid, shallow breathing ("air hunger"); thirst; restlessness; giddiness; fainting; unconsciousness

First aid for external haemorrhage

  1. Wear gloves; reassure; lay the casualty down
  2. Direct pressure – press firmly over the wound with a clean pad, cloth or hand for at least 10 minutes
  3. Elevation – raise the bleeding limb above the heart (if no fracture)
  4. Add more pads if blood soaks through; do not remove the first pad
  5. Embedded object – do not remove it; press on either side and build padding around it
  6. Pressure bandage over the pad; check circulation beyond it
  7. Tourniquet – only for life-threatening limb bleeding that cannot be controlled by direct pressure (e.g. traumatic amputation); applied 5–7 cm above the wound, tightened until bleeding stops, time of application noted and not loosened by the first aider
  8. Treat for shock and transfer urgently

First aid for nosebleed (epistaxis)

  • Sit up and lean forward (not backwards – blood would be swallowed)
  • Pinch the soft part of the nose for 10–15 minutes; breathe through the mouth
  • Cold compress over the bridge of the nose; do not blow the nose for some hours
  • Refer if bleeding continues for more than 20–30 minutes

First aid for internal haemorrhage

  • Lay the casualty down with legs raised (if possible), keep warm, nothing by mouth, loosen tight clothing, monitor pulse and breathing, and transfer urgently – surgery may be needed

(e) First aid management of shock (3 marks) Shock: a life-threatening condition in which the circulation fails to supply enough oxygenated blood to the tissues and vital organs.

Types (causes)

  • Hypovolaemic – loss of blood or fluids: haemorrhage, burns, severe diarrhoea and vomiting
  • Cardiogenic – failure of the heart's pumping: heart attack
  • Septic – severe infection
  • Anaphylactic – severe allergic reaction (insect sting, drugs, food)
  • Neurogenic – spinal cord injury
  • Psychogenic (fainting) – sudden emotional shock, pain or fear

Signs and symptoms

  • Pale, cold, clammy skin; sweating; rapid, weak (thready) pulse; low BP
  • Rapid, shallow breathing; thirst; nausea and vomiting
  • Restlessness, anxiety, confusion, giddiness; reduced urine output
  • Cyanosis of lips; finally unconsciousness and death if untreated

First aid

  1. Call 108 immediately; treat the cause – stop bleeding, cool burns
  2. Lay the casualty flat and raise the legs about 30 cm (unless there is injury to the legs, pelvis, spine or head)
    • In breathlessness or heart attack, a half-sitting position is more comfortable
  3. Loosen tight clothing at the neck, chest and waist
  4. Keep warm with a blanket – but do not overheat or use hot water bottles
  5. Nothing by mouth (surgery may be needed); moisten the lips if thirsty
  6. Reassure – keep calm and stay with the casualty
  7. Monitor breathing, pulse and level of response every 5–10 minutes and record
  8. If unconscious but breathing – recovery position; if breathing stops – CPR
  9. Anaphylaxis – help him use his adrenaline auto-injector if he has one
  10. Transport to hospital quickly and safely

Summary of priorities

Condition Key first aid
Wound pressure, clean, cover, bandage, tetanus
External bleeding direct pressure, elevation, pressure bandage, tourniquet as last resort
Internal bleeding lie down, legs raised, nil by mouth, urgent transfer
Shock lie flat, legs raised, keep warm, nil by mouth, monitor, 108

Conclusion First aid is immediate, temporary care to preserve life, prevent worsening and promote recovery. Its principles are safety, quick assessment (DR ABC), treating life-threatening problems first, reassurance, minimal handling and early transfer. Wounds are managed by controlling bleeding, cleaning and covering; haemorrhage by direct pressure, elevation and, as a last resort, a tourniquet; and shock by laying the casualty flat with legs raised, keeping him warm, giving nothing by mouth, monitoring and arranging urgent transport.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Define fracture. Classify fractures. Explain the signs and symptoms and the first aid management of fractures, dislocations and sprains. (2 + 3 + 3 + 7)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • A fracture is a break in the continuity of a bone, complete or incomplete
  • Causes:
    • Direct force – the bone breaks at the point of impact (a blow, being hit by a vehicle)
    • Indirect force – the bone breaks away from the point of impact (a fall on the outstretched hand fracturing the collar bone)
    • Muscular violence – sudden violent muscle contraction (fracture of the kneecap)
    • Pathological – weak bone breaks with little force (osteoporosis, bone tumour)
    • Stress (fatigue) – repeated stress (soldiers, athletes)

(b) Classification of fractures (3 marks)

1. According to the skin and complications

  • Closed (simple) – the skin is intact
  • Open (compound) – there is a wound leading to the fracture; bone may protrude; high risk of infection
  • Complicated – associated injury to nerves, blood vessels, joints or organs (e.g. a broken rib puncturing the lung)

2. According to the pattern of the break

  • Transverse – straight across the bone
  • Oblique – at an angle
  • Spiral – twisted around the bone (twisting injuries)
  • Comminuted – the bone is broken into several fragments
  • Greenstick – incomplete fracture; the bone bends and cracks on one side; seen in children
  • Impacted – one fragment is driven into the other
  • Depressed – a piece of skull bone is pushed inwards
  • Compression – a vertebra is crushed
  • Avulsion – a fragment of bone is pulled away by a tendon or ligament

3. According to the cause – traumatic, pathological, stress

(c) Signs and symptoms of fracture (3 marks)

  1. Pain and tenderness at the site, worse on movement
  2. Swelling and bruising
  3. Loss of function – inability to use the part
  4. Deformity – angulation, shortening, rotation, irregularity of the bone
  5. Abnormal mobility at the fracture site
  6. Crepitus – a grating sound or feeling of bone ends rubbing together (do not test for it)
  7. Wound with or without visible bone ends (open fracture)
  8. Signs of shock – especially in fractures of the femur and pelvis, which cause heavy internal blood loss
  9. History of a snap heard or felt at the time of injury

(d) First aid management (7 marks)

A. General first aid for fractures

  1. Safety and DR ABC – airway, breathing and circulation come first; call 108
  2. Do not move the casualty unless he is in danger – "treat him where he lies"
  3. Control bleeding in open fractures – cover the wound with a sterile dressing; apply pressure around the bone ends, never on them; do not push protruding bone back
  4. Immobilise the fracture
    • Support the injured part above and below the fracture; immobilise the joints above and below
    • Use splints – padded wooden boards, rolled newspapers or magazines, umbrellas, sticks – long enough to cover both joints
    • Use the body as a splint – tie an injured leg to the good leg; secure an injured arm to the chest
    • Pad the hollows between splint and limb; tie bandages firmly but not tightly, with knots on the splint side, not over the fracture
    • Use slings for upper limb injuries
  5. Check circulation beyond the bandage – colour, warmth, pulse, sensation of fingers or toes; loosen if they become blue, cold or numb
  6. Elevate the limb after immobilisation if possible; a wrapped cold pack reduces pain and swelling
  7. Treat for shock; keep warm
  8. Nothing by mouth – an anaesthetic may be needed
  9. Reassure and transport carefully on a stretcher

B. First aid for specific fractures

  • Collar bone (clavicle) – support the arm on the injured side in an arm sling (or elevation sling); bandage the arm to the chest
  • Upper arm and forearm – splint, then support in an arm sling; for an elbow that cannot bend, splint in the position found
  • Wrist and hand – padded splint and arm sling; remove rings early
  • Ribs – support the arm on the injured side in a sling; half-sitting position, leaning towards the injured side; watch breathing
  • Spine – the most serious; do not move the casualty unless absolutely necessary; keep the head, neck and trunk in a straight line; support the head with both hands; move only by log roll onto a spinal board with trained helpers
  • Pelvis – lay flat with knees slightly bent and supported; place padding between the legs; do not let him walk; treat for shock; transfer urgently
  • Thigh (femur) – lay on the back; pad between the legs; tie the legs together at the ankles, knees and above and below the fracture; a long padded splint may be placed from the armpit to the foot on the outer side; treat for shock
  • Lower leg – pad between the legs and tie the injured leg to the good leg, or use a padded splint
  • Skull and jaw – maintain the airway, place the casualty in a position that lets fluid drain from the mouth, support the jaw with a pad; watch the level of consciousness

C. Dislocation

  • Definition: displacement of the bone ends at a joint; common at the shoulder, elbow, fingers, jaw and hip
  • Signs: severe pain, deformity, swelling, inability to move the joint, abnormal position of the limb
  • First aid:
    • Do not try to put the joint back (reduce it) – this may damage nerves and vessels or cause fracture
    • Support the limb in the most comfortable position with pillows, a sling or a splint
    • Apply a wrapped cold pack; check circulation beyond the injury
    • Nothing by mouth; transfer to hospital

D. Sprain and strain

  • Sprain – stretching or tearing of ligaments around a joint (ankle, wrist, knee)
  • Strain – stretching or tearing of a muscle or tendon (back, hamstring)
  • Signs: pain, swelling, bruising, difficulty in moving the joint or muscle
  • First aid – RICE (or PRICE):
    • P – Protect the part from further injury
    • R – Rest the injured part
    • I – Ice – a wrapped cold pack for about 15–20 minutes every 2–3 hours for the first 24–48 hours
    • C – Compression – a crepe bandage, firm but not tight
    • E – Elevation – raise the part above the heart level
  • Refer if there is severe pain, deformity, inability to bear weight, or suspicion of fracture

Comparison

Point Fracture Dislocation Sprain
Structure bone joint ligament
Key sign deformity, abnormal mobility, crepitus joint deformity, fixed position swelling, pain on movement
First aid immobilise with splints support in position found, no reduction RICE

Conclusion A fracture is a break in the continuity of a bone. Fractures may be closed, open or complicated, and transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted, greenstick or impacted. Pain, swelling, deformity, loss of function and abnormal mobility are the main signs. First aid is to maintain ABC, control bleeding, immobilise the part with splints and slings including the joints above and below, check circulation, treat shock and transport carefully; dislocations are supported without reduction, and sprains are managed with RICE.

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: State the first aid for a foreign body in the eye.
answer_html:
Signs: pain, watering, redness, a gritty feeling, frequent blinking and blurred vision.

First aid

  1. Do not let the casualty rub the eye; wash your hands
  2. Seat him facing the light; gently separate the eyelids and examine the eye while he looks up, down and to each side
  3. If the particle is loose on the white of the eye, wash it out with clean water poured from the inner corner outwards, or lift it off with the moistened corner of a clean handkerchief or cotton swab
  4. If it is under the upper lid, ask him to pull the upper lid down over the lower lid – the lashes may brush it out
  5. Do not try to remove a particle embedded in the eye or lying on the coloured part, or any penetrating object – cover the eye with a clean pad (without pressure) and take him to hospital
  6. Chemicals in the eye – wash with plenty of clean running water for at least 15–20 minutes, with the affected eye lower, and refer urgently

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: State the first aid for a foreign body in the ear and nose.
answer_html:
Foreign body in the ear

  1. Do not probe with pins, matchsticks or earbuds – this pushes the object deeper and may damage the eardrum
  2. Live insect – tilt the head with the affected ear upwards and pour a little lukewarm water or oil to float it out (not if the eardrum may be damaged)
  3. Other objects – tilt the head with the affected ear downwards and gently shake it
  4. Do not use water for seeds or grains – they swell
  5. If not removed, take the casualty to a doctor

Foreign body in the nose

  1. Ask him to breathe through the mouth
  2. Ask him to blow the nose gently while closing the other nostril
  3. Do not probe or try to pull the object out
  4. Keep a child calm (crying may make him inhale the object) and take him to hospital if it is not removed

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: State the first aid for choking in an infant.
answer_html:
Signs: the infant (below one year) cannot cry, cough or breathe, makes weak sounds and turns blue.

First aid

  1. If the infant is coughing effectively, let him cough and watch closely
  2. If not:
    • Back blows – hold the infant face down along your forearm, head lower than the chest, supporting the head and jaw; give up to 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand
    • Chest thrusts – turn the infant face up, head lower; give up to 5 chest thrusts with two fingers on the lower half of the breastbone, just below the nipple line
    • Repeat back blows and chest thrusts until the object comes out or the infant becomes unresponsive
  3. Do not give abdominal thrusts to infants and do not do blind finger sweeps
  4. If the infant becomes unresponsive – call for help (108 or 112) and start CPR, checking the mouth for a visible object before giving breaths

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: State the first aid for frostbite.
answer_html:
Definition Frostbite is the freezing of body tissues due to exposure to extreme cold, usually of the fingers, toes, nose, ears and cheeks. It occurs at high altitudes and in very cold climates (soldiers, trekkers).

Signs: pins and needles, then numbness; skin becomes white or greyish-yellow, waxy, hard and cold; later blisters and blackening.

First aid

  1. Move the casualty to a warm place; remove wet clothing, rings and tight items
  2. Rewarm the part in warm (not hot) water at about 37–39 °C for 20–30 minutes, or with body heat (e.g. hands in the armpits)
  3. Do not rub or massage the part, and do not use direct dry heat (fire, heater)
  4. Do not rewarm if there is a risk of refreezing
  5. Do not break blisters; cover with dry, sterile dressings, placing gauze between fingers and toes
  6. Give warm, sweet drinks if conscious; treat for hypothermia; take to hospital

subject: Nursing Foundation I (including First Aid module)
question: Explain the first aid for an unconscious person.
answer_html:
Introduction Unconsciousness is a state in which a person is unaware of himself and his surroundings and does not respond normally to stimuli, due to interruption of normal brain activity. The main danger is blockage of the airway by the tongue, vomit or blood.

Common causes – memory aid FISH SHAPED:

  • Fainting, Infantile convulsions, Shock, Head injury
  • Stroke, Heart attack, Asphyxia, Poisoning, Epilepsy, Diabetes (high or low blood sugar)
  • Also heat stroke, electric shock, alcohol and drug overdose

Level of response – AVPU: Alert, responds to Voice, responds to Pain, Unresponsive.

First aid

  1. Danger – make the area safe (switch off electricity, move away from traffic)
  2. Response – tap the shoulders and shout, "Are you all right?"
  3. Call for help – 108 or 112; ask someone to bring an AED if available
  4. Airway – open it with head tilt–chin lift (jaw thrust if neck injury is suspected)
  5. Breathing – look, listen and feel for no more than 10 seconds
    • Not breathing normally → start CPR (30 compressions : 2 breaths)
    • Breathing → place in the recovery position (unless spinal injury is suspected) to keep the airway open and let vomit drain
  6. Control severe bleeding; look for injuries and for a medical card or bracelet (diabetes, epilepsy)
  7. Loosen tight clothing at the neck, chest and waist; protect from cold or heat
  8. Give nothing by mouth; do not slap, shake hard or pour water on the face; do not try to make him sit or stand
  9. Never leave him alone; check and record breathing, pulse and level of response every 10 minutes
  10. Hand over to the medical team – what happened, when, changes noticed and first aid given

Specific situations

  • Fainting – lay flat and raise the legs about 30 cm; recovery is usually quick
  • Fits – protect from injury, do not restrain him or put anything in his mouth; place in the recovery position after the fit
  • Known diabetic – if fully conscious, give sugar; if unconscious, give nothing by mouth and transfer urgently
  • Suspected spinal injury – keep the head and neck in line; move only if essential

Conclusion In an unconscious person, the first aider ensures safety, calls for help, opens the airway, checks breathing, starts CPR or places him in the recovery position, gives nothing by mouth, monitors him closely and arranges urgent transfer.

question: Explain the first aid for heat exhaustion and heat stroke.
answer_html:
Introduction Heat illnesses occur when the body cannot lose heat fast enough in hot, humid weather or during strenuous work. They are common in the summer months in Vidarbha and other hot regions, where temperatures often cross 45 °C. People at highest risk are the elderly, infants and children, outdoor workers and farmers, people with chronic illness, those who drink alcohol and those taking diuretics.

A. Heat cramps (mild)

  • Painful muscle spasms due to salt loss in sweat
  • First aid – rest in a cool place, ORS or salted lemon water, gentle stretching

B. Heat exhaustion

  • Cause – loss of water and salt through heavy sweating
  • Signs:
    • heavy sweating; pale, cool, clammy skin
    • headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, thirst, cramps
    • fast, weak pulse
    • body temperature normal or slightly raised (below 40 °C); mind remains clear
  • First aid:
    1. Move to a cool, shady place; lie down with legs raised
    2. Loosen and remove excess clothing
    3. Give ORS, water with salt and sugar, lemon juice or buttermilk if conscious
    4. Cool with a wet cloth and fan
    5. Rest; if there is no improvement within 30 minutes, or vomiting occurs, take to hospital – it can progress to heat stroke

C. Heat stroke – a life-threatening emergency

  • Cause – failure of the body's temperature-regulating mechanism; body temperature rises to 40 °C (104 °F) or more
  • Signs:
    • hot, dry, flushed skin (sweating may stop)
    • very high temperature
    • confusion, irritability, slurred speech, fits, unconsciousness
    • rapid, strong pulse
  • First aid – "cool first, then transport":
    1. Call 108 immediately
    2. Move to the coolest place; remove clothing
    3. Cool rapidly – sponge or spray with cool water and fan vigorously; ice packs wrapped in cloth on the neck, armpits and groin; immersion in cool water if available
    4. If unconscious but breathing – recovery position; if not breathing – CPR
    5. Nothing by mouth if confused or unconscious
    6. Check temperature; stop active cooling when it falls to about 38.5–39 °C
    7. Paracetamol and aspirin do not help in heat stroke

D. Heat exhaustion and heat stroke compared

Point Heat exhaustion Heat stroke
Skin pale, cool, sweating hot, dry, flushed
Temperature normal or below 40 °C 40 °C or above
Mental state clear confused, fits, unconscious
Pulse fast and weak fast and strong
Urgency needs prompt care medical emergency

E. Prevention

  • Drink plenty of water, ORS, buttermilk and lemon water even when not thirsty
  • Avoid going out in the sun between 12 noon and 3 pm
  • Wear light-coloured, loose cotton clothes; cover the head with a cap, cloth or umbrella
  • Avoid alcohol, tea, coffee and carbonated drinks in the heat
  • Rest breaks and shade for outdoor workers
  • Never leave children in parked vehicles; check on the elderly
  • Follow local heat action plans and weather warnings

Conclusion Heat exhaustion causes heavy sweating, weakness and dizziness with a clear mind and responds to cooling and fluids, while heat stroke – very high temperature with confusion – is an emergency needing rapid cooling and urgent transfer; both are preventable with fluids, shade and avoiding the midday sun.

question: Explain the first aid for drowning.
answer_html:
Introduction Drowning is respiratory impairment caused by submersion or immersion in liquid. Lack of oxygen leads to unconsciousness and cardiac arrest within minutes. In India many drownings occur in rivers, ponds, wells, lakes and during floods, and young children are especially at risk.

First aid

1. Rescue safely – do not become a victim yourself

  • "Reach, throw, row – don't go":
    • reach with a stick, rope, pole or cloth
    • throw a floating object – tube, plastic can, rope
    • row a boat to the person
  • Enter the water only if trained

2. Remove from the water

  • Keep the person horizontal if possible
  • Suspect a neck or spinal injury after diving or falls into shallow water – keep the head and neck in line

3. Call for help – 108 or 112

4. Check response and breathing

5. If not breathing normally

  • Open the airway; give five initial rescue breaths
  • Then start CPR – 30 chest compressions to 2 breaths
  • Use an AED if available, after drying the chest
  • Continue until help arrives or the person starts breathing

6. Do not try to drain water from the lungs

  • Do not press the abdomen, hold the person upside down or roll him over a drum or pot – this wastes precious time and causes vomiting and inhalation of stomach contents

7. If breathing

  • Place in the recovery position; vomiting is common – clear the mouth
  • Remove wet clothes and cover with dry blankets to prevent hypothermia

8. Always send to hospital

  • Even if the person seems to recover, lung complications (fluid in the lungs, pneumonia) may develop within hours

Prevention

  • Fence or cover wells, ponds and water tanks; cover buckets and drums at home – toddlers can drown in a few centimetres of water
  • Constant supervision of children near water; crèches for young children in high-risk villages
  • Swimming lessons and water-safety education for school children
  • Life jackets in boats; do not overload boats
  • No swimming after alcohol; follow flood warnings

Conclusion In drowning, safe rescue, early rescue breaths and CPR, prevention of hypothermia and hospital observation save lives; draining water by pressing the abdomen must be avoided, and most drownings can be prevented by supervision and barriers.

question: Explain the principles of bandaging and the basic turns of a roller bandage.

diagram.caption: Basic turns of a roller bandage

answer_html:
Introduction A bandage is a strip of material used to hold dressings or splints in place, support a part, apply pressure, control bleeding and swelling and limit movement. Correct bandaging is safe and comfortable; wrong bandaging can block circulation.

A. Principles of bandaging

  1. Explain and reassure; place the part in a comfortable, functional position in which it will remain
  2. Face the casualty and work from the injured side
  3. Hold the roll with the rolled part (head) uppermost; unroll a few centimetres at a time
  4. Start with a firm anchoring (circular) turn below the injury
  5. Bandage from below upwards (distal to proximal) and from the inner to the outer side of a limb
  6. Each turn should cover about two-thirds of the previous turn, with even pressure – firm but not tight
  7. Cover the dressing completely, but leave fingertips and toes exposed to check circulation
  8. Pad bony prominences and between skin surfaces; never bandage over a wet dressing
  9. Finish with a circular turn; secure with tape, pin, clip or a tie away from the wound and not where the patient will lie on it
  10. Choose the right width – about 2.5 cm for fingers, 5 cm for the hand and arm, 7.5–10 cm for the leg and 10–15 cm for the trunk
  11. Check circulation after bandaging and regularly – colour, warmth, sensation and capillary refill; loosen if there is numbness, tingling, pallor, blueness or swelling

B. Basic turns of a roller bandage

  1. Circular turn – each turn lies directly over the previous one; used to anchor and finish a bandage and for small parts such as the wrist
  2. Spiral turn – the bandage spirals upwards, each turn overlapping two-thirds of the one before; for parts of even thickness – finger, upper arm, trunk
  3. Reverse spiral turn – a spiral with a half twist (reverse) in each turn so it lies flat; for parts of varying thickness – forearm, calf
  4. Figure-of-eight turn – alternate ascending and descending turns crossing like the figure 8; for joints – elbow, knee, ankle – giving support while allowing some movement
  5. Spica – a figure-of-eight where a limb joins the trunk or the thumb joins the hand; for the shoulder, hip and thumb
  6. Recurrent turn – the bandage passes back and forth over the end of a part and is anchored by circular turns; for the head (capeline), an amputation stump or a fingertip

C. Triangular bandage – common uses

  • Arm sling – supports the forearm in injuries of the arm, wrist and hand
  • Elevation sling – keeps the hand raised (bleeding hand, collarbone injury)
  • Head bandage for scalp wounds; folded as broad or narrow bandages to tie splints

D. Dangers of incorrect bandaging

  • Impaired circulation, nerve damage, pressure sores, or a bandage that slips and fails to hold the dressing

Conclusion Good bandaging follows the principles of correct position, distal-to-proximal application, even pressure, complete coverage and regular circulation checks, using circular, spiral, reverse spiral, figure-of-eight, spica and recurrent turns to suit the part.
